Monitoring of banking system 
* 322. SHRI CP. THIRUNAVUKKA RASU: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to set up an independent agency to 
monitor the banking system effectively; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have reviewed the working of Debt 
Recovery Tribunals;

[16 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) if so, the details thereof, alongwith the success achieved by DRTs in 
the recovery of debts; 
(e) whether Government received sugges tions from the All India Bank 
Officers' Association on improvement of banks' functioning; 
(f) if so, the details thereof; and 
(g) what is Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) Reserve Bank of India, which is 
an autonomous institution, already exists to regulate and supervise banking 
system. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. The performance of Debt Recovery Tribunals (DRTs)

3.527 crores have been recovered.

Indirect  agricultural  advances  by  private banks 
* 323. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the names of the private sector banks which have extended indirect 
agricultural advances far in excess of  the maximum percentage while their 
direct agricultural advances fell far short of prescribed amounts or even 
negligible compared to indirect lending contrary to the advice of the Reserve 
Bank of India; and 
(b) the action Government have taken or propose to take against such 
erring banks? 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [16 April, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) Rese rve Bank of India (RBI) has 
reported that 11 private sector banks have extended indirect agricultural 
advances in excess of the stipulated percentage of 4.5 per cent of their Net 
Bank Credit (NBC) while failing to achie ve the overall agricultural lending 
target, i.e. 18 per cent of their NBC. These banks are: 
1. Bank of Rajasthan 
2. Vysya Bank 
3. Lord Krishna Bank 
4. Ratnakar Bank 
5. Benaras State Bank 
6. SBICI Bank 
7. HDFC Bank 
8. Centurion Bank 
9. Bank of Punjab 
10. Dcvclopmcnf Credit Bank 
11. IDBI Bank 
(b) All the domestic scheduled commercial banks, both in the public and 
private sectors, are required to make contributions to the Rural Infrastructure 
Development Fund (RIDF) based on the shortfall, if any, in their lending to 
the priority sector and/or agricultural lending. Effective RIDF-VII. the rate 
of interest payable on RIDF deposits has been linked to the banks' 
performance in lending to agriculture. Accordingly, banks now receive 
interest on their contribution to RIDF-VII onwards at rates inversely 
proportional to their shortfall in agricultural lending. 
RBI has also set a deadline of two years i.e. by March, 2003 for 
defaulting private sector as well as public sector banks for achieving their 
priority sector, including agricultural lending, targets for extending more and 
more institutional finance to the development programmes for rural areas.

Power of arrest and Prosecution to Enforcement Directorate 
* 324. SHRI AMAR SINGH: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government have received any demand from the Directorate 
of Enforcement for restoration of power of arrest and prosecution in terrorist 
related cases; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what is Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA), 1973 which provided 
for arrest and prosecution has been repealed. Under the sunset clause, two 
years time i.e. upto.31 May, 2002 has been given to complete investigations 
in the ongoing cases under the FERA. Foreign Exchange Management Act 
(FEMA), 1999 had come into force from June, 2000 and provides for civil 
liability for violation of foreign exchange regulations. In keeping with its 
commitment to implement the United Nations Security Council Resolutions 
for combating terrorism, the Government is taking, from time to time, 
various legal and administrative steps to deal with the situation.

Restoration of flights to Tanjore, Tamil Nadu 
* 326. SHRI S. AGNIRAJ: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be 
pleased to to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that airlink to Tanjore is not operational; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the number of tourists visiting this area of 
Tamil Nadu is on the rise; 
(d) if so, the steps being taken to restore the flights to Tanjore; arid 
(e) by when it will be operational? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SYED SHAHNAWAZ 
HUSSAIN): (a) to (e) Tanjore Airport belongs to Ministry of Defence and at 
present no civil flights are operating through this airport. 
Vayudoot Ltd. operated D0228 aircraft to Tanjore during the period 
January, 1987 to September, 1989. Tanjore Airport was, however, handed 
over by Ministry_of Civil Aviation to Ministry of Defence (IAF) on 20th 
September, 1989. Airports Authority of India (AAI) has retained only 26.50 
acres of land and transferred the remaining land area measuring 448.69 acres 
to Indian Air Force (IAF). AAI ha s not constructed any civil enclave 
consisting of Passenger Terminal Building, Apron and Link Taxiway for 
handling of civil flights. Though, the number of tourists visiting Tamil Nadu 
is on the rise, no scheduled airline operator has evinced interest to operate 
to/from Tanjore. Therefore, AAI has no plans to develop any civil enclave or 
other infrastructure at Tanjore. 
Tanjore is only 55 km. from Trichy Airport, Indian Airlines 
provides the following regular services to/from Trichy:—  /

Adulteration in diesel 
† 328. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have recei ved complaints regarding the 
adulteration of kerosene in diesel due to the difference in the prices of 
diesel^nd kerosene; and 
(b) if so, the steps being taken by Government to solve this problem? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Steps such as blue dyeing of PDS Kerosene, 
periodical inspection of the retail outlets, introduction of tamper proof locking 
system for tanker-trucks, special vigilance drives, etc. are taken by the Oil 
Marketing Companies. Action is taken by the Companies against erring 
dealers under the provisions of the Marketing Discipline Guidelines and/or 
Dealership Agreement. Also under the provisions of the "Kerosene 
(Restriction on Use and Fixation of Ceiling Price) Order, 1993". Oil 
Companies and State Governments can initiate action against any dealer 
indulging in adulteration and also for misusing public distribution kerosene 
for purposes other than those permitted. In addition, the Government have also 
constituted Anti Adulteration Cell to overview the issues arising out of 
adulteration.

Import of agricultural products 
* 331. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHMED KHAN (DURRU): Will the 
Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government arc monitoring the import of agricultural 
products; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, indicating the imports of different categories 
of products from various countries during 1999-2000, 2000-2001 and 2001-
2002; 
(c) whether any instance of dumping of agricultural products has come to 
Government's notice; and 
(d) if so, the action taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Government has constituted an Inter-Ministerial Standing Group of 
Secretaries which is monitoring the import of identified 300 Sensitive Items. 
The said list contains certain agricultural products also. A Statement showing 
import of major agricultural products during 1999-2000, 2000-2001 and 
2001-2002 (upto Jan. 2002) is enclosed {See below). Wherever abnormal 
increases in import arc noticed, the Standing Group has been recommending 
increases in tariffs. Thus, for instance, in the budget for the year 2000-2001, 
import of duties on many of the agricultural items, (Chapter 1 to 24 of ITC 
(HS) Classifications of Export and Import Items, 1997-2002), were increased 
to provide protection to domestic farm ers. Duty on rice was increased from 
0% to upto 80% on maize from 0% to 50% on apples from 35% to 50% and 
on wheat raised to 50%. Similarly, in the budget for the year 2001-2002, the 
custom duty on coconut, copra, tea and coffee was raised from 35% to 70%. 
In the budget for 
14 

[16 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
the year 2002-2003, the custom duty on tea and coffee has been further 
raised from 70% to 100%. on natural rubber latex (code no. 4001.10) from 
35% to 70% on cloves, cardamom, pepper and poppy seeds from 35% to 70% 
and on pulses from 5% to 10%. 
(a) and (d) According to Anti-Dumping Rules the initiation of Anti-
Dumping investigations is normally undertaken when the domestic industry 
files a fully documented petition to the Designated Authority with Prima-facie 
evidence of dumping, injury and casual link between the dumping of the 
imported goods and injury to the domestic producers. 
In so far as Agriculture products arc concerned, a request was made by the 
National Cooperative Dairy Federation of India Ltd/ National Development 
Dairy Board in Nov. 1998 for imposition of Anti-Dumping duty on Skimmed 
Milk Powder and Butter Oil imported from European Union. The same was 
subsequently withdrawn by the petitioner. So far as dumping of other 
agricultural products into Indian markets is concerned, no fully documented 
petition has been received from the domestic industry indicating any dumping 
or injury to the domestic producers.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE

agricultural commodities and plantation crops in Kerala. The decline in

the banks whose financial position was dwindling; and

112 

[16 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) As reported by Reserve Bank of India 
(RBI) and National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) 
there are 359 primary Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs), 1 State Co-
operative Bank (SCB) and 18 District Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs) 
functioning in the State of Gujarat. 
(b) and (c) While NABARD has reported that the SCB and DCCBs have 
not committed any default, about nine urban banks as reported by RBI have 
faced liquidity problems and have defaulted in meeting their commitments to 
their depositors. RBI has taken various action against these banks like issuing 
direction for protecting the interest of the depositors and to avoid preferential 
payment to favoured depositors, placing of restrictions on withdrawal of 
deposits and sanction of fresh loans, superceding the Board of Directors and 
appointment of administrator filing of criminal complaints against the 
management of the bank, etc. 
(d) and (e) RBI is regularly monitoring the functioning of these banks. 
However, the urban co-operative banks function under a regime of dual 
control. While their administrative function fall under the jurisdiction of the 
registrar of Co-operative Societies, their banking related functions are 
controlled by the RBI. RBI regulates the banking related functions through 
prescribed statutory returns which are submitted at periodical intervals. 
Violations observed during the course of inspection are brought to the notice of 
the bank concerned for rectification and compliance report is obtained from 
them. 
(f) RBI has reported that it has taken various regulatory supervisory 
measures to avoid such defaults in future. These include restricting the 
operations of co-operative banks in call money market, revising the norms of 
investment in Government and other approved securities, restricting the 
investment of funds as deposit with other cooperative banks, restricting the 
issue of bankers' cheques by urban co-operative banks, introduction of a 
system of Off-site surveillance on scheduled urban banks, etc.

Tourism Industry 
2494. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of TOURISM 
AND CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government are going to adopt any well-
planncd/wcll-considcrcd method for boosting tourism industry; 
(b) if so, whether it is also a fact th at the funds earmark ed for promoting 
tourism industry is not sufficient; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether it is also a fact th at there arc ample employment 
opportunities in the tourism industry; and 
(e) if so, what arc Government's plans in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF TOURISM AND CULTURE (SHRI JAGMOHAN): 
(a) The Department of Tourism, Government of India has formulated the 
following short term and long term plans to encourage the foreign as well as 
domestic tourists in the country:—  
(1) Positioning and maintaining tourism development as a National 
priority activity; 
(2) Enhancing and maintaining the competitiveness of India as a tourism 
destination; 
(3) Improving  India's  existing   tourism   products  and  expanding these 
to meet new market requirements; 
(4) Creation of world class infrastructure; 
(5) Developing    sustained    and    effective    market    plans    and 
programmes; 
(6) Special thrust to rural and small segment tourism; and 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [16 April. 2002] 
(7) Attention to civilizational issues and issues pertaining to civic 
administration and good governance and also of social and cultural 
values. 
(b) and (c) The budget of the Department of Tourism is allocated based on 
the availability of funds and competing demands. 
(d) Tourism industry generates large scale employment opportunities both 
direct and indirect through multiplier effect by involving  almost all the 
service sectors. 
(e) The proposed strategy in the Tenth Five Year Plan is to: 
 
* Position tourism as a major engine of economic growth. 
* Attempt to harness the direct and multiplier effects of tourism for 
employment generation, economic development and providing impetus 
to rural tourism. 
* Provide a major thrust to domestic tourism which will act as a spring 
board for growth and expansion of international tourism. 
* Position India as a global brand to take advantage of the burgeoning 
global travel and trade and the vast untapped potential of India as a 
destination. 
* Acknowledge the critical role of private sector with Government working 
as an active facilitator and catalyst. 
* Create and develop integrated tourism circuits based on India's unique 
civilization, heritage and culture in partnership with the States, private 
sector and other agencies. 
* Ensure that the tourist to India gets physically invigorated, mentally 
rejuvenated, culturally enriched, spiritually elevated, and "feels India 
within him".

Draft National Water Policy 
2513. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a draft National Water Policy has been 
formulated; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether and to what extent certain views on ownership of water 
reportedly finanliscd in the two-day 'Jal Sammclan' held recently at New 
Delhi under the aegis of Tarun Bharat Sangh, a Non-Governmental 
Organisation and others has been accept ed and incorporated in the draft 
policy; and 
(d) the details of views of other Non-Governmental Organisations/ 
experts etc. ascertained and incorporated  in the draft policy and the specifies 
of those which have been left out with the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) and (b) The National Water Policy which was originally adopted 
in 1987 has been revised in view of the issues/ emerging challenges during 
the last 14 years in water resources sector. The draft (revised) National Water 
Policy was considered by the    National    Water    Resources    Council    
(NWRC)    under    the 
173 

RAJYA SABHA [16 April, 2002] 
Chairmanship of the Prime Minister in its 5th Meeting held on 1st April, 
2002 wherein the (revised) policy has been unanimously adopted by the 
Council. 
(c) National Water Policy provides a broad frame-work as well as a 
road map for water resources development and its management in the 
country and is not a statutory instrument. The issue of ownership of 
water, which is a legal issue, has to be addressed through a 
legislation, which according to Entry 17 of List II of the Seventh 
Scheduled of the Constitution falls within the jurisdiction of the State 
Governments. 
(d) National Water Policy is an outcome of wide consultation 
process. The First draft of the National Water Policy is prepared by 
the National Water Board where all the States and Union Territories 
are represented by their Chief Secretaries and which is chaired by the 
Union Secretary of Water Resources. The draft policy is first 
discussed in the NWRC. where Chief Ministers of all the States, Lt. 
Governors/Administrators of all Union Territories and Union 
Ministers of Central Ministries d ealing with water arc the members, 
and then adopted. In addition, wide consultations at various levels 
bring in views of various experts from within and outside the 
Government. 
Government of India had constituted a Commission for 'integrated Water 
Resources Development Plan" in 1996. As part of the consultation process, 
the Commission organized four regional level seminars, wherein not only the 
officials from the State G overnments were present but also the professionals 
and experts from outside the Government, the professional bodies, the non-
governmental organizations (NGOs) working in the water resources sector 
were also present and participated in the discussions. In addition, the 
challenges before the water sector ar c discussed at various forum. The non-
governmental professional organizations like Indian Water Resources 
Society, India Water Works Association, Institution of Engineers discuss 
various aspects of water resources development and management in details 
where not only the engineers but also the social scientists, economists, 
representatives of the people and the 
174 

[16 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
voluntary organizations take part. The recommendations of these workshops 
and seminars also form the basic input for the formulation of the policies. 
The majority of suggestions by the NGOs arc in the form of mechanism to 
be worked out for implementation of the provisions of the policy. Certain 
issues raised by the NGOs that arc cither outside the ambit of the National 
Water Policy or arc contradictory and represent a minority view such as: 
defining the rights on water, relaxation of pollution norms for certain 
activities, pricing of all inputs to agriculture sector, taxing of exports on 
water intensive crops, application of the recommendation of the Pay 
Commission regarding improvement of efficiency and accountability of 
irrigation departments and preferring migration of people from water short 
areas instead of bringing water to such areas by inter-basin transfer and, as 
such, arc not included in the National Water Policy-2002. 
It is also pertinent to point out that the National Water Policy is finally 
adopted by the National Water Resources Council where all the States and 
Union Territories arc represented and unless the recommendations arc 
acceptable to the NWRC it cannot be incorporated in the Policy.

† 2516. SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: 
SHRI RAM JETHMALANI: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have got formulated any guidelines for 
preparing unanimously acceptable formula with regard to water sharing; 
(b) if so, the details of the said guidelines; 
(c) when these guidelines were prepared; 
(d) whether action has been taken to bring consensus of all the States on 
these directions; and 
(e) if so, the details of the action taken and when such an action was 
taken alongwith the result thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) to (c) The draft National Policy guidelines for water allocation 
amongst States were form ulated by the National Water Board in 1994 and 
were discussed by the Board during its 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
180 

[16 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
6th and special meetings held on 17th March, 1994, 16th and 22nd June, 
1994 respectively. The guidelines enumerate various concepts and definitions 
related to rivers, river valleys arid river basins, co-basins States, watersheds 
and catchments, storage, withdrawal, consumptive use and utilisation. The 
broad objective of the guidelines is to optimally harness the inter-State river 
waters for the betterment of the people of the co-basin States/Union 
Territories to the extent such development are not detrimental 4o the interests 
of other co-basin States. General principles incorporated in the guidelines for 
allocation of water are; equitable apportionment, allocation amongst States 
vis-a-vis allocation amongst uses, right of water use, inter-basin diversion, 
protection of existing uses, existing inter-State agreements, parties to the 
process of allocation, water quality, long distance water transfer (LDWT) etc. 
The guidelines also enumerate various factors for equitable distribution of 
water such as contribution of each of th e basin States in the water resources 
of the basin, demand made by the States and its practicability for utilisation, 
availability of alternative sources etc. It  also has provision for review of the 
allocation once made. 
The draft guidelines were considered by National Water Resources 
Council (NWRC) during its 3rd meeting held on 6th February, 1996. The 
State expressed divergent views on th ese guidelines. The draft guidelines 
were reviewed by the National Water Board in its 8th and 9th meetings held 
on 6th November. 1996 and 19th November, 1997 respectively after detailed 
deliberations and certain modifications , a majority of the members of the 
Board arrived at a broad consensus in its 9th meeting. The draft guidelines so 
modified were placed before NWRC in its 4th meeting held on 7th July, 
2000 where no consensus could be arrived at. The National Water Resources 
Council in its 5th meeting held on 1st April. 2002 has again referred the draft 
guidelines to the National Water Board for having a re-look and arriving at a 
consensus on the draft guidelines.

Inter-basin water transfer 
2522. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNITA: Will the Minister of 
WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government arc considering inter-basin water transfer in 
different regions of the country to tackle drought and floods in the face of 
growing water demands due to increase in population; 
(b) if so, the details of efforts made by Government for achieving 
consensus among basin States; and 
(c) the fresh steps taken for early implementation of the proposal in order 
to avoid cost escalation? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) to (c) In 1980. the Ministry of Water Resources, then known as 
the Ministry of Irrigation, formulated a National Perspective Plan for 
integrated water resources development through intcr-linkagcs of several 
southern based Peninsular rivers and the Himalayan rivers. Through this 
programme it is intended to assess the surplus basins as of now for possible 
transfer of water from surplus to deficit basin in order to optimally utilize 
the water resources of the country. With this purpose the Government of 
India has established the National Wa ter Development Agency (NWDA) in 
1982 as an autonomous society to carryout water balance and feasibility 
studies of the Peninsular and Himalayan rivers. Union Minister of Water 
Resources heads the Society and Chief Ministers/ Irrigation Ministers of the 
States arc its Members. The Society meets regularly to review progress 
made in National Perspective and to decide the further course of action. 
NWDA has identified 30 links under Na tional Perspective for preparation of 
Feasibility Report and has completed Feasibility Report of 6 links. 
Implementation of the water transfer links would only be possible if the 
concerned co basin

necessary for project implementation and availability of fund. It has been 
decided recently to constitute a group headed by Chairman, Central Water 
Commission (-CVVC) and consisting of other officers of CWC and Secretaries 
of Irrigation/Water Resources Department from concerned States to discuss 
with the States the issues of arriving  at a consensus regarding sharing of 
surplus water and the preparation of detailed project report by NWDA.

Restructuring the Power Sector 
*355. SHRI RAMAMUNI REDDY SI RIGIREDDY: Will the Minister 
of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the power sector is facing do or die situation; 
(b) if so, what steps the Ministry are taking or propose to take to 
restructure the power sector to make it commercially viable; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the SEBs losses amount to 1.8 per cent 
of the GDP of the country; and 
(d) if so, how the Ministry propose to recover the dues from the SEBs? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SURESH PRABHU): (a) to (d) 
Power sector is passing through a critical phase. The Gross Domestic 
Product (GDP) at current price during the year 2000-01 was Rs. 18,78,429 
crores. As against this cumulative commercial losses of SEBs upto March, 
2001 (without subsidies) were Rs. 26,013 crores (1.38 per cent of GDP). 
Government of India has recently approved a scheme for liquidating the 
present and future outstanding dues of the CPSUs against SEBs. Under the 
scheme 60% of the interest/surcharge on 
23 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2002] 
the delayed payments as on 30.09.2001 would be waived off and the rest of the 
dues would be securitised through tax-free bonds issued by the respective State 
Government.There would also be incentives to the States for timely payment 
of current dues. 
The Ministry of Power after wide ranging consultations with all stake holders 
namely state governments, State Electricity Boards, utilities, experts, trade 
unions, private investors and political leaders has evolved a compressive and 
detailed action plan for turning around the power sector. A broad strategy for 
this purpose was finalized in a Conference of Chief Ministers/Power Ministers 
taken by the Prime Minister on 3rd March, 2001. 
To tackle the problem of technical inefficiency at the level of distribution 
involving erratic power supply, frequent distribution transformer failures and low 
voltage with high technical losses, the Govt, of India has stepped into assist the 
States under the new Accelerated Power Development Programme (APDP). In 
the first phase of this programme 63 distribution circles in the States have been 
taken up for intensive upgradation. These identified circles are being developed as 
"Centres of Excellence" so as to serve as models for remaining distribution circles 
in the country for improvement in a phase manner. This programme has now 
become the Accelerated Power Development and Reform Programme (APDRP) 
and also provides for transitional financing. In this programme the Govt, of India 
had made an allocation of Rs. 3500 crores during 2002-03. The programme is being 
monitored by central level consultants who are required to undertake field level 
inspections. The intention is to replicate this programme in all the distribution 
circles of the country gradually. 
To support the reform efforts of all the States the Centre has been entering into 
MOUs with the states. These are State specific. In the MOUs, which have been 
signed by 21 States so far, the concerned States have committed to achieve 
milestones in reforming the power sector. The milestone include setting up of the 
State Electricity Regulatory Commission, timely payment of subsidies, metering 
of all 11 KV feeders, 100% metering of consumers, energy audit, reduction 
24 

[17 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
of technical and commercial losses etc.  Government of India has committed 
its support through additional allocation of power from Central Generating 
Stations, assistance for development of transmission system and financial 
assistance. 
A mechanism has been institutionalized for intense monitoring of the 
capacity addition programme both in the Central Sector as well as in the 
State Sector. The progress is being reviewed regularly. With the provision of 
adequate Plan funds and close monitoring, performance in capacity addition 
in the Tenth Plan is expected to show considerable improvement. Renovation 
and modernisation of existing plant is given priority. With the other 
measures for reducing technical losses in distribution and demand side 
management through energy efficiency and energy conservation, it should be 
possible to make the country free of power shortages. Basin-wise ranking 
studies have been undertaken by CEA so as to optimally utilize the total 
potential of feasible hydro projects over next few decades. 
Standing Committee on training has been eonsitutcd to formualte National 
Action Plan for Power Training. The Committee has submitted its report. A 
Committee has been constituted to draw up a perspective  research  and  
development  plan. 
The Conference of Chief Ministers held on 3rd March, 2001 resolved that 
Village Electrification may be completed by the end of the 10th Plan i.e. by 
year 2007 and full coverage of all households may be targeted for the end of 
the  11th Plan r.e.,  by year 2012. 
Rural electrification has not been included under Prime Minister's 
Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY) from the year 2001-02. 
In the Chief Ministers Conference, it wa s agreed that there is urgent need 
to dcpoliticisc power sector reforms and speed up their implementation. To 
explain the problems of the power sector  and the action that is required for 
resolving these problems, road show s have been organized across the 
country for generating public awareness and understanding. More than 2000 
road shows have been organized at the district level all across India. This has 
been considered necessary, as, without public understanding and support, it 
would be 
25 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2002] 
difficult to implement to meausres necessary for turning around the financial 
and operational health of the power sector. 
The forward looking reform oriented electricity Bill 2001 has been 
introduced in Parliament. The Bill, inter-alia, contains stringent provisions 
for penalty in case of power thefts. The Bill also includes provision for 
reduction of cross subsidies, and for payment of subsidies up front by the 
State Governments to the State Power Utilities where such subsidies are 
considered unavoidable. 
Subsidised Power supply to agriculture 
†356. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the 
Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether subsidized power supply to agriculture is only benefiting the 
large and affluent farmers who own electric pumps; 
(b) whether Government have made any survey or assessment in this 
regard; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether State Governments are being advised in this regard; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof and steps proposed so that benefit reaches 
small and poor farmers equally? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SURESH PRABHU): (a) to (e) 
Electricity is a concurrent subject and distribution is the responsibility of the 
State Government. Retail tariff is determind by the State Electricity 
Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) or  by the State GovemmenfState 
Electricity Board where Regulatory Commissions have not been set up. 
Supply to agriculture sector in the country is by and large subsidized. Even 
in States where SERCs determine ta riff, the law empowers the State 
Government to give subsidies to a targeted group, if it so desires. The World 
Bank in its report on "Power supply to agriculture: case studies of Haryana 
and Andhra Pradesh" has observed that  the electricity subsidy exclusively 
benefits electric pump owning farmer especially the medium to large farmers 
as they 
26 

[17 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
predominantly own electic pumps and account for the larger share of the 
electricity consumption. A copy of the report has been circulated to all the 
States for taking appropriate action. 
The resolution of the co nference of Chief/Power Minister held on 3rd 
March, 2001 inter alia contained that the subsidies may be given only to the 
extent of State Governments capacity to pay the subsidies explicitly through 
budget provisions and the decisions of CMs of a minimum agricultural tariff 
of 50 paise may be implemented immediately. The ERC Act, 1998 mandates 
the Regulatory Commissions to decide the tariff so that it progressively 
reflect the cost of supply. The tariff orders passed by some SERCs reflect a 
trend in this direction. 
In the new Electricity Bill, 2001 which has been introduced in the Lok 
Sabha, there is a specific provision that tariff should progressively reflect the 
cost of supply and cross subsidies be progressively reduced and eliminated.

WRITTEN ANSWERS TO UNSTARRED QUESTIONS Land 
taken from Tribes by BALCO 
†2523. SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV: Will the Minister of COAL AND 
MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) the land taken from the Scheduled Tribes in Korba (Madhya Pradesh) 
by the Bharat Aluminium Company; 
(b) whether the State Government has taken any action to return this land 
to its owners; and 
(c) if so, the owners to whom the land has been given back? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL AND 
MINES (SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) to (c) Bharat Aluminium 
Company Limited (BALCO) did not take any land directly from the 
Scheduled Tribes in Korba, Madhya Pradesh. The Government of Madhya 
Pradesh acquired land and handed over the same to BALCO, together with 
the tenure land, around 1968. In 2001, the Government of Chattisgarh issued 
notices purportedly to take back some of the land thus given to BALCO. The 
matter was agitated before the Supreme Court in Transferred Case (Civil) 
No. 8 of 2001 with TC(C) No. 9 and 10 of 2001 and W.P.(C) No. 194 of 
2001. The Supreme Court decided that "In the instant case, either the land 
was acquired and then given on leas e by the State Govt, to BALCO or 
permission was given by the District Collector for transfer of private land in 
favour of BALCO. This was clearly permissible under the provisions of 
Section 165(6) as it then stood and it is too 
†Original notice of the Question was received in Hindi. 

[17 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
late in the day, 25 years after the last permission was granted, to hold that 
because of this disinvestment, it must be presumed that there is a transfer of 
land to the non-tribal in the year 2001 even though the land continues to 
remain with BALCO to whom it was or iginally transferred. The giving of 
land to BALCO on lease was in compliance with the provisions of Section 
165(6) of the Revenue Code. Moreover, change of management or in the 
shareholding does not imply that there has now been any transfer of land 
from one company to another. If the original grant of lease of land and 
permission to transfer in favour of BALCO between the years 1968 and 1972 
was valid, then, it cannot now be contended that there has been another 
transfer of land with the Government having been redtfced its stake to 49%. 
Even if BALCO had been a non-public sector undertaking, the transfer of 
land to it was not in violation of thefvl.P. Land Revenue Code." 
In view of the dear finding of th e Supreme Court the question (a) & (b) 
does not arise.

NHRC concern on Gujarat violence 
2575. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether NHRC has recently expressed its serious concern on the 
pathetic condition of communal riot victims in Gujarat and urged the Union 
Government to directly intervene in the matter; 
(b) if so, whether the State Government has totally failed to curb 
communal violence in the State; 
 
(c) if so, whether demands have been made to investigate communal 
clashes in the State by a sitting Judge of the Supreme Court; and 
(d) if so, the reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): (a) and (b) The 
National Human Rights Commission in its Preliminary Report on the 
incidents in Gujarat has taken note of the rescue, relief and rehabilitation 
measures undertaken by the State Go vernment and the strenuous efforts 
having been made by the Collectors and other District officials, often acting 
on their own initiative, to control the situation. Numerous complaints were 
received by the Team of the Commission during their visit regarding lack of 
facilities in the Camps set up for the victims. The Commission has noted the 
range of activities and measures taken by the State Government to pursue the 
relief and rehabilitation of those who have suffered. The Commission has 
further appreciated the positive steps that have been taken and has also 
commended those officials and other NGOs that have worked to ameliorate 
the sufferings of the victims. The Commission has made a number of 
recommendations for implementation by the State Government in order to 
bring normalcy back to Gujarat. 
The Commission has in its report observed that there was a serious failure of 
intelligence and action by the State Government which marked the events 
leading to Godhra tragedy and subsequent deaths 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2002] 
and destruction that occurred. The Commi ssion has also observed that in the 
light of the fact that numerous allegations have been made, both in the media 
and before the Team of the Commission , about the lack of faith in the 
integrity of the investigating process and the ability of those conducting 
investigation, there was need for gr eater transparency and integrity to 
investigate the instances of death and destruction of property and to instill 
confidence in the minds of the general public. 
(c) and (d) The Commission has not recommended investigation of the 
communal clashes in the State by a sitting Judge of the Supreme Court. 
However, there have been demands from certain quarters including some 
political parties for an inquiry by a sitting Judge of the Supreme Court. The 
Government of Gujarat has to take a view on this demand.

Use of Geographic Information Systems, Geo-Positioning Systems and 
Remote Sensing 
2584.  SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) how the Ministry is using Geographic Information Systems, Geo-positioning 
Systems and Remote Sensing to improve the distribution networks, restoration 
of services as well as to harness the hydro power potential in the country to 
achieve "Power for all by 2012"; 
(b) how the Ministry is utilizing the IT to help developing solution and solve 
the problems of power sector; 
(c) whether it is a fact that approximately $200 million fresh investment is 
required for the growth of the sector; and 
(d) if so, how the Ministry is thinking of mobilizing such huge amount? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) The Geographic Information Systems (GIS), 
Geo-positioning System and Remote Sensing technique could be applied to 
develop hydro power projects, augmentation of transmission capability and for 
reforming distribution. In order to quickly identify the projects, which, need to 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2002] 
be taken up for development in the next 10-20 years, ranking/pre-feasibility 
studies have been carried out for 399 schemes (1,07,000 MW). Some of these 
studies to hydro electirc projects have been conducted by considering details of 
land use cover, Infrastructure etc. utilizing Satellite Imageries based data 
obtained from National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA). 
Software for GIS and remote sensing are available in the market for the 
distribution system network. Utilities are in the process of making use of such 
software for distribution system. 
Information Technology (IT) is used in Power System Planning for carrying out 
Load Flow Studies, Short Circuit Studies, Stability Studies and 
Electromagnetic Transient Phenomena studies. On the basis of these studies, the 
performance for the power system is simulated and the most optimum solutions 
for transmission system expansion and/or augmentation are formulated. 
(c) and (d) To meet the demand during 10th and 11th Plan, an incremental 
capacity around 1,00,000 MW would be required for which investments to the 
tune of Rs. 8 lakh crore (US$200 Billion) approximate are required which will take 
into account the cost for associated transmission and distribution system for this 
capacity addition. The investment needs would be met through budgetary 
support, market borrowings (both domestic and external), retained earnings, 
suppliers' credit and financing through bilateral and multilateral agencies.

2590. SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU. Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government proposes to en ter into agreements with State 
Electricity Boards throughout the country for payment guarantees for 
drawing power from " national power distribution agencies; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the views of SEBs on such agreements have been obtained; 
and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) The Government of India 
has recently approved a modified scheme to sccuritisc the outstanding dues 
payable by the State Electricity Boards (SEBs) to the Central Public Sector 
Undertakings (CPSUs) as on 30.9.2001 for supply of power and coal and a 
mechanism that would ensure payment of current dues in future. The scheme 
for sccuritisation of 
116 

[17 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
outstanding dues of SEBs as on 28-2-2001 was circulated earlier to the States 
in August, 2001. 
The salient features of the scheme, now approved, are: 
(a) The scheme would come into force from the date of orders or from the 
date when the State Governments sign the tripartite agreement (with the 
Ministry of Finance in the Government of India and the Reserve Bank of 
India), whichever is later. 
(b) For the states participating in the scheme, 60% of the interest/ 
surcharge on the delayed payments as on 30-09-2001 would be waived off. 
(c) The rest of the dues amounting to the full principal amount as well as 
the remaining 40% of the interest/sur charge will be securitised through 
bonds issued by the respective State Governments. 
(d) The bonds will be issued through RBI at a tax-free interest rate of 
8.5% per annum. The terms of bonds should be structured to achieve a 
moratorium of 5 years on repayment of principal with the entire principal 
being repaid between the 6th and 15th year. These bonds will be identical to 
bonds issued in connection with the market borrowings of State Governments, 
with the attendant discipline in repayments. The bonds will be subject to lock-
in restrictions that will allow release of  only 10 per cent of the bonds in the 
secondary market each year. 
(e) For ensuring timely payment of current dues in future, defaults in 
current payment for power/fuel will attract a graded reduction in the supply 
of power from central power stations  and in coal supplies. Where such 
defaults exceed 90 days from the date of billing, the Ministry of Finance will 
recover these dues through adjustment against releases due to them from the 
centre. 
(f) In order to initiate steps towards reform of the sector, the SEBs shall 
accept reform based performance milest ones such as setting up of SERCs, 
metering of distribution feeders, improvement in revenue realization specified 
in the MOUs to be signed with the Ministry of Power. 
117 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2002] 
(g) The States will be offered incentives for complying with the scheme. If 
SEBs do not default on their current dues and adhere to the performance 
milestones, CPSUs will pay them, bi-annual cash incentives equal to 3 per 
cent of the value of bonds in the first year, 2.5% in the second year and 2% in 
the third and fourth years. Further, if SEBs open and maintain Letters of 
Credit (LCs), CPSUs should pay them a one time cash incentive equal to 2 
per cent of the value of bonds. In addition, States undertaking reforms will 
also be assisted through Accelerat ed Power Developm ent and Reform 
Programme (APDRP) grants and discretionary allocation of power. 
(h) The States that withhold their consent beyond 60 days after this scheme 
enters into force will be denied any share in the discretionary allocation of 15 
per cent from the power stations of CP SUs, as well as any assistance under 
APRDP. If the overdues of such States  exceeded Rs. 50 crore in respect of 
any CPSUs, they will also attract reduc tion in power and coal supplies, as 
applicable to the States participating in this scheme. 
(i) The scheme covers the outstanding dues of payable by the SEBs to the 
National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC), National Hydro-electric 
Power Corporation (NHPC), North Eastern Power Corporation (NEEPCO), 
Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) and Power Grid Corporation of India 
Ltd. (PGCIL) under the Ministry of Po wer, Coal India Limited (CIL) and its 
subsidiaries and Neyveli Lignite Corporation (NLC) under the Department of 
Coal, Nuclear Power Corporation (NPC) under the Department of Atomic 
Energy and the Ministry of Railways. 
(c) and (d) The state governments have been apprised of the scheme for 
one-tie settlement of SEBs dues on 03-08-2001. Andhra

Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Goa, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand,

Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Jammu and Kashmir have

metering of consumers, energy audit, reduction of technical and commercial

of India has committed its suport through additional allocation of power from

Statement 
Resolutions of the Chief Ministers/Power Ministers Conference on 
3rd March, 2001 
I. The Chief Ministers/Power Ministers took note of the challenges 
confronting the Power Sector. It was agreed that there is urgent need 
to dcpoliticise power sector reforms and speed up their 
implementation. For this purpose, an all-party consensus needs to be 
created. The Prime Minister is requested to convene all-party 
meetings including leaders of opposition in State Assemblies. 
II. The following Resolutions were adopted: 
A. COMPLETING   ELECTRIFICATION   OF   ALL   VILLAGES 
AND HOUSEHOLDS 
(i) Rural Electrification may be tr eated as a Basic Minimum Service 
under the Prime Minister's Gramodaya Yojana; 
122 

[17 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) Rural Electrification may be completed by the end of the 10th Plan 
i.e. by year 2007; 
(iii) Full coverage of all households may be targeted for the end of the 
11th Plan i.e.  by year 2012. 
(iv) For the attainment of full electrification. States may be given flexibility 
for using funds under Rural Development Programmes with the 
consent of the Village/Block Panchayats for undertaking the task of 
electrification where it is required. 
(v) It was agreed that electrification of remote villages in the States 
would need a special mode of financing including an element of 
grant. 
B. DISTRIBUTION REFORMS 
The real problem of management and the challenge of reforms lies in the 
distribution sector. 
(i) Energy audit at all 11 KV feeders must be made effective within the 
next 6 months and accountability fixed at the local level. 
(ii) An effective Management Information System for this purpose. 
needs to be made operational. 
(iii) On the basis of the above, an effective program needs to be launched 
for identifying and eliminating power thefts in the next 2 years. 
(iv) Full metering of all consumers had been targeted for completion by 
December 2001. Special efforts sh ould be made to complete the 
programme. 
(v) The quality of power supplied esp ecially in rural areas needs to be 
improved through the APDP and other programmes quickly; 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2002] 
(vi) Commercial viability has to be achieved in distribution in 2-3 years 
through any or all of the following. 
—Creating Profit centres with full accountability. 
—Handing over of local distribution to Panchayats/Local 
Bodies/Franchisees/Users Associations, wherever necessary. 
—Privatisation of distribution. 
—Or any other means. 
(vii) Efforts by States, if necessary, at inviting private investment in the 
power sector need to be focusscd towards the distribution sector. 
(viii) Current operations on distribution would need to reach break even in 
two years and achieve positive returns thereafter. 
C. TARIFF DETERMINATION BY REGULATORY 
COMMISSIONS AND SUBSIDIES 
(i) State Electricity Regulatory Commissions may be made functional in 
the next six months and tariff filings made. Tariff orders issued by 
Central Electricity Regulatory Co mmission and State Electricity 
Regulatory Commissions need to be implemented fully unless 
stayed or set aside by Court order. It is necessary to move away from 
the regime of providing free power. 
(ii) Subsidies may be given only to the extent of State Government's 
capacity to pay the subsidies explicitly through budget provisions. 
(iii) The past decision of CMs of a minimum agricultural tariff of 50 
paise may be implemented immediately(*). 
D. GENERATION 
(i) Special efforts need to be ma de to increase the PLF of existing 
plants through Renovation and Modernisation. 
(*) Punjab and Tamil Nadu did not agiee. 
124 

[17 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) In the short run, there is no alte rnative to increase in public sector 
investment in generation, as large-scale private investment in 
generation would flow only afte r reforms succeed in restoring 
financial viability. The Centre and the States need to take suitable 
decisions regarding increase in outlays for the 10th Plan. Priority 
should be given for investments at those locations which produce 
the cheapest power specially for hydro projects and pit head thermal 
generation. CEA has estimated the requirement for an additional 
100,000 MW of generating capacity by 2012. 
(iii) Where the States and Financial Institutions arc in agreement about 
the need for development of IPPs, they need to work together to 
achieve financial closure at the earliest. The Centre would facilitate 
the finalisation of reforms based multi-partite agreements. 
(iv) The evolution of a National Grid for intcr-rcgional transfer of power 
needs to be taken up on priority. 
(v) Some provisions of the Forest Conservation Act may require to be 
revised for expeditious completion of power and other projects. 
E. ENERGY CONSERVATION AND DEMAND SIDE 
MANAGEMENT 
An effective program in the field of demand side management through — 
energy efficient bulbs, tube lights and agricultural pumpsets, 
— time of the day metering and differential tariff for peak and off peak 
hours needs to be implemented with suitable mass awareness and 
extension efforts. 
F. SUPPORT FROM GOVERNMENT OF INDIA 
(i) The Government of India would support the States in their reform 
efforts. This support would be linked to time bound power reform 
initiatives in the States and achievement of definite milestones 
towards restoration of financial viability. 
125 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2002] 
(ii) Interest rates of PFC and REC should be brought down to reflect 
market conditions. 
(iii) An Expert Group would be set up to recommend one time settlement 
of all power sector past dues to CPSUs and dues from CPSUs to 
State Power Utilities. This would be linked to implementation of 
reforms with time bound milestones. The Group will give its report 
within three weeks of its constitution. 
G. SUPPLY FROM CENTRAL GENERATING STATIONS 
Continued supply of power from Central Generating Stations would have 
to be linked to demonstration of capacity to make payments for current 
purchases and sccuritisation of past dues. 
H. HIGH LEVEL EMPOWERED GROUP 
A High Level Empowered Group comprising of Minister of Power and 
Chief Ministers of some States may be set up to coordinate, monitor and 
review the implementation of Reforms.

Statement 
Details of Project "Sustainable Community-Based Approaches to 
Livelihoods Enhancement" (SCALE) 
1. Objective, Duration and Area of Operation 
The SCALE project aims at undertaking field intervention to promote and 
demonstrate community-based natural resources management approaches around 
key resource issues for tangible and sustainable benefits at the local level, and at 
improving the policy framework as well as the implementation of policies impacting 
rural livelihoods through targeted research, advocacy, net working and training. 
The project components would be field implementations and an outreach 
programme. 
The field implementation component will be implemented in three districts in 
Gujarat and a fourth district in a semi-arid region in Gujarat or a neighbouring 
state to be selected during the Inception Phase. 
The wider outreach programme will be implemented in the semi-arid areas of 
India. 
The duration of the project will be 10 years. 
2. Implementation arrangements 
The Aga Khan Foundation (India) will have management res ponsibility for 
the project supported by relevant AKF offices elsewhere and other voluntary 
organisations. 
Components that fall under "Field Implementation" will predominantly be 
implemented through Aga Khan Rural Support Programme, India (AKRSP), is 
working in 450 villages in three districts of Gujarat, reaching out to over 
40,000 households.

strengthen and promote textile exports including readymade garment. Some of the 
important initiatives are:— 
(i) The Government has de-reserved the woven segment of readymade 
garment from the SSI sector. It has also announced the de-
reservation of knitted segment in the Budget 2002-03. 
(ii) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and 
upgradation of this sector so that it can become more competitive 
in international trade. 
(iii) Weaving, processing and garment machinery, which are covered under 
TUFS, have been extended the facility of accelerated depreciation 
at the rate of 50%. 
147 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2002] 
(iv) With a view to encouraging backward integration, the custom 
duty on shuttleless looms has been brought to 5%. A 
programme has also been announced to induct 50,000 
shuttleless looms and to modernise 2.5 lakh powerlooms in the 
decentralised sector by 2004. 
(v) Foreign equity participation upto 100% through automatic route 
has been allowed in the textile sector with certain exceptions. 
(vi) Reduction in the cost of machinery through fiscal policy measures 
announced in the budget 2002-03. 
(vii) Technology Mission for Cotton has been launched for initiating 
focussed steps for boosting production, productivity and quality 
of cotton for manufacture and export of competitive 
downstream textile products, 
(viii) National Institute for Fashion Technology (NIFT), its six branches 
and Apparel Training & Design Centres (ATDCs) are running 
various courses/programmes to meet skilled manpower 
requirements of textile industry especially apparel in the field of 
design, merchandising and marketing. 
(ix) The import of a large number  of garment machinery has been 
allowed under concessional custom duty. 
(x) To prepare and sensitise our textile and garment industry to 
conform to the ecological requirements of improving countries 
by providing facilities by way of eco-testing laboratories. 
(xi) The National Textile Policy-2000 (NTP-2000) has been announced 
to provide the policy direction for orderly and sustained 
development and growth of the textile industry in a harmonious 
way and to give a thrust to textile exports.

Foodgrains Management Policy 
*363. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-report, 
captioned, "Foodgrains Management Policy in limbo" appearing in the Hindu 
dated the 8th March, 2002; 
(b) if so, by when a firm Foodgrains Management Policy is likely to be put 
in place; and 
(c) whether the opinion of the various State Governments with regard to the 
Foodgrains Management Policy is likely to be solicited before finalising the same 
and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) The High Level Committee constituted by the Government of India under 
the Chairmanship of Prof. Abhijit Sen to formulate a Long Term Grain Policy is 
now expected to submit its report in May, 2002. The recommendations made by the 
said Committee will be duly examined and a new Grain Policy formulated 
expeditiously.

Governments. Further consultations with the State Governments will be held by 
the Government of India, if considered necessary, after the receipt of the report 
of the High Level Committee.

†*365. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: W ill the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the agriculture experts have demanded Government for 
immediate repeal of the Essentia' Commodities Act, with a view to providing 
for unhindered transit of foodgrains in the country; 
(b) whether such demands had also been made previously; 
(c) if so, what are the reasons for not repealing the same; and 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
                                                     8 

[18 April, 2002]                 RAJYA SABHA 
(d) the action taken by Government on the demands raised by the experts? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) and (b) An expert 
Committee on Strengthening and Developing of Agricultural Marketing was set 
up by Government in the Ministry of Agriculture in December, 2000. The 
Committee in its report dated 29th June, 2001 recommended that the Essential 
Commodities Act, 19S5 under which restrictions have been imposed on storage and 
free movement of stocks, should be repealed to make way for play of free market 
forces in the real sense. 
(c) A standing Committee of some Union Ministers and Chief Ministers has 
been set up to look into issues relating to food management and agricultural 
exports. One of the issues identified was "Review of the Essential Commodities 
Act and Control Orders to ensure free movement of agricultural products". The 
Committee has suggested that the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 may continue 
as an umbrella legislation for the Centre and the States to use when needed, but a 
progressive dismantling of controls and restrictions was also required. 
(d) The Central Government have issued an Order under the Essential 
Commodities Act, 1955 allowing dealers to freely buy, stock, sell, transport, 
distribute, dispose, etc. any quantity in  respect of wheat, paddy/rice, coarse 
grains, sugar, edible oilseeds and edible oils without requiring any license or permit 
therefor under any order issued under the Act. The Order took effect after thirty 
days from the date of its issue (15.2.2002) notwithstanding anything to the 
contrary in any Order made by a State Government before the commencement of 
the Order.

         *368.  SHRI RAJU PARMAR: 
                    SHRI BHAGATRAM MANHAR: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER  AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the buffer stock of foodgrains by the end of this year 
is estimated to rise from the existing 580 lakh tonnes to more than 
675 lakh tonnes; 
(b) if so, what steps Government have taken or propose to take to tackle 
this problem; and 
(c) whether Government would consider to revamp the Public 
Distribution System (PDS) and if so, the details thereof? 
11 

RAJYA SABHA [18 April, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) The total stocks of wheat 
and rice in the Central Pool as on 1.1.2002 were 580.32 lakh MTs. Keeping in 
view the likely procurement and off take during the year 2002, it was estimated 
that the total stocks of wheat and rice in the Central Pool as on 1.1.2003 would 
be 675.12 lakh MTs. 
(b) and (c) The Central Government  has recently taken the following 
measures to tackle this problem :— 
(i)  The allocation of foodgrains for Antyodaya and other BPL families 
under the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) has been 
increased from 25 kg. per family per month to 35 kg. per family per 
month. Further, the allocation for APL families has also been fixed at 
35 kg. per family per month with effect from 1.4.2002. 
(ii)    The Central Issue Prices (CIPs) for APL category have been reduced by 
Rs. 100 per quintal in respect of both rice and wheat with effect from 
1.4.2002. 
(iii)   The allocation for all welfare institutions and SC/ST/OBC hostels has 
been fixed uniformly at the rate of 15 kg. per head per month. An 
additional allocation equal to 5% of the BPL allocation of States/UTs 
has been made on this account at BPL rates. 
(iv)    50 lakh MTs of wheat and 10 lakh MTs of rice will be sold under the 
Open Market Sales Scheme during the year 2002-03. 
(v)  Quantitative restrictions on the export of rice, wheat and wheat 
products have been removed subject to the condition that the stocks in 
the Central Pool will not be lower than the buffer stock of 243 lakh MTs 
(100 lakh MTs of rice and 143 lakh MTs of wheat) at any point of time. 
Besides, to increase the export of wheat and rice, WTO compatible 
subsidies will be provided. 
12 

[18 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(vi) A decision has been taken to enter into counter trade and/or commodity 
assistance to other countries on te rms to be decided on case to case 
basis.

from the Central Pool will increase by 160 lakh MTs in a full year.

Statement-II 
Steps   taken   by   the   Government   to   promote   the   Information 
Technology Sector 
1. Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme (EPCG) has been rationalised 
and extended uniformly to all sectors without any threshold limit on 
payment of 5% duty. 
2. Approvals for all foreign direct investment proposals relating to the 
Information Technology Sector, with the exception of Business-to-consumer 
(B2C) e-commerce are under the automatic route. 
3. Electronics Hardware Technolog y Park (EHTP) and Software 
Technology Park (STP) Schemes are implemented under the aegis of the 
Department of Information Technology, Ministry of Communications and 
Information Technology, through a si ngle window mechan ism of the Inter-
Ministerial Standing Committee (MSC). 
4. Supplies of Information Technology Agreement (ITA-1) items in the 
Domestic Tariff Area (DTA) by EHTP/EOU/EPZ units shall be counted 
towards fulfillment of minimum Net Foreign Exchange earning as a 
Percentage of exports (NFEP) and the minimum Export Performance (EP), 
provided that the items ar e manufactured in the unit and attract zero rate of 
basic customs duty. Positive NFEP is required to be achieved in 5 years 
instead of every year. 
5. DTA access upto 50% of the FOB valu e of export is permitted for 
electronics hardware units under EOUEPZ-EHTP schemes and the software 
units under EOLPEPZ/STP schemes. 
 
6. Accelerated depreciation norms exte nded to computers and computer 
peripherals to all units and capital goods of IT hardware units under Export 
Oriented schemes (EOIPEPZ^TP/EHTP).  These shall stand depreciated to 
overall limit of 90% over a period of 3 years. 
7. Special Economic Zones are bei ng set up to enable hassle free 
manufacturing and trading for export purposes. 
8. The Depreciation on Computers is allowed @ 60%.

*377. SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO: Will the Minister of

to state: 
(a) whether telephone is essential for lower middle class and retired 
employees; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to increase the number of free 
calls and reduce the rental charges to help the poor subscriber; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI PRAMOD M AH A J AN): (a) to (c) One of the 
objectives and targets of New telecom Policy' 99 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [18 April, 2002] 
is to ensure availability of affordable and effective communications for the 
citizens. It also contemplates to make available telephone on demand by the 
year, 2002. 
The fixation and regulation of tarrif is a function of Telecom Regulatory 
Authority of India (TRAI). For this purpose, TRAI issues telecom Tariff 
Order (TTO) from time to time. The Telecommunication Tariff Order (TTO) 
1999 as notified by Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) recognizes 
that social objectives of Telecommunication policy are important particularly in 
relation to those sections of the society for whom afordability is the most 
important issue. Thus, the TTO has specified monthly rentals, which are 
different for rural and urban subscriber s. Monthly rentals specified in TTO, 
1999 have been purposely kept below cost for rural and small sized exchanges 
so that basic telephone services are largely affordable. Presently, Government 
have no proposal to increase the numb er of free calls and reduce the rental 
charges.

Nepalese Prime Minister's visit to India 
*379. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the discussions that took place with the Nepalese Prime 
Minister during his recent five days official visit to India; 
(b) whether issues like increasing security on the border, removing trade barriers 
recently imposed by India, were discussed; 
(c) if so, the outcome thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) 
to (d) His excellency Mr. Sher Bahadur Deuba, Prime Minister of Nepal, paid an 
official good will visit to India from March 20-25, 2002 at the invitation of the 
Prime Minister of India. During the visit, PM Deuba called on the President and 
Vice President and held talks with the Prime Minister. The Home Minister, 
External Affairs Minister, Defence Minister, Commerce and Industries 
Minister, Human Resource Development Minister and Water Resource 
Minister called on the Nepalese Prime Minister. PM Deuba attended a business 
meeting organised jointly by the Confederation of Indian Industry and the Federation 
of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industries. He also visited Kolkata where 
he met the Governor and Chief Minister of West Bengal. The discussions were 
friendly and cordial, in keeping with the close relations between India and Nepal. 
2. The discussions held during PM Deuba's visit focused on issues relating to 
terrorism and bilateral trade and econom ic cooperation. Both Prime Minister 
reiterated the determination of the two countries to work closely in fighting the 
scourge of terrorism which was adversely affecting peace and stability in the 
region as also impeding socio-economic development. The Prime Ministers 
renewed the commitment of the two countries not to allow their respective 
territories to be used for activities inimical to the interest of the 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [18 April, 2002] 
other. In pursuance of their shared objective of combating terrorism and cross-
border crimes, the two Governments agreed to intensify their ongoing 
cooperation and to continue working closely with each other. 
3. As regards trade and economic co-operation, the two Prime Ministers noted 
with satisfaction the successful renewal of the India-Nepal Trade Treaty for a period 
of five years till March 5, 2007 with mutually agreed amendments to the Protocol to 
the Treaty without changing its basic framework. 
4. On the Pancheshwar Hydle Project, the two Prime Ministers noted that 
considerable work had been done on the field investigations for the Joint 
DPR. They agreed that all out efforts should be made to complete a Joint DPR 
before June this year. 
5. An Agreement on Cooperation in the Field of Science and Technology 
was also signed during the visit. 
6. The Ncpalcse Prime Minister invited the Prime Minister to pay an official 
visit to Nepal at an early dale. The invitation was accepted. The dates of the visit 
would be decided through diplomatic channels.

TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) No, Sir.

(Projection) is about Rs. 1537 crores. The high deficit of the Department is 
due to continuous increase in the cost of operations which are largely manual 
and periodical increase due to revision of salaries, wages, dcarness allowance

purposes, there is justification for raising tariffs to generate revenue for 
cross-subsidizing the socially useful services. Keeping in view the urgent

Statement—II 
To dispose of old and surplus Stocks of foodgrains available in the 
Central Pool and increase the off take of Food grains from the Central 
Pool,  Government has taken the following measures:— 
(i) The allocation of Foodgrains for Below the Poverty Line (BPL) 
families was revised w.e.f. 1.12.2000 on the basis of population projections 
of the Registrar General as on 1.3.2000. As a result, the number of BPL 
families eligible for subsidized foodgr ains has increased from 5.96 crore 
families to 6.52 crore families. 
(ii) The Antyodaya Anna Yojana was announced on 25.12.2000 for the 
one crore poorest of the poor BPL families. The Scheme is now under 
implementation in all States/UTs. Each of the Antyodaya families is given 
25Kg of Foodgrains @ Rs. 2 per Kg. for wheat and Rs. 3 per Kg. for rice. 
(iii) Government launched the Food for work Programme in January, 
2001 in the drought affected areas of the country. Later, it was extended to 
States affected by other calamities lik e floods and cyclones as well 38.33 
lakh M.Ts of foodgrains have been made available for distribution under this 
scheme. 
(iv) Government of India has decided to give additional allocation of 
Foodgrains at BPL rates to drought aff ected States for distribution to all the 
drought affected families (BPL & AP L) @ 20 Kg. Per family per month for 
a period of three months in the current financial year. The Govts, of Andhra 
Pradesh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh,

additional Foodgrains. The State Government of Bihar has been given

(v) The entitlement for BPL families was raised from 10 Kg. Per family per 
month to 20 Kg. Per family per month from April, 2000 and further to 25 Kg. 
Per family per month from July, 2001. 
(vi) The Central Issue Price (CIP) of wheat and rice was reduced as under

(viii) Foodgrains are made available at BPL rates for allotment to State

M.Ts. of wheat and 10 lakh M.Ts of rice under the Open Market Sale 
Scheme(Domestic) of wheat has been allowed.

Decontrol of Sugar 
2688. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government  are planning to decontrol Sugar 
from PDS; 
(b) if so, whether Government have conducted any study to know whether 
the Sugar Industry and Sugarcane growers would be benefited by this move; 
and 
(c) whether Government are aware that in Karnataka thousands of tonnes 
of Sugar has been stored in godowns for sale; if so, in what way Union 
Government propose to help the State in clearing the stocks? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. 
SREENIVASA PRASAD): (a) and (b) The Central Government has decided 
to effect complete decontrol of sugar during 2002-03 financial year after the* 
opcrationalisation of future/forward trading in sugar. The Government has 
taken the said decision in the light of the recommendations of the High 
Powered Committee headed by Shri B.B. Mahajan, the retired Food 
Secretary. The Committee studied the entire gamut of sugar economy. The 
proposed decontrol of sugar is intended to remove restrictions on sale of 
sugar. 
(c) The Government is aware of the high level of sugar stocks held by 
sugar factories in the country including the factories located in the State of 
Karnataka. As intimated by the State Government of Karnataka, about 9.08 
lakh MTs of sugar is lying in the various 
128 
 

[18 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
godowns of Karnataka, worth about Rs. 1174 crores as on 31.10.2001. In 
order to reduce sugar stocks, the Government is, inter alia, encouraging the export 
of sugar. The following measures have been taken in this regard:— 
(i) Levy exemption has been given on the quantity of sugar exported. 
(ii) The quantity of sugar exported is treated as advance free sale release and 
is adjusted after a period of 18 months from the date of release. 
(iii) Duty Entitlement Pass Book (DEPB) at the rate of 5% value of f.o.b. 
price of sugar was allowed, which has now been reduced to 4%. 
(iv) Quantitative ceiling on export of sugar has been removed. 
(v) Requirement of Registration-cum-Allocation Certificate from the 
Agricultural and Processed Food Export Development Authority 
(APEDA) has been dispensed with effect from 1.4.2001. 
(vi) State Governments of the major sugar producing States have been 
requested to give remission in purchase tax on sugarcane on the 
quantity of sugar exported. 
The sugar factories have been provided temporary relief by way of permitting 
them to sell equivalent quantity of unlifted levy sugar stocks as free sale sugar in 
tlfe open market. During the sugar season 2000-01, out of 1,62,631 MTs of 
unlifted levy sugar stocks so far permitted to be sold as free sale sugar, the share of 
sugar factories in Karnataka works out to be 48,803.6 MTs. 
Advance releases of free sale sugar have been made, subject to adjustment and 
5% levy obligations, to needy sugar mills to enable them to clear cane price 
dues of the farmers and to reduce their stock. Besides, the factories have been 
allowed to sell upto 10% of their quarterly quota over and above their normal quota 
to clear their cane price dues.

2713. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: W ill the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Pakistan has appealed to India to break barriers and resume 
flight operation, Samjhauta Express, peace process and reduce army build-up 
at the borders; 
(b) whether Pakistan of late has offere d to normalise their relations with 
India before taking up Kashmir issue as appearing in the Press Media; and 
(c) if so, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): 
(a) Yes, Sir. Pakistani leaders have frequently resorted to 
150 

[18 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
propagandist rehetoric and empty public relation gimmicks of this nature, in 
their futile bid to deflect internaitonal focus from Pakistan's ongoing 
sponsorship of cross border terrorism in India. 
(b) and (c) No, Sir. Pakistan's negative and hostile approach towards India 
remains completely unchanged. During a public address on Sth February 
2002, the President of Pakistan stated that "the Indian Position that Kashmir 
is an integral part of India is untenable and therefore unacceptable". He also 
emphasized that the issue of Jammu and Kashmir remained central to India-
Pakistan relations. It is also quite evident that despite its positive assurances 
to the international community to end the use of terrorism as an instrument of 
state policy, Pakistan is unwilling to take effective and irreversible steps to end 
its sponsorship of cross border terrorism in India.

occupation of Pakistan. Government are firmly resolved to take all necessary 
steps to preserve the security and territorial integrity of the country.

countries have been resolved in his visit?

Labour Reforms 
2728. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to go for labour reforms; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have got any proposal from the trade unions and 
labour organisations in this regard; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
MUNI LALL): (a) and (b) Rcvicw/updation of labour laws is a continuous 
process in order to bring them in tune with the prevailing situation and 
emerging needs of the economy. Reforms in labour laws in recent years have 
been necessitated with a view to make  Indian industry efficient, cost 
effective and internationally competitive in  the face of globalisation process. 
Accordingly, the Trade Un ions Act, 1926 has been amended to reduce the 
multiplicity of trade unions and to ensure their orderly growth and internal 
democracy. A Group of Ministers (GOM) on Labour Reforms has approved 
amendment proposals in respect of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 and the 
Payment of Wages Act, 1936. The Bills to this effect arc likely to be 
introduced in the current Session of Parliament. Besides, the amendment to 
the Contract Labour Act has been discussed in detail by the GOM. The GOM 
is to further deliberate on this issue. The Government has also set up the 
Second National Commission on Labour with a view to suggest 
rationalization of existing laws relating 
164 

[18 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
to labour in the organised sector and to suggest an umbrella legislation for 
ensuring a minimum level of protection to the workers in the .unorganised sector. 
The Commission is expected to submit its report shortly. 
(c) and (d) The. Central Trade Union Organisations have been generally 
opposing amendments in labour laws unless these are perceived as beneficial 
to the working class.
