Efficient, Corruption-free Government Machinery 
2731. SHRI SATISH PRADHAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased 
to state the details of the steps taken or proposed to be taken for making 
Government's administrative machiner y free from inefficiency, corruption 
and lethargy? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA 
RAJE): It has been the continuing Endeavour of the Government to check 
irregularities and malpractices in Government Departments. Policies in this 
regard have been formulated and are continuously monitored and modified in 
order to make them more effective and responsive to the needs of the 
changing environment. In the Government, the Ministry of Personnel, Public 
Grievances and Pensions acts as a Nodal Agency and coordinates the efforts 
of the Ministries/Departments in the fields of vigilance and anti-corruption 
activities of various agencies involved in the task. The Annual Action Plan 
prepared by the Ministry of Personne l, Public Grievances and Pensions 
envisages a three-pronged strategy fo r combating corruption in public life. 
The broad features of the Action Plan are: 
(i) Preventive vigilance; 
(ii) Surveillance and detection; and 
(iii) Deterrent punitive action. 
For conferring a statutory status on Central Vigilance Commission, CVC 
Bill has been introduced in Parliament. After the Bill was reported by the 
Joint Parliament Committee, it is awaiting consideration and passing by the 
Parliament. 
Lok Pal Bill, 2001 was introduced by the Government in the Lok 
167 

RAJYA SABHA [18 April, 2002] 
Sabha on 14.8.2001. After it was referred to the Department related 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs for examination and 
report, the Standing Committee has presented its Report to the Speaker, Lok 
Sabha and Chairman, Rajya Sabha on 31.12.2001. 
The Central Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964, inter alia, provide that 
every Government servant shall at all times (i) maintain absolute integrity; (ii) 
maintain devotion to duty; and (iii) do nothing which is unbecoming of a 
Government servant. These provisions are intended to make the Government 
servants function efficiently. Similar provisions have also been made in the 
rules governing other Services. Violation of these Rules by the Government 
servants is dealt with in accordance with  the provisions of the Central Civil 
Services (Classification, Control & Appeal) Rules, 1965 etc. 
The Government has also taken several steps in the recent past to improve the 
accountability and efficiency of the bureaucracy and also the quality of public 
service delivery. Some of these steps are as follows: 
(i) Based on the recommendations of the Commission on Review of 
Administrative laws, set up by the Government in May, 1998 and 
which submitted its report in September, 1998, the Government has 
taken up simplification of laws, rules and procedures including 
repeal of irrelevant and dysfunctional laws with a view to improve 
service delivery and transparency in the functioning of the 
Government. 393 Acts, including five War-time Permanent 
Ordinances, have been repealed so far. 
(ii) A large number of Ministries/D epartments etc. with considerable 
public interface have introduced Citizen's Charters indicating 
broadly the quality of service the people would be entitled to within 
a specified time-frame. So far 68 Citizens' Charters have been 
formulated by various Ministries/Departments etc. Information and 
Facilitation or Help Counters have been set up by 75 Ministries/ 
Departments/Organizations to provide information and assistance 
to the public regarding procedures, programmes 
168 

[18 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
and schemes of the concerned organizations as well as access to 
information pertaining to the status of individual cases. 
(in) The Freedom of Information Bill, 2000 has been introduced in the Lok 
Sabha on 25 July, 2000. 
(iv) Information Technology is being used in the functioning of the 
Government for improving administrative efficiency as well as hassle-
free services to citizen.

National Highway Accident Relief Service Scheme 
2748. SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA: Will the Minister of ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of schemes for NGO's participation under his Ministry; 
(b) the details of the amount released under the "National Highways 
Accident Relief Service Scheme" since 1998-1999 till 2000-2001, State-wise, and 
the details of beneficiaries; 
(c) whether Government have came to know about misuse of these funds in 
recent years; and 
(d) if so, "the steps taken by Government to stop such incidents? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF ROAD TRANSPORT 
AND HIGHWAYS (MAJ. GEN. (RETD.) B.C. KHANDURI): (a) There are 
three schemes for Road Safety under this Ministry in which an NGO can 
participate. Details of these schemes are as given below :— 
(i) Grants-in-aid for administering Road Safety Programmes 
Under this scheme grants-in-aid is provided to NGO's to undertake various types 
of road safety programmes for raising road safety consciousness among the road 
users, publicity campaigns on road safety, providing training facilities and 
medical aid to the victims of road accidents. Any registered Voluntary 
Organization engaged in research activity or field programmes relating to road 
safety for a period of at least two years can apply for financial assistance. 
189 

RAJYA SABHA [18 April, 2002] 
(ii) Refresher Training to Heavy Vehicle Drivers In Unorganised Sector 
This scheme was formulated in 1997-98 for providing Refresher Training to 
Heavy vehicle Drivers in Unorganized Sector, as most of the drivers of heavy 
vehicles do not have access to recognized training institutes and are generally 
uneducated and untrained. The scheme aims at educating/motivating the drivers to 
inculcate safe driving habits, rules of the road, understand the road signs and 
signals, road marks as well as rules and other provisions of Law, to keep the 
vehicle in road worthy condition and to develop understanding regarding the 
critical parts of the vehicles namely  brake system, steer ing system, electric 
system, Tyre etc. Apart from this, medical check up is also done. 
(iii) National Highway Accident Relief Service Scheme (NHARSS) 
With a view to provide immediate medical assistance to the victims of road 
accidents and removing damaged vehicles from the National Highways, a National 
Highway Patrolling Scheme was finalised during 1993-94, under which Rupees 
Twenty Five lakhs was provided to States as one time financial assistance for 
procurement of one 16 ton crane and one ambulance. This scheme has been 
reviewed and modified in 2000-01 and now is • implemented through States 
Govemment/UTs and established NGOs in  the field of road safety, by 
providing equipment in place of cash grant. 
(b) Requisite details are given in the statement (See below). 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) Does not arise.

Standard of school education 
† * 384. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA : Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that standard of school education in various parts of 
the country is deteriorating day by day; 
(b) if so, whether Government are considering to take any steps for 
improving the same; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) it not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. 
MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) to (d) "E ducation" is in the Concurrent 
List of the Constitution, and manage ment and academic arrangements in 
schools are primarily the concern of St ate/UT Governments. Information is 
received from time-to-time that quality of  education is deteriorating at some 
places. National Policy of Education, 1986 (as modified in 1992) has laid 
special emphasis on quality of education. In pursuance of the policy, the 
Central Government has been emphasizing the need to constantly improve 
the quality of education. 
A number of schemes are being implemented for improving quality of 
primary/elementary education in cooperation with the State/UT Governments. 
District Primary Education Programme (DPEP) is a holistic programme for 
development of primary education. The programme at present covers 273 
districts in 18 States. The project provides several interventions for quality 
improvement. These inter- 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
4 

[19 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
ventions include textbooks development, teacher training, capacity building, 
supply of teaching learning materials, appointment of additional teachers, 
improvement in the school environment etc. In all the DPEP States, new 
textbooks have been developed and several rounds of improved teacher training 
have been conducted. New ins titutions of Block Resource Centres and Cluster 
Resource Centres have been established to provide academic resource support at 
sub-district levels. A joint Government of India — United Nations programme 
namely, Jan Shala is being implemented in 105 blocks in 9 States. It is a 
community-based programme, which aims at improving the quality of 
primary education. 
A new scheme of Sarva Shikha Abhiyan has been launched with the 
objective of providing quality elementary education to all the children in 6—14 
age group by 2010. District Elementary Education Plans have been sanctioned 
under the scheme for 512 districts for the year 2001-2002. The scheme of 
Restructuring and Reorganisation of  Teacher Education is being implemented 
to create a viable institutional infrastructure, academic and technical resource bas 
orientation, training and continuous up gradation of know] competence and 
pedagogical skills of school teachers in the country. So far, 470 District Institutes 
of Educational Training have been sanctioned and more than 16 lakhs teachers 
trained under this scheme. 
In the field of Secondary Education, a number of Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes like Computer Literacy and Studies in Schools (CLASS), 
Improvement of Science Education in Schools, Environmental Orientation to 
School Education etc. are being implemented for improving the quality of 
education.

SFAC Scheme 
2778. DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: Will the Minister of 
AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are implementing the Central Sector Scheme, 
namely setting up of Small Farmers Agri-Busincss Consortium (SFAC); 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Andhra Pradesh has formed the State level SFAC; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof?  
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI HUKUMDEO NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Central Sector Scheme provides Grants-in-Aid to the Small 
Farmers Agri-Business Consortium (SFAC), which is a Public—Private 
Joint Venture Society , declared as a financial Institution under section 
17(8A) of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Act, 1934 and under Section 
9(l)(c) of the Industrial Development Bank of India (IDBI) Act, 1964. It was 
registered on the 18th January, 1994, under the Societies Registration Act, 
1860, as a Society by the Ministry of Agriculture, Department of Agriculture 
and Co-operation. It has a diverse membership, with the Department of 
Agriculture and Co-operation, Reserve Bank of India (RBI), IDBI, National 
Bank for Agriculture & Rural Development (NABARD), State Bank of India 
(SBI) and Oriental Bank of Commerce (OBC) being the Promoter Members, 
and Canara Bank, 
45 
 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2002] 
National Agricultural Co-operative Marketing Federation of India Limited 
(NAFED) and M/s United Phosphorous Ltd. (a private company) as its 
primary members. Other banks, Financial institutions, Statutory and 
Autonomous Organizations, dealing in agriculture and agro industries, private 
companies and co-operatives, exporters, NGO/farmcrs organizations working

2806. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS

profit, whereas the PSU fertilizer units arc in losses;

commercial production of fertilizer for the last several years;

profitability of fertilizer plants depe nds upon the various factors such as 
vintage of plant, technology, feedstock, product profile, human resources, 
managerial expertise, sources of finance and many other factors within the 
control of management. The cooperative sector plants have an advantage in 
some of these areas vis-a-vis some PSUs, making them profitable. However, 
some of the fertilizer PSUs such as Ra shtriya Chemicals and Fertilizers Ltd.

never be commissioned due to insufficient quantum of power sanctioned by 
West Bengal State Electricity Bo ard and breakdown of number of 
equipments. Thereafter, various alternatives were explored to revive the 
project, but its revamp was not found to be techno-economically viable. The 
cost of Haldia Project was Rs. 520.90 crore as in April, 1986.

Population control of leopards 
2815. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased state: 
(a) whether Government have taken note of a quantum jump in the 
leopard population from 1324 to 1961 in Uttaranchal and the increasing 
incidence of human beings falling prey to man-eaters in the recent years; 
(b) if so, whether Government  propose  to adopt some sort of 
88 

[19 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
population control measures to check  the increasing number of leopards 
keeping in view the enormous depletion of forest cover and disappearance of 
herbivorous; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) Chief Wildlife Warden, Uttaranchal has reported that 
the population of leopard has increased in the State from 1324 to 1961. 
However, it will not be appropriate to attribute in increased incidence of 
human killings by leopards to this increase in population. The study 
conducted by Wildlife Institute of India, Dehradun has identified the 
following reasons for the increase in number of human killings:—  
(i)   Reduction   in   prey   base   due   to   increase d   poac hing   of  
herbivorous. 
(ii) Large scale forest fires. 
(iii) Degradation of wildlife habitat. 
Most of the incidents of human killings have been reported from the areas 
where forests have degraded severely and the area in invaded by weeds like 
Lantana and Parthcnium. The measures suggested by the above study for 
preventing human killings by leopards are—  
(i) Clearing the bushes like Lantana and Parthcnium and other species 
around human habitations. 
(ii) Refrain from going into the forests between dusk and dawn, (iii) 
Prevent forest fires, (d) Does not arise.

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir. A Wildlife Crime Cell has been set up at National

(b) and (c) The Central Government Constituted a Committee under the 
chairmanship of Dr. S. Subramanian on 24th May, 1994. The Committee 
submitted its final report on 8th August 1994 i.e., in 2 months and 16 days.

due regard to the available financial resources and the policy on right sizing 
the infrastructure has set up a Wildlife Crime Cell under the charge of Joint 
Director (Wildlife).

(1) Intelligence gathering on wildlife, poaching and illegal trade from 
various NGOs in the field of wildlife conservation and various 
enforcement agencies and intelligence organisations of Government of 
India.

various enforcement organisations.

Ban on import of ash 
2821. SHRI B. J. PANDA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the import of ash, waste and scraps of zinc and lead are banned; 
(b) if so, since when and the reason for such ban; and 
(c) whether any petition was filed in the Apex Court for 
continuance of import of such material and if so, what is the court's 
ruling? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) As far as import is concerned, zinc and lead scrap are 
on Open General Licence (OGL). Zinc ash and skimmings with 65 per cent 
or above zinc content and lead and cadmium contents being equal to or less 
than 1.25 per cent and 0.1 per cent respectively, which are also on OGL, can be 
imported by units registered with the Ministry of Environment and Forests as 
recyclers having environmentally sound management facilities for reprocessing 
such wastes. Import of lead acid batteries, whole and crushed and lead ash is 
not allowed, in view of their potential to cause harm to human health and 
environment, if not handled in a scientific manner. However, import of any 
of these wastes is not permitted for dumping or disposal as per the provisions 
of the Hazardous Wastes (Mangement & Handling) Rules, 1989 as amended 
in 2000. 
(c) No sir, the Ministry is not aware of any such petition in the Apex 
Court in this regard.

(a) whether a final decision has been taken to allow farmers to cultivate 
genetically modified Bt Cotton seeds which reportedly had the potential to 
dramatically improve crops, while cutting down the use of pesticides;

the reasons therefor;

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir.

re-consideration of the matter. 
(c) The  broad  parameters/conditionalitics  laid  down   inter-alia included: 
(i) Every field where Bt cotton is planted shall be fully surrounded by a 
belt of land called 'refuge' in which the same non-Bt cotton variety 
shall be sown. The size of the refuge belt should be such as to take at 
least five rows of non-Bt cotton or shall be 20% of total sown area 
whichever is more. 
(ii) To facilitate this , each packet of seeds of the approved varieties 
should also contain a separate packet of the seeds of the same non-Bt 
cotton variety which is sufficient for planting in the refuge defined 
above. 
(iii) Each packet should be appropriately labelled indicating the contents and the 
description of the Bt hybrid including the name of the transgencs, the 
GEAC approval reference, physical and genetic purity of the seeds. 
The packet should also contain detailed directions for use including 
sowing pattern, pest management, suitability of agro-climatic 
conditions etc., in vernacular language. 
(iv) MAHYCO will enter into agreements with their dealers/ agents, that 
will specify the requirements from dealers/ agents to provide details 
about the sale of seeds, acreage cultivated, and State /Regions where 
Bt cotton is sown. 
(v) MAHYCO will prepare annual reports by 31st March each year on the 
use of Bt cotton hybrid varieties by dealers, acreage, locality (State and 
Region) and submit the same in electronic form to GEAC, if asked for 
by the GEAC.

Environmental concerns and priorities 
2828. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: W ill the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have identified air pollution as 
the top priority area of concern in a National State of Environment Report, 
prepared for the United Nations Environment Programme, to be considered 
at the second Earth Summit, 2002; 
(b) if so, the details of practical strategics outlined to check the rising air 
pollution level, especially in the metropolitan cities; and 
(c) the details of other specific areas of environmental concern 
108 

[19 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
identified, priorities allocated and practical steps outlines, to correct the 
growing environmental imbalances? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (c) The State of the Environment Report prepared for India 
for the forthcoming Earth Summit 2002 broadly covers five priority issues 
pertaining to the environment. These issues include land degradation, bio-
diversity, air pollution with special reference to vehicular pollution in cities, 
management of fresh water resources and hazardous waste management with 
special reference to municipal solid waste management. However, in the  
priority area of air pollution, top priority is given to vehicular pollution as 
70% of air pollution is from vehicular emissions in the metropolitan cities of 
the country. The details of the practical strategies as outlines in the report to 
check the rising air pollution level, especially in the metropolitan cities, 
include the following: 
• The measure to control vehicular pollution include promotion of public 
transport and mass rapid transport systems together with traffic 
planning and management, taxes on fuels and vehicles, stringent 
emission norms and fuel quality specifications, promotion of cleaner 
fuels such as CNG, replacement of two-stroke engines, and a 
strengthening of the inspection and maintenance (I&M) system. 
• Measures to control industrial air pollution include promotion of 
cleaner technologies, st rengthening of emission standards. introducing 
economic incentives, strengthening of the monitoring and reporting 
system, waste minimisation and utilisation and appropriate sitting of 
industries so as to minimise the impacts of activities on ecosystems and 
human health. 
• Formulation of a comprehensive urban air quality management strategy 
using information related to urban planning, ambient air quality, an 
emission inventory, and air quality dispersion models Strengthening 
the monitoring network and institutional capabilities to facilitate an 
improvement in the enforcement mechanism. 
 
109 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2002] 
• Use of cleaner fuels such as LPG in  households to reduce indoor air 
pollution. 
• Launching of the epidemiological studies to develop dose-response 
relationships, which will help in developing appropriate air qua lity 
standards. 
• Institutions of economic instruments to encourage industries to adopt cleaner 
technologies and other conservation practices and to discourage the over-
utilisation of natural resources.

Removal of KV Teachers Under Education Code CODE 
Article 81  (D).   Voluntary Abandonment of Service 
(1) If an employee has been ab sent/remains absent without 
sanctioned leave or beyond the period of leave originally 
granted or subsequently extended, he shall provisionally lose 
his lien on his post unless:—  
(a) he returns within fifteen calendar days of the commencement 
of the absence or the expiry of leave originally granted or 
subsequently extended, as the case may be; and 
(b) satisfies the appointing authority that his absence or his inability 
to return on the expiry of the leave as the case may be was for 
reasons beyond his control. The employee not reporting for duty 
within fifteen calendar days and satisfactorily explaining the 
reasons for such absence as afor esaid shall be deemed to have 
voluntarily abandoned his service and would thereby 
provisionally lose lien on his post. 
(2) An employee who has provisionally lost lien on his post in 
terms of the aforesaid provisions, shall not be entitled to the 
pay and allowances or any other benefit after he has 
provisionally lost lien on his post provided that payment of 
such pay and allowances will be regulated by such directions as 
150 

[19 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
the appointing authority may issue while ordering reinstatement of 
the employee in terms of Sub-clause (6) of this Article. 
(3) In cases falling under Sub-clause (1) of this Article, an order 
recording the factum of voluntary abandonment of service by the 
employee and provisional loss of his lien on the post, shall be made 
and communicated to the employee concerned at the address recorded 
in his service book and/or his last known address, to show cause why 
the provisional order above mentioned may not be confirmed. 
(4) The employee may make a written representation to the appointing 
authority, within ten days of r eceipt of the order made under Sub-
clause (3). 
(5) The appointing authority may on receipt of the representation, if any, 
and perusal of materials, available on record as also those submitted 
by the employee, grant, at his discretion, an oral hearing to the 
employee concerned to represent his case. 
(6) If the appointing authority is satisfied after such hearing that the 
employee concerned has voluntarily abandoned his service in terms of 
the provisions of Sub-clause (1) of th is Article, he shall pass an order 
confirming the loss of employee's lien on his post and in that event, 
the employee concerned shall be deemed to have been removed from 
the service of the Kendriya Vidyal aya Sangathan with effect from the 
date of his remaining absent. In case the appointing authority is 
satisfied that the provision of Sub-clause (1) of Clause (d) of this 
Article arc not attracted in the facts and circumstances of the case, he 
may order rc-instatcment of employee to the post last held by him, 
subject to such directions as he may give regarding the pay and 
allowances for the period of absence. 
(7) APPELLATE AUTHORITY: An employee aggrieved by an order 
passed under Sub-clause (6) of this Article may prefer an appeal to the 
Appellate Authority as notified by the Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan 
from time to time. 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2002] 
(8) PERIOD OF LIMITATION FOR APPEALS : No appeal preferred 
under this Article shall be entertained unless it is preferred within a period 
of 45 days from the date on which a copy of the order appealed against is 
served on the appellant provided that the Appellate Authority may entertain 
the appeal after the expiry of the said period, if it is satisfied that the 
appellant was prevented by sufficient cause from not preferring the appeal 
in time. 
(9) FORM AND CONTENTS OF APPEAL: Form and contents of appeal 
shall mutatis mutandis be the same as prescribed under the CCS (CCA) 
Rules 1965. 
(10) CONSIDERATION OF APPEAL:  The appellate authority 
shall consider: 
whether the requirements laid down under Sub-clause (1), (3), (5) and (6) 
of this Article have been complied with and, if not, whether such non-
compliance has resulted in failure of justice; 
whether the order confirming loss of employee's lien on his post and his 
consequent removal from service is warranted on record; and 
pass order confirming modifying or setting aside the order passed under 
Sub-clause (6) of this Article. 
(11) IMPLEMENTATION    OF    ORDER    OF    APPEAL:    The 
appointing authority shall give effect to the order passed by the 
Appellate Authority. 
(12) FINALITY OF ORDER PASSED IN APPEAL:  The order of the 
Appellate Authority made under this Article shall be final and shall not be 
called in question by way of any further application/petition for revision, 
review etc. 
(13) APPLICABILITY OF THE CCS (CCA) RULES: In matters falling 
under this Article and in those matters alone the procedure prescribed 
for holding inquiry in accordance with the CCS (Classification, Control & 
Appeal) Rules 1965 as applicable to the employees of the Kendriya 
Vidyalaya Sangathan as also other provisions of the said rules which arc 
not consistent with the provisions of this Article shall stand dispensed 
with.

(14) REMOVAL OF DIFFICULTIES: Notwithstanding anything contained 
in any rule or order for the time being in force in KVS, the 
Commissioner KVS may, with the approval of the Vice-Chairman, 
KVS issue such instructions as  he may deem fit to remove 
difficulties in the implementation of these provisions. 
(15) POWER TO ISSUE INSTRUCTIONS : Without prejudice to the 
generality of the foregoing provisions, the Commissioner, Kendriya 
Vidyalaya Sangathan may, with the approval of the Vice-Chairman, 
Kendriya Vidyalaya Sangathan, issue, from time to time (whether by

railway stations more accessible to handicapped people in Andhra Pradesh;

160 

[19 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) to (c) Large number of requests / s uggestions are 
received from the general public and people's representatives for provisions of 
additional facilities for handicapped people at stations by implementing the 
provisions of Equal Opportunities (Protection of Rights and Full Participation) 
Act, 1995 and it is Railways' endeavour to accommodate as many suggestions as 
possible while formulating their action plan. 
Amenities to make stations more accessible to handicapped has been planned 
to be provided through an action plan. In short term action plan, Zonal Railways 
have been directed to provide facilities like standard ramp for barrier free entry 
earmarking parking lots for vehicles used by disabled persons, non-slippary 
walkway, signages, toilets and water taps suitable for needs of handicapped persons. 
In long-term action plan, Railways have planned to provide facility of inter-platform 
transfer by providing ramps on FOB/Subway or lifts and engraving edges of 
platforms. 
Some of the works for provision of above facilities have been completed and 
the rest are in progress at major stations, in the first phase, all over Indian Railways 
including Zonal Railways serving the State of Andhra Pradesh. 
No separate fund allocation is done for the above works and these are 
financed from the Plan Head "Passenger Amenities." 
Zonal Railways have been directed to complete the above works on priority. 
However, required works, as per laid down norms, are being undertaken 
progressively at identified major stations based on relative priorities and 
availability of resources.

Health facilities to physically handicapped 
2876. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether health facilities are available for the physically 
handicapped, aged and children at main railway stations in the 
country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; station-wise; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the effective measures being taken by Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) to (b) Health of the general public is not within 
the purview of Railways and is a subject dealt with by the State Governments. At 
railway stations, health services are not maintained for passengers. However, 
first aid facilities are available for emergencies for which a First Aid Box is 
available with the Assistant Station Master/Deputy Station Superintendent. 
Frontline railway staff are trained in providing first aid. Besides, Assistant Station 
Master/Deputy Station Superintendent maintains a list of medical practitioners and a 
list of nearby hospitals with particulars such as telephone numbers, distance from 
station etc. for availing treatment in emergency. No exclusive health care services 
are provided to the physically handicapped, aged and children at railway 
stations. Wheel chairs and stretchers are, however, provided at important stations 
for the convenience of physically handicapped and aged persons. Further, 
amenities for physically handicapped passengers like signages, ramps with railing for 
barrier free entry, low level water taps, user friendly toilets, non-slippery walkways, 
parking spaces have been/are being progressively provided at important stations 
subject to the availability of funds. The details of the same are given in the 
Statement.

Decongestion of saturated rail routes 
2892. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news report, 
"Railway Panel wants saturated routes decongested", published in the Hindu 
dated the 13th March, 2002; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and Government's reaction thereto; 
(c) steps proposed to be taken in this regard; and 
(d) the amount of investment required to revamp the basic 
infrastructure, like routes? 
 186 

[19 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. The news report is regarding 
the recommendations contained in the Fourth Report of the Railway Convention 
Committee (1999) on Development of Alternative Routes for Decongesting 
Existing Routes. Highlighting the need to strengthen the Rail network on the 
Golden Quardrilateral and the two diagonals, the article has also brought out the 
precarious financial position of the Railways and the extremely thin spread of the 
available resources. The article has also talked about the need for a more 
rational use of the available resources and a concerted effort to explore all 
possible avenues for additional resources. 
The need to enhance line capacity on saturated routes in general, and on the 
Golden Quadrilateral in particular, is one of the priority areas for Indian Railways. 
In this regard, for following specific areas of investment have been identified: 
■ Doubling of remaining single line sections 
■ Additional lines on selected routes. 
■ Electrification of the unelectrified sections 
■ Grade separation at important road-rail crossings 
■ Signalling Improvements & Manning of Level Crossings. 
■ Increasing speed of freight trains to reduce speed differential between 
freight trains and Mail/Express trains. 
■ Introduction of High Horse Power Locomotives 
■ Track upgradation. 
The total requirement of funds for strengthening the Golden Quadrilateral on 
the above lines is approximately Rs. 16,000 Crores. 
A number of steps have also been taken to improve the resource availability and 
utilisation position. 
187 

RAJYA SABHA [19 April, 2002] 
• The probclm of large shelf of on going projects leading to thin spread of 
resources is more acute in respect of New Lines and Gauge Conversion 
projects. In order to enable judicious allocation of resources these 
projects have been prioritised on the basis of their operational requirements, 
physical progress, national and strategic importance and social desirability. 
• Special Railway Safety Fund of Rs. 17,000 Crores has been created to 
undertake renewal of overaged assets, which the Railways were unable to 
undertake in the normal course due to shortfall in internal generation. 
• By rationalizing the passenger fare in the current year's budget the resource 
base of the Railways is expected to be augmented by Rs. 910 crores. 
• In order to contain the staff costs, railways have been progressively 
reducing their staff strength. During the tenth Plan it is proposed to achieve 
2% reduction in staff strength every year. 
• Railways have already started drawing power directly from NTPC at a 
few locations. Railways arc also exploring the possibility of setting up 
captive power houses for generating electricity for traction purposes. These 
steps are likely to bring down high cost of electric traction. 
• Steps are being taken to involve the private sector and the State Governments in 
execution of Railway projects through financial participation by means of 
SPVs or through cost sharing. In addition projects are also sought to be 
executed through the BOT scheme.

collections during 2002-2003?

approximate results in this regard will be available by end of April, 2002. 
However, the results lo end of February, 2002 show marginal shortfall of Rs. 2.73

Estimates) of Rs. 33851.85 crorc. The main reason for this shortfall is lesser

freight traffic.

Railway terminals with private participation, etc. 
3. Drive against ticket-less travel.

and air space, leasing of advertising rights at railway stations and on the 
rolling stock etc.

zoning map of India published by Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS), the Koyna 
Dam falls under zone IV. This zone is broadly associated with earthquakes of 
intensity up to VIII on the Modified Mercalli Scale. At present, there is no 
scientific technique available anywhere in the world which can prediet the

mechanism in the region.

Balbir Punj Committee on National Youth Policy 
2921. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of YOUTH 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have constituted a Committee under the 
Chairmanship of Balbir Punj to help draft National Youth Policy; 
(b) if so, what arc its terms of reference and by when it is going to submit 
its Report; 
(c) whether the Committee has been aske d to review the youth-related 
schemes and programmes being implemented by various Ministries; and 
(d) if so, the details of such programmes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF YOUTH 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI P. RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) Government 
have constituted a National Commission for Youth under the Chairmanship 
of Shri Balbir Punj vide Resolution dated the 15th March, 2002. 
(b) to (d) The terms of reference of the Commission arc annexed as 
statement (See below). The tenure of commission is six months from the date 
of its constitution. 
Statement 
Balbir Punj Committee of National Youth Policy 
The terms of reference of the Commission arc as follows: 
1. To construct and recommend an action oriented strategy and approach 
for the development of youth  and suggest  new policy 
232 

[19 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
measures and programmes, which arc multi-dimensional and cross-cutting, 
after an in-depth analysis of the pr oblems faced by them, with particular 
reference to the problem of youth unemployment, suggesting measures to 
identify, encourage and build up the capacity of talented youth in the North-
Eastern Region. 
2. To review existing youth related schemes and programmes 
implemented by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports as well as 
by other Ministries/Departments of the Government of India with 
particular reference to their potential for employment generation and 
to recommend measures to make th em more effective and increase 
their outreach and coverage in line with Government thinking to 
cover the entire youth population with one or the other Youth 
Programme such as NCC, TA, NSS. 
3. To conceptualise a frame-work for coordination of youth rcldtcd 
activities of State Governments, Ministries/Departments of the Government 
of India, NGOs and the private sect or and to recommend measures for 
convergence. 
4. To look into the recommendations of the Working Groups on Adolescents 
set up by the Planning Commission and suggest specific intervention strategics 
for catering to the needs of this group. 
5. To suggest measures for the implementation of the Plan of Action of 
the new National Youth Policy. 
6. While framing its recommendations, the Commission shall be guided 
by a realistic assessment of the resources  that can be made available by the 
Government.

Facilities in Hospitals 
*402. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-
item captioned "Facilities in hospitals  exist only on paper: panel", 
which appeared in the Hindu, dated the 18th March, 2002; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken to implement the 
recommendations of the Parliament ary Committee to provide quality 
medical facilities in the various me dical institutes and hospitals of 
Government? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
C.P. THAKUR): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The Press Report has referred to 
the recommendations of Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Human Resource Development. A statement indicating 
the status on the points raised in the Press Report is enclosed. 
2 

[22 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement  
Status of the points raised in Press Report 
1. Non-Functional Equipments:—  
Monthly review/monitoring of stat us of non-functional equipments 
costing more than Rs. 1.00 lakh in respect of Central Government 
Hospitals is being undertaken at the Directorate General of Health 
Services. Most of the costly and vital equipments are placed under 
Annual Maintenance Contracts. The reasons for any equipment being 
non-functional are normal wear and t ear and use of the equipments. 
As on date, in the Central Govern ment hospitals (Dr. Ram Manohar 
Lohia Hospital; Safdarjung Hospital; Associated Hospitals of Lady 
Hardinge Medical College), out of 838 equipment of a value above 
Rs. 1 lakh each, only 6 are non-functional. 
2. Coordination between Hospitals:—  
A nodal officer is designated in the emergency control room of each 
hospital. The emergency control r oom is manned by Chief Medical 
Officer/Senior Medical Officer round the clock to attend and 
coordinate the treatment facilities required for the serious patients 
coming to the casualty. Besides, a senior officer takes an evening 
round to oversee the arrangement of the casualty and emergency 
facilities in each of the hospital. 
A proper referral system of treatm ent and follow-up already exists 
between Safdarjung Hospital and A ll India Institute of Medical 
Sciences (AIIMS). In emergency cases, Hospital Administrations has 
been communicating and coordinating regularly for referring of 
patients from AIlRlS casualty to Safdarjung Hospital and similarly 
from Safdarjung Hospital to AIIMS. If need be. Further, coordination 
is also being maintained as regard s the major investigative procedures 
like CT, MRI etc. in case such equipments are out of order in any of 
these hospitals. 
 3. Increase in Patients with no increase in number of beds:—  
There is a considerable increase in the number of OPD and indoor 
patients in Central Government Hospitals. 47 indoor beds in Dr. RML 
Hospital and 51 beds in LHMC and Associated Hospitals have been 
increased in the Ninth Five Year Plan. For reducing the waiting 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [22 April, 2002] 
time, more registration counters are run during the rush hours. In 
LHMC, number of registration counters have been increased from 4 to 
6 and in Safdarjung Hospital from 6 to 14. Besides, 14 to 18 special 
clinics are run in Dr. RML Hospital. Safdarjung Hospital and LHMC 
and Associated Hospital in the afternoon. 
To cope with the patients rush , AIIMS is expanding its hospital 
services in specialities like Dr. R.P. Centre, C.T. Centre, Neuro-
Sciences Centre etc. It is also pr oposed to have a screening OPD near 
to the present OPD building. 
Keeping in view the large patient-load, the Government of NCT of 
Delhi has constructed/commissi oned/upgraded 15 hospitals/Trauma 
Centers (9 Peripheral hospitals, 4 existing major hospitals and 2 
Trauma Centers) during the Ninth Five Year Plan i.e. 1997—2002. 
Seven new hospitals and one dental  college building at Lok Nayak 
Hospital Complex are under constr uction, eight hospitals are under 
expansion and three colony hospita ls are under upgradation. Land for 
five hospitals has been purchased and the facilities are under 
planning/SFC stage. Construction of these hospitals is to start during 
2002-2003. 
4. Overcrowding adversely  affecting  research  activities in  AIIMS, 
PGI Chandigarh and JIPMER Pondicherry:—  
Despite the burden of patients, AIIMS has been rated as the top 
Institution in clinical, medical and bio-medical research in the 
country. The specific measures fo r encouraging research activities 
include:—  
(i) Identification of priority areas of research. 
(ii) Increasing Plan Outlay on research. 
(iii) Revamping the Scheme/Research Cell: 
The function and working of the research/scheme cell has 
already been reviewed and the same is being revamped in 
order to respond to the challenges of the new millennium. 
4 

[22 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(iv) Creation of an advanced centre for Molecular Medicine 
during the Tenth Plan period:—  
An advanced centre for Molecular Medicine is being 
planned for development molecular diagnostics and 
therapeutics, cell and tissue engineering, progeonics and 
genomics, transplantati on immunology, molecular 
epidemology, new drug discovery and bioinformatics. This 
centre is expected to give a real boost to research in 
AIIMS. 
In PGIMER, Chandigarh, during the Ninth Five Year Plan with a view 
to boost medical education and resear ch activities, various measures 
had been taken which include the following:—  
(i) Upgradation of various departments. 
(ii) To develop new Centres, namely, Advanced Cardiac Centre, 
Advanced Eye Centre, Advanc ed Trauma Centre, Bone 
Marrow Transplant Centre and 2nd phase of Advanced 
Paediatrics Centre 
The PGI is trying its best to carry out the research work, which is one 
of the basic objectives of the Institute and over 400 research papers are 
published from the Institute every year. The Institute has a separate fund 
of its own for sanction of Institute Research Projects to the Faculty 
Members. The Institute also en courages and motivates the Faculty 
Members of seek funding from National/International Agencies for their 
research projects i.e. D.S.T. (Govt, of India), D.B.T. (Govt, of India), 
C.S.I.R., New Delhi, ICMR, New Delhi and the W.H.O. etc. etc. 
JIPMER, Pondicherry is also undertaking similar initiatives to boost 
the research activities in the institute. 
5. Screening OPD at AIIMS:—  
The new Master Layout Plan for screening OPD of AIIMS has been 
prepared and the same has been subm itted to concerned authorities for 
their approval. It is expected that the construction work shall start by 
September 2002. 
5 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

RAJYA SABHA [22 April, 2002] 
6. Computerization  of OPD  Registration  in  Central government 
Hospitals:—  
The computerization of various de partments in Safdarjung Hospital 
has been started. Computerizati on has been started in Dr. RML 
Hospital and LHMC and Associated Hospital for Administration and 
Medical Stores. A proposal for comput erization of all services in Dr. 
RML Hospital, Safdarjung Hospital and LHMC and Associated 
Hospital is under process. 
Computerization of patient care system at AIIMS has been entrusted 
to consultant and the consultant has already submitted their report. 
Based on the reports, tenders for co mputerization have already been 
floated. It is expected that the pa tient care system of AIIMS will be 
fully computerized within 2 years of  finalisation of tenders. Adequate 
funds are available for computerization. 
7. Separate  Queues  for Senior  Citizens  in  Central government 
Hospitals:—  
A provision for separate queue for priority treatment to senior 
citizen patients is already in ex istence in the OPD of Central 
Government Hospitals. 
8. Cleanliness and hygiene and lack of coordination between Local 
Bodies and Hospital Authorities:—  
Senior level Medical Officers have been made responsible for 
overseeing the cleanliness of hospital premises. The premises have 
been divided into zones and r esponsibility assigned to Sanitary 
Inspectors for the upkeep of the premises and laboratories. Hospitals 
arrange cleanliness drives periodically. Incinerators are being used for 
the disposal of bilogical waste like dead foetus, etc. and other infected 
waste including physical material lik e syringes, needles, bottles etc. 
As regards non-infected, non-hazardous waste, the NDMOlocal 
bodies are responsible for its coll ection and disposal. The hospital 
authorities have been liaising with local bodies for disposal of this 
waste. The matter is also being taken up in the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests to bring the problem into focus and give a 
direction to the hospitals, local bodies and other engaged 
6 

[22 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
in the task of hospital waste manage ment. Adequate attention is being 
paid by LHMC for the management of hospital waste. The cleanliness 
and hygiene of the hospital is being improved and wherever 
necessary, renovation of toilets has been undertaken. Under the 
Comprehensive Redevelopment Plan, proposals for latest amenities for 
sewerage, water supply and management of hospital waste have been 
incorporated. 
9. Creation of an 'Ombudsman' Type of machinery:—  
A public grievances committee has been functioning in each of the 
Central Government hospital for looking into the complaints of 
patients and there is a public grievances committee in the Dte. GHS 
headed by the D.G. A citizen charter is also in existence in each of the 
Central Government Hospital.

Non-existent voters' names in West Bengal 
*404. DR. ARUN KUMAR SARMA: Will the Minister of LAW, 
JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the CEO of West Bengal detected 
seventy lakhs non-existent voters' names as reported in the Statesman, 
Kolkata edition, dated the 5th February, 2002; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and status of those indicating their 
existence, citizenship status, modus operandi adopted for their 
inclusion in the list and implication on the Assembly Poll, 2001 
results; 
(c) the steps taken to prevent such happening in future; and 
(d) the reported incidents of such fi ndings, if any, in other States 
including Assam? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY 
AFFAIRS (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): (a) The last intensive revision of 
electoral rolls in the State of West Bengal was undertaken in 1994 
with reference to 01.01.1995 as the qualifying date. It may be added 
that since then only summary revisions of the electoral rolls have been 
taken place in the years 1997, 1998, 1999, 2000 and 2001 with reference   
to   01.01.1997,   01.01.1998,   01.01.1999,   01.01.2000   and 
01.01.2001 respectively as the qualifying date. 
The special revision of electoral rolls of an intensive nature with 
01.01.2002 as the qualifying date, was undertaken in West Bengal. 
An house to house verification and enumeration was conducted from 
5th November to 4th December, 2001. Through the process of 
verification of voters, whose names appeared in the preliminary list, 
69,30,851 voters were reported as either dead or not residing at the 
addresses shown in the electoral ro lls published in 2001. Hence, the 
names of these voters (69,30,851) were deleted from the draft 
electoral rolls with 01.01.2002 as the qualifying date, which was 
published on 4th February, 2002. 
(b)  During  the  house  to  house  verification  cum  enumeration 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [22 April, 2002] 
conducted as a part of Special Revision of Electoral Rolls of an 
Intensive Nature-2002, names of 69, 30,851 electors were deleted at 
the stage of publication of draft rolls. Deletion of these names was 
carried out on the above grounds only and not on the basis of 
verification of citizenship. The name s of these deleted electors might 
have been included during the continuous process of revision of rolls 
which started with the de novo intensive revision of electoral rolls of 
1995 and continued with the summ ary revision of 1996 and special 
revision of 1998, 1999, 2000 and 2001. It is evident that during the 
summary revision, no house to house verification is done and names 
of the electors oa grounds of death and shifting of residence get 
accumulated unless a specific request for deletion is filed. 
In the general electir- %o the Legislative Assembly of West Bengal- 
2001, 75.05% electors voted and it is not possible prima facie to 
identify as to whether any of those electors, whose names have since 
been deleted, cast their vote in that election. 
(c) The summary or intensive revision of electoral rolls is taken up 
every year as per the provisions of the Representation of the People 
Act, 1950 and toe Registration of Elec tors Rules, 1960 with a view to 
making them up-to date as far as possible. Due publicity is also given 
at the time of revision to create awareness and copies are displayed at 
all the polling stations of the Assembly Constituencies so as to help 
the electors to find out as to whether their names exist in the electoral 
rolls or not and they may get their names enrolled or get the names of 
the members of their family deleted if they have either expired or 
shifted their residence. As a result of the special revision of electoral 
rolls of an intensive nature in 2002, the electoral rolls were rectified. 
In future too, the efforts would contin ue to be made to ensure that the 
problem of non-existent voters do not find place in the electoral rolls. 
(d) As regards the reported incidents of  such nature in other States 
including Assam, information with re gard to all the States and Union 
Territories except Bihar and Tripura, may be treated as NIL. In respect 
of Bihar, during the summary revision of the electoral rolls, 
2002, names of 9,39,761 electors were deleted under Rule 21A of the 
18 

[22 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. Similarly in Tripura, the names 
of 52,614 electors have been deleted under Rule 21A of the 
Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. 
Model Land Use Policy for urban areas 
*405. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTI A: Will the Minister of 
URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering to formulate a Model 
Land Use Policy for urban areas to meet the aspirations of the 
economically weaker sections; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) by when the Model Land Use Policy is likely to be >ught 
before the Parliament? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION (SHRI ANANTH KUMAR): (a) to (c) Land is a 
State subject. Union Government can only provide guidelines in the 
matter. It is for Slate Governments to formulate a comprehensive 
policy in the matter. National Housing & Habitat Policy 1998 takes 
into account the interests of ec onomically weaker sections of the 
society, while defining action areas in the Land matters as follows:—  
(i) Land is the most critical input for housing. Public agencies 
should continue to undertake land acquisition proceedings for housing 
and urban services. Other more feasible alternatives like land sharing 
and land pooling aiiangemcjs, particularly in the urban fringes, should 
be considered through public and private initiatives with appropriate 
statutory support. Land assembly and development by the private 
sector should be encouraged. 
(ii) The repeal of the Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act, 1976 
is expected to ease the availability of land for all including the urban 
poor. 
(iii) Town and Country Planning regulations may be modified to 
19 

RAJYA SABHA [22 April, 2002] 
provide a portion of land at affordable rates for housing those poor 
people who provide essential services. This will also help in checking 
the growth of slums. 
(iv) Urban Land use needs to be optimized. Town and Country 
planning regulations should be ame nded to provide for higher density 
use. 
(v) Designation of no development zones in high population areas 
of cities and towns have led to the growth of slums. Planning 
authorities should re-plan these zones to meet the need of a growing 
population after taking adequate care for provision of green areas.

Cereal Banks in villages 
†*409. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: W ill the Minister of TRIBAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to set-up Cereal Banks in the 
villages; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) in what manner it will help to provide food security to the 
villagers, particularly poor villagers? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JUAL ORAM): 
(a) to (c) A Central Sector Scheme of Grain Banks in tribal villages 
was launched during 1996-97. The Scheme was started on a pilot basis 
in selected areas out of the areas identified by CPC for preventive 
measures against deaths of childre n in remote and backward tribal 
areas by providing a safeguard against fall in nutritional standard to 
Scheduled Tribes living in remote rural areas. Under this scheme the 
Ministry of Tribal Affairs provides a one time grant towards purchase 
of food grains of locally preferred variety 
for the initial stock of the bank, setting up of storage facilities of 
traditional type and purchase of weight and scales. Member families 
can take loans of food grains in instalment during the period of 
scarcity and can repay it, in cash or kind, with noin nnl i terest at the 
time of the next successful harvest. The Grain Banks are to be 
managed by Working Committees elected by beneficiaries themselves. 
All tribal families in the concer ned village as well as interested 
Scheduled Caste families living below the poverty line can be 
members of a particular Grain Bank under the Scheme. The Scheme 
was initially started in 13 States viz. Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, 
Bihar, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Or issa, Tripura, Rajasthan. Tamil 
Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and Manipur. 
Funds are released by the Ministry to the State Governments 
through TRIFED which is the channelising agency under the scheme. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
24 

[22 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
So far an amount of Rs. 1024.38 lakhs has been released to 11 States 
for establishment of 1876 Grain Banks to benefit 1888S1 families. 
As per the scheme the member families of the Grain Bank are 
entitled to take loans of food grai ns in four instalments upto 25 kg 
each during the rainy season or in any other period of scarcity. The 
loan is required to be returned with interest in cash or kind at the time 
of the next harvest season. Thus the present scheme provide for food 
security to the poor tribal villagers, within the village itself.

District Mental Health Programme is presently being implemented in

respective State Government/Urban Local Bodies to plan, formulate,

respective areas and to make adequate provision in their respective State 
Plans. The Government of India supplements the efforts of the State

various towns and cities owing to a multitude of factors such as huge 
resource gap for investment in water sector, poor distribution system, 
excessive unaccounted for water (UFW ), depletion of ground water 
resources and poor operation and ma nagement of water utilities by 
Urban Local Bodies.

laws.

of reducing the birth rate to the extent necessary to stabilize the 
population at a level consistent with the requirement of the national 
economy. 
Since the year 1996 several policy initiatives and programme

replaced by a "Community Need Based Assessment Approach". This major 
shift in programme emphasis has promoted a decentralized, need based, 
area specific and participatory plan and monitoring approach, which

Government has now adopted the National Population Policy, 2000 
on 15th February, 2000. The policy recognizes the fact that stabilizing 
population is an essential requirement for promoting sustainable 
development with more equita ble distribution. The National 
Population Policy, 2000 enumerates certain socio-demographic goals 
to be achieved by 2010, which will lead to achieving population 
stabilisation by 2045. 
The immediate objective of the National Population Policy is to 
address the unmet needs of contraception, health infrastructure, health 
personnel and to provide integrated service delivery for basic 
reproductive and child health care. The medium term objective is to 
bring the total fertility rate to replacement level by 2010, through 
vigorous implementation of inter sectoral operational strategies. The 
long-term objective is to achieve a stable population by 2045, at a 
level consistent with the requi rements of sustainable economic 
growth, social development and environmental protection.

†2949. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND

(b) From 1st April, 1996, the Family Planning Programme is being 
implemented all over India as per the recommendation of the National 
Development Council Committee on Population. The Committee 
recommended: 
1. Decentralized area specific planning based on an assessment of 
community needs.

The Department of Family Welfare of Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare, accordingly implemented the following: 
(a) The Centrally defined methods specific targets for family 
planning were abolished. 
(b) Emphasis shifted to decentralized planning at district level, 
based on community needs assessment. 
(c) The implementation of programmes was aimed at fulfilling 
these needs. 
(d) Quality of care is now a major is sue and so is skill upgradation, 
training for all health care providers, and also the building up of 
a referral network. 
(e) Monitoring and evaluation has become a routine part of the 
programme and the data is used for mid term corrections. 
During the 10th Five Year Plan the focus is on enabling couples to 
achieve their reproductive health goals, to address the unmet needs for 
contraception to reduce unwanted pre gnancies and to integrate health 
care for women and children with special emphasis on community 
needs assessments. There would be decentralized, area specific, micro 
planning with greater emphasis on quality of care. The 10th Five Year 
Plan would also make efforts to meet the health care needs of the 
families with emphasis on involvement of men in Planned 
Parenthood. The emphasis would be to address the unmet need, by 
inter-alia, improving logistics to ensure adequate and timely supplies 
of health care products, commodities and services.

researchers for last three years, State-wise, year-wise and category-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) Yes, Sir. Recently there 
was an outbreak of acute febrile illness with haemoptysis (blood in 
sputum) in Hatkoti village of Shimla district which has been confirmed by 
National Institute of Communicable Diseases as pneumonic plague. 
From 4th February till 14th March, 2002 out of the sixteen cases of 
69 

RAJYA SABHA [22 April, 2002] 
plague detected in Himachal Pradesh and the four suspected cases 
with plague like symptoms from Ch andigarh and its adjoining areas 5 
have died, 15 have discharged after recovery. 
On receiving report from the nodal officer for National Surveillance 
Programme for Communicable Diseases a team from National 
Institute of Communicable Diseases consisting of epidemiologist, 
microbiologist and entomologist proceeded to the affected areas of 
Himachal Pradesh 14.2.2002 and on 22.2.2002 another team 
consisting of 6 public health expe rts was sent to Chandigarh. The 
teams visited the affected areas and examined the patients in the 
hospitals. They assisted and advise d the State health autorities in 
containing the spread of infection. 
The following action were taken: 
(i) The emergency medical require ments of the Government of 
Himachal Pradesh were promptly met with. 
(ii) Guidelines were issued to h ealth authorities of Government of 
Himachal Pradesh, Uttaranchal, Punjab, Haryana and U.T. of 
Chandigarh for containing the spread of infection. 
(iii) Door to door interaction with the population in the affected 
and adjoining village for dispensing antibiotics, informations 
about the new cases and educating the people was conducted. 
(iv) Fumigation of the patients' houses were carried out using 
            Formalin (10%).  
     (v)  About   28,000   to   30,000    people    have    been    provided                                                    
chemoprophylaxis. 
The significant components of these guidelines were: 
*Quarantine of the affected village and close contacts of the 
patients. 
*Chemoprophylaxis (using Doxyc line/Tctracyclinc/Broad Spectrum 
antibiotics) administered to th e close contacts of the patients 
residents of the affected and neighbouring villages, doctors/ 
paramedics and health workers in Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, 
Haryana and Uttaranchal, Fumigation of the patients' houses have

as the transport vehicles.  
* IEC campaign for reassuring the general public not to panic, and also      
advising them to report to health facilities in case there was fever, 
cough, etc. 
In order to identify outbreak of communicable diseases and 
appropriate and timely response to these outbreaks Government of India 
launched National Surveillance Programme for Communicable Disease 
(NSPCD) during 1997-98. The main objectives of this programme is 
capacity building at State and district levels for early identification of 
outbreaks and rapid response. The Programme is currently under 
operation in 80 districts.

Stringent laws to prevent sale of spurious drugs 
2973. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will th e Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is an urgent need for more stringent laws to 
prevent the sale of spurious and banned drugs in the country; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to enact a legislation in this 
regard; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the other steps Government propose to take to prevent the sale 
of spurious and banned drugs in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) Under the 
provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules thereunder, 
State Government have been empowered to enforce quality of durgs 
including check on manufacture or sale of spurious and banned drugs. 
The said Act was amended in 1982 to provide for specific definition 
of spurious drug. Manufacture and sale of spurious drug, if detected, 
is punishable with imprisonment fo r a term which may extend to a 
term of the life and with fine 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [22 April, 2002] 
which shall not be less than Rs. 10,000/-. Hence there are adequate 
stringent provisions available in the said Act to tackle the problem of 
spurious drugs. 
Section 26-A of the said Act empowers Central Government to 
prohibit manufacture, sale or distribution of drugs whose use is likely 
to involve any risk to any human being or it does not have the 
therapeutic value claimed or does not have therapeutic justification. 
72 categories of drugs have already been prohibited by the 
Government. The Act provides one year imprisonment but which may 
extend to two years and fine if any person is found contravening the 
provision of manufacture, sale or distribution of prohibited drug. 
(d) Since manufacture and sale of spurious medicine is a clandestine 
activity indulged in by anti-social persons, steps are taken from time to 
time by the enforcement authorities of the States to detect and unearth 
spuriousfake drugs in the interstate commerce. The Drugs Controller 
General (India) has advised the st ate drugs controller to take the 
following measures for curbing the incident of spurious drugs:— 
(i) Constitution and reactivation of State Drug Advisory 
Committees in which various trade and industry associations 
as well as consumer associations should find representation. 
(ii) Establishment of separate intelligence-cum-legal machinery 
with police assistance. 
(iii) To provide training to se lected officials of Drug Control 
Administration in the modalities of intelligence work 
prosecution etc. in respect of spurious counterfeit drugs. 
(iv) To ensure speedy analysis of drug samples by establishing 
own State level drug testing facilities. 
(v) State Drugs Control Authorities should be cautious while 
approving licenses for drug product to ensure that look-alike 
products are not encouraged. 
(vi) To develop efficient comm unication facilities and recall 
procedures. 
102 

[22 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(vii) To undertake Surveillance of suspected dealers. 
(viii) To engage experienced counsel for fighting spurious drug 
cases. 
(ix) To obtain Cooperation of Pharmaceutical Industry by regular 
interaction with them. 
(x) To collect survey samples under National Survey Quality 
Evaluation of Drug (NSQED) Programme. 
In addition the following steps have been taken:—  
1. Association of Pharmaceutical Industry and All India 
Organisation of Chemists and Druggists have been asked to take 
necessary initiative to collectively combat the menace of 
spurious drugs. 
2. The problem of manufacture and sale of spurious drugs and the need 
to ensure its checking has been specifically explained to State 
Health Ministers during the meeting of Central Council of Health and 
Family Welfare held on 12th and 13th July, 2001 in New Delhi. 
3. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare constituted a 
Committee under the Chairmanship of DGHS on July 18, 2001 
associating members from industry, trade, drug regulatory officials 
and public representative to go into all aspects of the menace of 
spurious drugs and suggest reme dial measures. Meeting of the 
Committee were held on October 25, 2001 and March 14, 2002 and 
various underlying issues concer ning manufacture and sale of 
spurious drugs in the country were examined.

†2993. SHRI JANESHWAR MISHRA: Will the Minister of

good sanitary habits and health seeking behaviour, which will 
contribute to reduction of inciden ce of water borne diseases. The 
Government has also initiated an Oral Rehydration Therapy 
Programme and a National Su rveillance Programme for 
Communicable Diseases as a pilot project in selected districts for 
detection of early warning signals of outbreaks of cholera and other 
diarrhoeal diseases and rapid response for prevention and control of

Functioning     of    the     Committee     for     development     of     the 
Entertainment Sector 
3011. DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: Will the Minister of 
INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a Committee for development of the Entertainment 
Sector including films has been constituted under her Ministry; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the number of meetings of the Committee held, so far, and 
decisions arrived at with details thereof; and 
(d) whether these decisions will be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING (SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (d) In 
accordance with the recommendations of the 24th Conference of 
States and Union Territory Ministers of Information (SIMCON) held in 
New Delhi on 21.01.2001, a Committee for Development of the 
Entertainment Sector was set up with nine State Information Ministers 
under the Chairpcrsonship of Minister for Information and Broadcasting, 
to suggest a policy framework both at the Centre and in the States for 
realizing the potential of the entertainment sector. The Committee met 
twice in New Delhi and as a result of its deliberations recommended 
that: 
(i) State Governments may consider fixing a realistic ceiling level 
of 60 per cent for the entertainment tax rates. 
(ii) Each State Government should explore the best method of 
introducing computerized ticketing to remove tax evasion 
and incorrect disclosure of sales volumes. 
(iii) The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting should evolve 
training modules regarding copyright enforcement for both 
senior police officers and junior personnel and 
144 

[22 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
circulate it to all the States to enable them to  include these 
in their training curriculum for the Police. 
(iv) The existing policy of film and exhibition infrastructure of 
all States should be examined with a view to formulate an 
ideal structure of rules, regulations and incentives to act as a 
updated reference point for the States. 
(v) State Governments could id entify shooting locales and build 
sufficient infrastructure so as to encourage film makers and 
producers to shoot films in such locales. 
The recommendations of the Committee have been circulated to all 
State Governments/Union Territory administrations for action, as most 
recommended actions fall within their purview. 
The Indian Institute of Mass Communication has been entrusted with 
the task of preparing training modules rgarding copyright enforcement to 
be included in the curriculum of police officers.

†3034. SHRI VUAY SINGH YADAV: Wi ll the Minister of LAW,

THE MINISTER OF LAW, JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): (a) to (c) The issue regarding departmental 
inquiry on the same charge in r espect of a matter which is under 
consideration of the High Court has been considered by the Supreme 
Court in the case of Kusheshwar Dubey, Appellant Vs. M/s Bharat 
Coking Coal Ltd., and other, (AIR 1988 Supreme Court 2118) and it 
was held that 'while there could be no legal bar for simultaneous 
proceedings being taken, yet, there may be cases where it would be 
appropriate to defer disciplinary pr oceedings awaiting disposal of the 
criminal case. In the latter class of cases it would be open to the 
delinquent-employee to seek such an order of stay or injunction from 
the Court. Whether in the facts and circumstances of a particular case 
there should or should not be such simultaneity of the proceedings

the given circumstances of a pa rticular case as to whether the 
disciplinary proceedings should be interdicted, pending 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [22 April, 2002] 
criminal trial. As we have already stated that it is neither possible nor 
advisable to evolve a hard and fast, straight-jacket formula valid for all 
cases and of general application wit hout regard to the particularities 
of the individual situation'.

Supreme Court 30) .it was held that the initiation and continuation of 
disciplinary proceedings in good faith do not obstruct or interfere with the 
course of justice in the pending court proceedings. The employee is free 
to move the court for an order restraining the continuance of the 
disciplinary proceedings. If he obtains a stay order, a willful violation of 
that order would of course amount to contempt of court. In the absence 
of stay order the disciplinary author ity is free to exercise its lawful 
powers.

3044. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of SHIPPING be

(d) whether Government have any plans to rectify this situation?

(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) Yes, Sir. About two-third of total 
containers carrying import/export cargo to/from India are transshipped at

advantage of economies of scale, which makes it viable to install 
modern handling equipment.

addition, because of detour involved in transportation by ship, extra 
ocean freight is incurred.

vessels to facilitate direct sailing from/to India.

1998 
3058. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the 
Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether following the National Housing and Habitat Policy, 
1998, a number of positive policy meas ures have been initiated on the 
financial, fiscal and legislative fronts; 
(b) if so, whether these are not adequa te to fulfil the Budget 2000-
2001 vision target of "Housing for AH' to be realised by the year 2010;

regard; and 
(d) the latest position about these projects? 
182

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) Yes, Sir. The Na tional Housing and Habitat Policy, 
1998 envisages Government's role as an enablcr rather than builder. 
Government aims to create an enabling environment by removing the legal, 
regulatory, technical, and financial constraints facing the housing sector. The 
State Governments are required to draw their own action plans to address the 
housing problems in their States. As a follow-up of the National Housing and 
Habitat Policy, 1998, several steps have been taken as given in Statement 
(See below). 
(b) to (d) Housing is a State subject. The Government through the National 
Agenda for Governance have declared Ho using for All as a priority area and 
has decided to focus on the housing needs of citizens in general and that of 
the poor and the deprived in particular. Towards this end, the Agenda sets a 
target of consturction of additional 2 million houses (7 lakh in Urban areas 
and 13 lakh in Rural areas) every year through State Government agencies on 
a demand-driven t approach. The steps taken by the Government to fulfil the 
target of 'Housing for All' arc given in Statement II. 
Statement 
Steps taken As a follow up of the National Housing and Habitat 
Policy, 1998.  
(i) Fiscal incentives under the Income Tax Act and in Customs and Excise 
duties are available. 
(ii) Legal reforms have been initia ted to facilitate housing. The Urban 
Land Ceiling Act has been repealed. Model Rent Control Legislation has 
been prepared and circulated among State Governments for its adoption. 
States have also been advised to amend town planning and building laws to 
encourage housing. This Ministry is also pursuing amendments to 
foreclosure laws to facilitate easy foreclosure and for developing a secondary 
mortgage market. 
(iii) The Government, through grea ter interaction with the National 
Housing Bank and Housing Finance Institutions is seeking 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [22 April, 2002]

strengthen the cooperative sector through the National Cooperative 
Housing Federation.

technology.

'Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana' (VAMBAY) for providing housing and 
upgradation of existing housing for the below-poverty line families in 
urban slums with a component for construction of community toilets.

3068. SHRI VIJAY SINGH YAD AV: Will the Minister of 
URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be

erring persons with the time frame by which it would be completed;

DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI 
BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Government has received, from time to time, grievances on 
various issues relating to the functioning of DDA like delay in 
possession of flats, non-rcccipt of letters, etc. DDA has taken number 
of steps to rationalize its working and to make it more transparent.   
This   has   been   done   through   adoption   of   certain 
193 

RAJYA SABHA [22 April, 2002] 
e-govemance practices and computerisation. This improvement in 
functioning and systems is an on-going process. 
(c) There have been complaints of illegal construction in Group 
Housing Societies mainly pertai ning to covering of balcony by 
glazing/grill, construction on terr ace of room/WC, covering of 
varandah, extension of Cupboa rd, extension of courtyard, 
encroachment of society land, cons truction of society office in stilt 
area and occupancy of flats without provisional occupancy 
certificate/completion certificate i.e. without No Objection 
Certificate from Delhi Fire Services etc. 
During the last 18 months action has been taken against illegal 
construction by DDA in Group Housing Societies and show cause 
notices were issued in 52 cases. After giving opportunity/hearing to
