detective and punitive to curb corruption in the organisation. To 
maintain integrity in the Dcptt., instructions regarding anti- 
corruption measures issued by the Dcptt. of Personnel and 
Training are being scrupulously followed. Measures for 
strengthening of Vigilance Admn. and anti-corruption work as 
advised by the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) are also being 
implemented. Several long-term measures have been initiated by 
DDA to train its work force, introduce computerisation and 
e-govemance as well as exercising strict vigilance at all levels. 
Various preventive measures have been taken to streamline the 
functioning of the organisation i.e. monitoring/implementation of time 
limits provided for various items/transactions in DDA as per citizen's 
charter. The System of acknowledging letters and documents has been 
put in place. The centralized Receipt and Despatch Section has been 
computerized and the public is issued a computerized 
acknowledgement  against  their  letters.   All  important  letters  like 
194 

[22 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
demand-cum-allotment letters, refunds etc. are being sent by Speed 
Post and proof of delivery is being obtained from Post Office. 
13 Counselors/Facilitators have b een permanently seated in the 
main Reception Hall of Vikas Sada n for personally attending to the 
public visiting DDA offices for various transactions. These 
Counselors apart from guidance also help in documentation. 
Steps have been taken to disse minate information regarding 
functions and facilities provided by  public dealing department to 
customers by way of issuing br ochures, hand books and notices in 
newspapers and public places. DDA has also created a Website 
(dda.delhi.com) to provide information to public. 
As a short-term measure, disciplinary action is being taken against 
defaulting officials. During the year 2001-02, the departmental action 
has been initiated against 100 offi cials. During the same period 
disciplinary cases of 152 officials were finalized, of which in 60 
cases, major penalty was imposed, which includes 5 cases of 
removal/dismissal from service and one case of compulsory 
retirement. In 59 cases, minor penalties were imposed.

Steps to reduce migration to Delhi 
3075. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: W ill the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that three lakh migrants come to Delhi in 
search of better employment opportunities; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the said phenomena not only add to 
the burden on the city's infrastructure but add to the congestion; and 
(c) if so, the steps being taken by Government to reduce the 
migration? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI 
BANDARU DATTATRAYA): (a) As per the Census of India, 1981, 
during the decade 1971—81, NCT Delhi received about 12.30 lakh 
migrants. Out of these, 34.48 per cent arc estimated to have migrated 
due to employment opportunities. 
As per the Census of India, 1991, during the decade 1981—91, 
NCT Delhi received about 15.86 lakh migrants (i.e. average of about 
1.59 lakh migrants per ye.ar). Of these 31.29 per cent migrated on 
account of better employment opportunities. 
According to report of expert sub-group of DDA to study 
demographic profile for NCT of De lhi, about two lakh persons arc 
migrating every year to Delhi. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The root cause of migration is attributable to the prevailing 
regional-economic-imbalanccs in the country which forces the 
population from rural hinterland to the urban centres in search of 
gainful employment opportunities. However, to decongest Delhi, the 
Government have set up the Nationa l Capital Region Planning Board 
in 1985 for development of the area known as the National Capital 
Region Area. Its objectives arc to promote a planned and harmonized 
development of this entire area to decongest Delhi. 
 
 
 
 
 200 
 

[22 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Some of the steps taken up by NCRPB include: 
(i) Preparation of Regional Plan-2001 which is being 
implemented by the NCR States and the Central Ministries. 
(ii) Preparation of 4 Functional Plans relating to transportation, 
telecommunication, industry and power. 
(iii) Prepartion of the Sub-Regional Plans of U.P. and Rajasthan 
sub-regions. 
(iv) Extension of loan facilities to State Governments/agencies to 
create infrastructure in the NCR area so that pressure on Delhi 
is reduced.

(c) and (d) The problem of slum dwellers has been engaging the 
attention of Government since the 2nd Five Year Plan. A number of 
programmes/schemes were launc hed by the Government for 
improving the economic and environmental conditions of the slum 
dwellers living all over the c ountry. Some of the important 
programmes are as under:—  
The Environmental Improvement of Urban Slums (EIUS) scheme is in 
operation in the States Sector th rough which basic facilities like water 
supply, sewerage, storm water drains, community facilities, widening and 
paving of paths/lanes, street lighting are provided in the existing slums 
by the State Governments. 
During 1996 to ameliorate the living condition of slum dwellers the 
Central Government launched a scheme namely National Slum 
Development Programme (NSDP), under which the funds are 
provided by the Central Government in the form of Additional Central 
Assistance (ACA) for provision of basic amenities like water supply, storm 
water drains, community bath, widening and paving existing lanes, sewers, 
community latrines, street light etc. including provision of community 
centres, to be used for pre-school education, non-formal education, adult 
education, recreational activities etc. in improving the condition of slum 
dwellers in States/Union Territories. 
202 

[22 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
A scheme called Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rojgar Yojana (SJSRY) which 
seeks to provide gainful employment to the unemployed and 
underemployed poor as per guidelines of the scheme, is under 
implementation since 1.12.1997. 
A new scheme called Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana 
(VAMBAY) has been launched in December, 2001 to provide 
shelter/shelter upgradation to the slum dwellers living below poverty line 
including economically weaker sections. This scheme has a component 
for providing community toilet facility also to slum dwellers. The 
Central Government provides a subsidy to the projects of the State 
Governments to the extent of 50 per cent while the balance to be met 
by the State Governments either through loans from HUDCO or other 
agencies or contribution from any other source.

AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the number of projects pending with the Central Government 
for clearance, State-wise; 
(b) what is the duration of their pendency, project-wise; and 
(c) what are the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SYED SHAHNAWAZ

indicated below: 
Maharshtra 
(i) Second International Airport in Navi Mumbai

Industrial Development Corporation of Maharashtra Ltd. (CIDCO) on

Interest rates on deposits in Urban Co-operative Banks 
*427. SHRI YADLAPATI VENKAT RAO: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Reserve Bank of India has issued a directive to the 
Urban Co-operative Banks to slash the interest rates on deposits to 
the level offered by the commercial banks; 
(b) if so, the rate of interest  Urban Co-operative Banks were 
paying before the directive of the RBI; and 
(c) what is the rate of interest of commercial banks at present? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) Urban cooperative banks are free 
to determine their rate of interest on term 
8 

[23 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
deposits with the approval of their Board of Directors. However, offering 
high rate of interest which is not in alignment with market rates, affects the 
profitability of banks and adds to their liability. Therefore, Urban 
cooperative banks were advised by RBI in January 2002 to review their 
interest rate structure on term depos its of different maturities and take 
appropriate action to make them comp arable with the rates offered by 
commercial banks. 
(c) With effect from October 22, 1997, RBI has given freedom to 
commercial banks to fix their own interest rates on domestic term deposits of 
various maturities. At present the term deposit rates of different banks are 
generally between 8% to 9% p.a. Howeve r, interest rate on savings deposits 
is still regulated by RBI and this rate has been fixed at 4.0 per cent per 
annum since April 1, 2000.

*431. SHRI SANJAY NIRUPAM: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Air India has made any profit for the year 2001-2002; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Air India has made any profit from non-operating revenue or its 
unutilised bilateral rights; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SYED SHAHNAWAZ 
HUSSAIN): (a) and (b) Air India has earned a net profit of Rs. 4.71 crores 
during the period April, 2001 to January, 2002. Based on Traffic trends during

2002 would be higher.

*432. SHRI B. J. PANDA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the export growth target has been slashed by 12 per cent for the 
current fiscal year as against the previously achieved growth rate of 19.83 per 
cent in 2000-2001; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) the country's targeted International share (in terms of 
percentage) for 2000-2001; 
(d) the share (in terms of percentage) of "ores and minerals" in India's total 
export in 2000-2001 and the projection for the current year; and 
(e) whether any study is made to qualify the improvement in export 
growth rate by exporting value added products of these "ores and minerals" 
instead of exporting them as it is? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI MURASOLI 
MAR AN): (a) and (b) Keeping in view the global ec onomic slowdown and 
events of September 11 and their aftermath, the annual export target was scaled down 
to 3% from 12% which was originally envisaged at the beginning of 2001-02. Export 
growth rate achieved during 2000-01 was 21% which was the highest growth rate 
in the last decade. 
(c) As per WTO Report, share of India's merchandise export is 
0.67% during 2000. 
(d) As per the data available from Directorate General of 
Commercial Intelligence and Statistics (DGCI&S), Calcutta, the 
export of ores and minerals accounted  for 2.61% share in total export 
during 2000-01. Export of minerals and ores sector is projected to be 
around US $ 1497 million in the financial year (2001-2002). 
(e) No formal study has been conducted specifically on the issue of 
improving export growth rate by exporting value added products 
rather than ores and minerals in their raw form.

*434. SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN:  Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that subsidy given to passengers of North-East in 
air travel has been withdrawn; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the fare hike to and fro North-East 
destinations are much higher than any other sector now; and 
(c) if so, what has forced the Ministry of Civil Aviation to do so? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SYED SHAHNAWAZ 
HUSSAIN): (a) The Government set up a Civil Aviation Development Fund 
on  1.4.1964 to provide subsidy for 
15 

RAJYA SABHA [23 April, 2002] 
operation of uneconomic routes by Indi an Airlines at th e instance of the 
Government, Indian Airlines was paid a subsidy of Rs. 11.30 crores in 1973-

systems and procedures for acquisition, maintenance and operation of small 
aircraft. The Committee has submitted its report on 08.11.2001. 
(c) In all, the Committee made 55 recommendations, details of which are 
available in the enclosed Statement. 
Statement 
Recommendation to undertake comprehensive review of sysems and 
procedures for acquisition, maintenance and operation of small aircraft 
Applicable to Airworthiness and Safety 
1. Each operator of small aircraft engaged in Non-Scheduled 
operations should be brought under approval system keeping in view 
the scope and type of operations, and should nominate an 
Accountable Manager as per the provisions of CAR where the 
operator has his own maintenance agency. 
2. All   operators   including   private   operator   should   have   a 
30 

[23 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
designated  Quality   Control  Manager  to  carry  out   all  attendant functions. 
3. All operators for a given type of aircraft should follow Standardised 
Maintenance Schedules approved by DGCA. 
4. Quality Control Manuals of the opera tors should have commonality to 
help in standardisation of Quality Assurance Practices and Programmes. 
5. The syllabus for granting Aircraft Maintenance Engineer's Licences should 
be reviewed for necessary amendments with specific emphasis on Quality Control 
functions awareness. 
6. The system of Defect Recording, Reporting, Investigation, Rectification and 
Analysis needs to be strengthened and monitored for private^hon-scheduled 
operators>flying clubs and State Government Aviation Department. Defect(s) 
carried forward under the provisions of MEL, if any, should be strictly 
monitored. 
The requirement related to Minimum Equipment List (MEL) should be 
stipulated for small aircraft operators also, wherever applicable, as per the type 
of aircraft. 
7. A system of carrying a standardised Flight Report Book on board the 
aircraft by all operators should be implemented. This document would have 
different sections to record flight, technical and maintenance related data. 
8. Certification of airborne radio equipment for all types of aircraft may be 
aligned with the issuance of Certificate of Flight Release for the aircraft 
wherever possible. 
9. The CAR issued relating to airworthiness of ageing aircraft should be made 
applicable to all types of aircraft in operation as per manufacturers requirement. 
The various associated control & prevention programme on this aspect should 
be integrated with regular maintenance schedules. The necessary 
documentation, if required in this regard, should be prepared-reviewed and approved 
by Regulatory Agency. 
10. Aircraft with all up weight of 5,700 kgs. and above should be 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [23 April, 2002] 
maintained by approved Maintenance Organisations. 
11. The fitment of CVR & FDR to be made mandatory even in small twin 
engine aircraft where STC is available. 
12. All aircraft permitted to fly in Instrument Meteorological C onditions 
(IMC>Night Conditions and carrying passenger(s) should mandatorily have 
serviceable weather radar, provided STC is available, and the pilots operating 
such flights should undergo prior training in operatin^lnterprelation of weather 
radar picture. 
13. Test flight requirements for aircraft flying with Private/Non-Scheduled 
Operators'Flying ClubsState Governments should be mandatory with every C of 
A renewal, whether on annual or six monthly basis as the case may be. 
14. Small aircraft operators should mandatorily prepare a Flight Safety Manual 
duty vetted by the DGCA is line with as required by the Scheduled Operators 
for enhancing safety of operations. 
15. Small aircraft operators should prepare Operations Manual Handbook for 
guidance of their personnel engaged in aircraft operations.

Trim Sheet on aircraft whose manufacturer provide the necessary documentation

should be strict compliance and monitoring by the operators themselves for 
adherence of laid-down standards through frequent Safety AuditsSurveillance 
Check*5pot Checks. Regular reports on related issues should be obtained from the 
operators by Regulatory Agency.

essential to comply with maintenance and flight safety standards,   as  stipulated  by   
the   Regulatory  Agency.   The  Human

[23 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA

operators. The norms for deployment of personnel in such organisations

3110. SHRI C.P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: 
  SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: 
Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to establish Common Intellectual Property 
Court (CIPC) to deal with Intellectual Property Rights cases across the country; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to set up CIPC on the lines of UK, 
USA and Japan; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the steps taken by Government foT effective and speedy enforcement of 
Intellectual Property Rights? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN SINGH) (a) to (d) Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs) 
cases are presently handled by the existing judicial system in the country. 
However, the Trade Marks Act, 1999 provides for the setting up of an 
Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB) with appellate jurisdiction over the 
decisions of the Registrar of Trade Marks. It will also have jurisdiction over the 
decisions of the Registrar of Geographical Indications under the Geographical 
Indications (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999. Its jurisdiction is further 
proposed to be extended to the decisions of the Controller General of Patents 
under the Indian patent law. The IPAB is modeled on the Central 
Administrative Tribunal. A Copyright Board exists under the Copyright Act 
with appellate jurisdiction over the decisions of the Registrar of Copyright. The 
Semiconductor Integrated Layout Design Act, 2000 also provides for setting up of 
a Layout Design Appellate Board.

(a) whether Government have examined the causes of recent failure of 
Co-operative Banks in the country, particularly in Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh 
and Karnataka: 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether Government have prepared the revival package for such Co-
operative Banks; 
(e) if so, the details thereof; and 
(f) the steps proposed to be taken to stop further collapse of Cooperative 
Banking Sector in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (e) The causes of the failure of Co-
operative Banks include, inter alia, Low Entry Capital, Unsatisfactory Credit 
Appraisal and Credit Monitoring Systems, Non-Observance of Prudential 
Norms, Poor Funds Management, High Level of NPA, Deficiencies in 
Management, etc. The Co-operative cred it system, therefore, suffers from 
systematic shortcomings and erosion of net worth. Government of India had 
constituted a Task Force (known as Capoor Committee) in April 1999 to 
study the functioning of co-operative credit system and suggest measures for 
its strengthening. The Task Force made wide ranging recommendations 
which have been examined by the Government in consultation with State 
Governments and deliberated upon in a Conference of Chief Ministers of 
States. It was decided in the above Conference to constitute a Joint 
Committee of the Cooperation Ministers of select States under the 
Chairmanship of Union Minister of State for Finance. This Committee has 
since submitted its report on the required reform and for improving the net 
worth of    these    institutions    which    is    under    consideration    of    the

Government. Meanwhile, Finance Minister has announced a provision of 
Rs. 100 crores in the Union Budget  for the year 2002-2003 for the 
revitalization of the Co-operatives. 
 (f) RBI has taken various regulatory/supervisory measures to avoid 
such failure in future. These include restricting the operations of Co

restricting the issue of bankers' cheques by urban Co-operative banks,

etc.

Category I— Projects where financia l closure had been achieved and 
formally documented 
Category II— Projects with original proj ect cost of Rs. 100 crore or more 
Category III— Projects with original project cost of less than Rs. 100 
 crore 
 In case of category-I (which would norm ally be infrastructure projects or large 
value manufacturing projects financed after 1 997), the asset may be treated as standard 
asset only for a period of two years beyond the date for completion of the project, as 
originally envisaged at the time of initial financial closure of the project. In case of

 In case of category-II projects sanctioned prior to 1997 and where

Filing of Income-tax returns by hospitals 
3177. PROF. M. SANKARAUNGAM: W ill the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made any effort to find out those private 
hospitals and nursing homes which have not filed their Income-tax returns in 
different parts of the country including Delhi; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) whether Government would provide details of the CAG Report with 
regard to non-filing of Income-tax returns by such private hospitals and nursing 
homes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Central Information Bran ch (CIB) of the Income Tax 
Department collects information regarding Private Hospitals and 
Nursing Homes as per CBDT Instruction No. 1943 dated 22.08.1997 
and passes on the same to the Commissioners of Income Tax 
concerned for further necessary action. 
The territorial Assessing Officers al so collect information regaiding 
ownership, assessment particulars, books of accounts, bank accounts, turnover, 
stock in trade, vehicles etc. u/s 133B of the Income Tax Act regarding all the 
commercial establishments including Private Hospitals and Nursing Homes 
operating in their territorial jurisdiction, from time to time. 
(c) Not applicable in view of (a) and (b) above. 
130 

[23 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) The CAG Report (No. 12A of 200 2) has already been placed before 
the House. 
The observations made in para 3.7.1. regarding non-filing of Income-tax 
returns by private hospitals and nursing homes do not reflect the true state of 
affairs. 
The list containing commercial names of the Hospitals/Nursing Homes 
has been primarily prepared from  Municipal Records and Telephone 
Directories, whereas th e Income-tax Records show names of assessable 
entities (Individuals/Firms/Trusts/Associations of Persons/Companies) 
having ownership of such Hospitals/Nursing Homes. Detailed 
verification/field enquiry in Delhi has shown that all the cases reported in the 
list are filing their tax returns except one case in which the reported 
HospitakNursing Home does not exist at the address given in the list. 
Similarly, 187 cases out of total 198 Private HospitalsWursing Homes in 
Jharkhand arc assessed to tax. Similar results have been reported after 
verification from different parts of the country namely Haryana, Uttar 
Pradesh, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Goa, Assam, 
Punjab and Madhya Pradesh. 
Inter-State Coordination Committee on Narcotics 
3178. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that seizures made by the enforcement agencies 
have clearly indicated that India has now become a producing country for 
heroin; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard and the efforts made by Government to 
curb opium drug trafficking; and 
(c) the main decision taken at the Inter-State Coordination Committee 
meeting held at Narcotics Control Bureau on 23rd February, 2002? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
GINGEE N. RAMACHANDRAN): (a) The seizure reports 
131 

RAJYA SABHA [23 April, 2002] 
of various Drug Law Enforcement Agencies indicate that heroin, besides being 
smuggled in from across the border, is also being manufactured illicitly in some 
parts of the country, especially in and around the opium producing States. 
(b) As reported by various Drug Law Enforcement Agencies, during the 
year 2001 eight illicit drug manufacturing facilities were detected in various parts of 
the country and dismantled by the said Agencies. The Government has taken a 
number of steps to curb opium drug trafficking, viz., (i) enactment of the 
Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act to combat drug 
trafficking, (ii) empowerment of a large number of Central and State 
Agencies under the NDPS Act to ensure effective implementation of the Act, 
(iii) intensive preventive and interdiction efforts, (iv) training to upgrade the 
skills of law enforcement officers, (v) a liberal reward scheme for informers, 
(vi) setting up of the Narcotics Control Bureau to ensure a coordinated 
approach towards drug law enforcement nationally, (vii) setting up special 
courts to try cases under the NDPS Act and (viii) international cooperation and 
coordination including a number of regional and bilateral agreements. 
(c) The main decisions taken at the Intcr-Statc Coordination Committee 
meeting, held on 22 February, 2002 by the Narcotics Control Bureau, are as 
under: 
 
(1) Agencies operating in the States bordering Pakistan shall increase vigil 
along the Indo-Pak border. 
(2) Agencies operating in the North Eastern States shall monitor the drug 
situation in the area, especially the trafficking of drugs and precursor chemicals along 
Indo-Myanmar, Indo-Bangladcsh border. 
(3) All agencies in the States of Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and 
Rajasthan shall keep a vigil on illicit opium product. 
(4) Financial investigations in all cases under the NDPS Act shall be 
accorded priority. 
(5) Illicit cultivation of opium poppy and cannabis shall be 
identified and destroyed. 

[23 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(6) Adequate steps shall be taken for speedy disposal of pending court cases 
booked under the NDPS Act. 
(7) Steps shall be taken for speedy establishment of Special Courts for trial of 
cases booked under NDPS Act. 
 
(8) All agencies shall furnish the requi site reports regarding sampling, 
storage and disposal of drugs. 
(9) All Agencies shall furnish seizure reports and monthly performance 
reports regularly and on time.

THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) to (c) No reserves of hydrocarbons have been established in

data, 1575 LKM of deep seismic sounding data, Aeromagnetic and Gravity 
Magnetic Surveys and 4980 LKM of Geo-chemical Survey and drilled four 
wells in onland areas and 11 wells in  offshore areas including North-East 
coast basin. 
In last two years, six blocks have been awarded to various public sector 
and private sector oil companies in  the offshore and onshore areas of 
Mahanadi basin in the first and second rounds of offer under New 
Exploration Licensing Policy (NELP-I&II). A total of 4182 LKM 2D 
seismic data has been acquired by the oil companies in these blocks.

Water to the Cantonment area is supplied by Hyderabad Metropolitan 
Water Supply and Sewerage Board (HMWSSB). Owing to repairs undertaken

there was disruption in regular water su pply which resulted in water scarcity

Secunderabad and Hyderabad.

lakhs towards connection charges to HMWSSB for increasing the qunatum of 
bulk water supply from 27 lakhs gallons per day to 37 lakh gallons per day 
which will commence shortly. Cantonmet Board is also executing a project for 
laying new distribution pipe lines to benefit 50 Housing colonies apart from 
digging 25 deep bore wells. This has been done in addition to the existing 110 
electric bore wells and 700 hand pump bore wells for water supply to the 
residents of Cantonment area. This will mitigate the severe shortage of water to 
a large extent

State Government of Gujarat, which have also been addressed directly to that

confidence building measures should be taken to instill a sense of security among 
the people of Gujarat and that relief and rehabilitation measures should be further 
strengthened.

Meetings of Inter-State Council 
* 444. SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of meeting Inter-State Council held during the last year; 
(b) the subjects which were discussed and the recommendations made; 
(c) the details of recommendations which are yet to be implemented; 
(d) if so, by when those recommendations will be implemented; and 
(e) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) The seventh meeting of the Inter-State Council was 
held on the 16th November, 2001 in New Delhi. 
(b) In this meeting, 59 recommendations contained in the report of 
Sarkaria Commission on various subjects viz, Legislative Relations, Role of 
Governor, All India Services, Inter-Governmental Council, Mines and Minerals, 
Mass Media etc. were considered. Some of the important recommendations 
made by the Council include the following:— 
(i) All residuary powers of legislation including those of taxation 
matters should be transferred from the Union List to the Concurrent 
List in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. 
(ii) For legislation in respect of subjects in the Concurrent List, there 
should be active consultation with the State Governments except in 
emergent cases. 
(iii) A comprehensive Central legislation should be brought up in regard 
to imposition of taxes by the local bodies on the properties of the 
Union Government, which are of industrial and commercial nature. 
(iv) Consultation with the State Chief Ministers in the selection of a 
person to be appointed as Governor should be made obligatory 
. through a Constitutional amendment. 
(c) to (e) Of the 59 recommendations of the Sarkaria Commission 
considered in the meeting held on the 16th of November, 2001, the Inter-State 
26 

[24 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Council recommended acceptance of 40 recommendations and the remaining 
19 were recommended for rejection. The recommendations of the Inter-State 
Council have been forwarded to the concerned Ministries and State Governments 
in January, 2002 for implementation. The major recommendations regarding 
legislative relations, role of Governors etc. would, if accepted by the Government, 
require amendments to the Constitution. Many of the aspects covered by the 
above recommendations of the Sarkaria Commission/Inter-State Council have 
also been examined by the National Commission set up to Review the Working 
of Constitution and they have given their recommendations. The Government 
will need to take a comprehensive view on these issues after examining the 
recommendations of the Inter-State Council as well as the Constitution Review 
Commission. Therefore, it is not possible to indicate a definite time-frame by 
which these recommendations of the Inter-State Council will be implemented.

* 455. SHRI AIMADUDDIN AHME D KHAN (DURRU): Will the 
Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government of Rajasthan has been demanding review of the 
allocation formula for power allocation from Central Power Stations; 
(b) if so, how far the power requirement of the State falls short under the 
present formula; 
(c) on what lines the formula is sought to be reviewed; and 
(d) the Government's response thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SURESH PRABHU): (a) to (d) 
According to the formula for sharing of power from Central Sector Power 
Stations, power was allocated among the States/UTs of a region in accordance 
with the Central Plan Assistance and actual energy consumption in the State of 
the region for previous five years, the two factors being given equal weightage. 
The matter was reviewed and it has been decided by the Government in April, 
2000 to treat the existing "formula" for allocation of power to the States/UTs 
from new Central sector power stations as "guidelines" so as to link the 
allocation of power with their need and capacity to pay. However, there is no 
change in the contents of the formula and it does not disturb the allocation 
already made from the Central sector power stations. Under the "guidelines" 
power from the new Central sector power stations will be made to the States/' 
UTs as per their entitlement subject to the Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) 
to be signed by them with the CPSUs concerned. No further review of the 
"guidelines" is presently envisaged. 
The power requirements of the State are met from its own generation, share 
in Central sector generating stations as well as share in joint sector power stations.

the existing Development Boards have worked in Maharashtra. Accordingly, 
the impact assessment report about functioning of these Development Boards

has informed the Ministry of Home Affairs that their Evaluation Study on

Liberalisation of coal policy 
3234. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRA1AH: Will the Minister of 
COAL AND MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Union Government has liberalised its coal policy and has 
given new guidelines recently; 
(b) if so, whether under this policy and guidelines, the State Government 
companies can now mine for coal and liginite through memorandum of article 
of association; 
(c) whether any restriction have been imposed on the companies in this 
regard; 
(d) if so,' the details thereof; and 
(e) to what extent the State Government have welcomed this move? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL AND MINES 
(SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) to (e) Yes, Sir. A revised Coal Mining 
Policy has been issued on 12th December, 2001. Under the revised policy, the 
50 

[24 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
State Government companies or undertakings are allowed to do mining of 
coking and non-coking coal or lignite reserves, either by opencast or 
underground method, anywhere in the country, subject to the following 
conditions: 
i)  The State Government company or undertaking (referred to as 
the 'company' hereafter) is authorised to do coal or lignite mining 
by its Memorandum and Articles of Association. 
ii) The company will do coal or lignite mining in accordance with 
the provisions of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, the 
Mines & Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957, the 
Contract Labour (Regulation & Abolition) Act, 1970, and all other 
mineral, environmental and labour laws and other regulations 
governing the Indian coal industry. 
iii) For coal, the company shall obtain a certificate from Coal India 
Limited to the effect that the later has no plan or willingness to 
undertake mining operations for coal in the concerned area. For 
lignite, the company shall obtain a certificate from Ney veli Lignite 
Corporation. 
iv) The proposed mining area has not been altotted to a captive mining 
compnay under the provisions of Section 3(3)(a)(iii) of the Coal 
Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973. 
v) No financial assistance from the Central Government or Coal 
India Limited or Neyveli Lignite Corporation shall be provided 
to the compnay for coal or lignite mining in the concerned area. 
vi) None of the coal or lignite mines operated by the company will 
be taken over by the Central Government or Coal India Limited 
or Neyveli Lignite Corporation in the event of closure of such a 
mine or otherwise. 
vii) No employee of the company, engaged in a coal or lignite mine 
operated by it, will be absorbed in Coal India Limited or Neyveli 
Lignite Corporation at any point of time. 
No reaction from any State Government has been received on the revised 
policy.

Statement 
Common Minimum Programme on Power 
The political parties signatory to this declaration agree on the following 
Common Minimum Programme on Power: 
• Every Indian has a right to uninterrupted and quality power supply at 
affordable rates. 
• The work of extending electrification needs to be accelerated so as to 
complete: 
. i) Electrification of all villages by the end of 10th Plan, 2007. 
ii) All households by the end of 11th Plan, 2012. 
• State Governments cannot afford to supply free power. 
— Electricity rates may be determined by independent Regulatory 
Commissions. 
 ----  Power supply may be given at subsidised rates to targeted groups 
only to the extent that the State Governments can afford to 
provide subsidies through the Budget for this purpose. 
• The real problem of management and the challenge of power sector 
reforms lies in the distribution sector where: 
a. All consumers need to be metered. 
b. Power theft has attained alarming proportions. Immediate steps 
need to be taken to eliminate theft. 
c. Technical losses need to be reduced. 
d. Energy audit arid accountability at the local level have to be 
ensured. 
e. Commercial viability needs to be achieved in the next 2-3 years 
through any or all of the following: 
—  Creating Profit Centres with full accountability 
—  Handing over of local distribution to Panchayats/Local Bodies/ 
Franchisees/Users Associations, wherever necessary 
—  Privatisation of distribution 
—  Or any other means. 
88 

[24 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
• State Governments may evolve their own path of reforms to suit their 
specific conditions. 
• Only commercially viable distri bution can sustain and attract the 
investments required in the sector. 
• Public sector investment in the Centre as well as in the States may be 
stepped up to ensure that in the 10th Plan the country is free of power 
shortages. This is critical for the Indian economy in the new globalised 
environment. 
• An effective programme for conserving energy through energy efficient 
lighting, pump sets and other equipment needs to be implemented 
with urgency. 
• Power sector is in a critical situation and reforms need to be undertaken 
to achieve the above objectives . Power sector reforms to be 
depoliticised in order to facilitate their speedy implementation.

Power theft 
† 3288. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: Will the Minister of POWER 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact.-that theft of power is still taking place in Delhi 
and the entire country des'pite change in meter policy; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to take steps to check this; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefore? . 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Yes, Sir. Theft of power takes place 
in varying magnitude in the country. Power distribution falls under the 
jurisdiction of State Governments and the activities to contain theft of power 
have to be undertaken by the power utilities. 
(b) and (c) The Central Government has given priority to reduction of 
transmission and distribution losses including power theft. The Central 
Electricity Authority has issued guidelines for reduction of transmission and 
distribution losses including power theft and for conducting Energy Audits in 
power systems. These guidelines have been circulated to all the power utilities, 
which are taking the following steps to prevent the theft of energy— 
a. Mass checking drive is carried out periodically by vigilance squads 
as well as field staff. Inspections are being carried out by district 
units of engineers and prosecutions of erring consumers are launched 
by Police Officers manning the anti Power theft Squads. 
b. Installations are being made pilfer proof. 
c. A scheme for incentive to informants is in operation. A scheme to 
recognize the performance of individuals to curb theft of energy by 
providing incentive to deserving officers/employees has also been 
introduced. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
94 

[24 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
d. Load inspection studies for major load centres are being conducted. 
e. Penalty for imprisonment is also being imposed on the culprits. 
f. With the help of computerization of billing process, abnormal 
consumption of consumers is being detected. If consumption is less 
than 15% of the average, case s arc immediately inspected for 
detecting tampering of meter/theft of energy. 
The Government of India has also launched a scheme for Accelerated 
Power Development Programme for renovation & modernization/life extension 
uprating of existing old power plants, and upgradation of sub-transmission & 
distribution network including energy audit activities and metering in the 
distribution circles in a phased manner. In the first phase of this programme, 
since rechristencd as Accelerated Power Development and Reform Programme 
(APDRP), 63 distribution circles in the States have been taken up for intensive 
upgradation so as to serve as models for remaining circles in the country for 
improvement in a phased manner. The Government has made an allocation of 
Rs. 3500 crores during 2002-03. 
The Government of India had al so set up a Steering Committee for 
preparing guidelines/manuals for improvement of Sub-transmission & 
distribution systems on a scientific basis. These include guidelines on Energy 
Accounting and audit, which would help in containing commercial losses. 
Necessary amendments have been enacted to the IE Act, 1910 to make 
theft of electricity a cognizable offence.  Stricter provisions and penalties are 
envisaged in the Electricity Bill, 2001 in case of power theft.

New policy to promote FDI in Hydro Power Sector 
3290. SHRI SATISH PRADHAN: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government is considering any new policy to promote foreign 
direct investment in hydro power generation sector by discouraging generation 
of costly power which is generated through the utilization of various petro 
products in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) to (c) The Government had 
formulated a policy in 1991 to encour age greater investment by the private 
sector in the power sector. Keeping in view the growing demand for power in 
the country and the need for more investment in this sector, the Government 
of India, as part of further liberalization of the Foreign Direct Investment 
regime, has on June 12, 2000, decided to remove the upper limit for foreign 
direct investment in respect of pr ojects relating to electric generation, 
transmission and distribution(other than atomic reactor plants). 
The use of certain liquid hydro carbon liquid fuels for generation of 
electricity was permitted under the liquid fuel policy announced in 
96 

[24 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
November, 1995 considering the shorter gestation period of liquid fuel based 
power projects as compared to thermal power projects and the need to have a 
quick capacity addition to avert a severe power crisis. Due to the spurt in 
international prices, naphtha is no longer considered a viable fuel for generation 
of electricity, also considering the difficulty in its handling. The State Governments 
are also now reluctant to encourage naphtha based power generation. 
In order to accelerate the pace of hydro power development in the country, 
a Policy of Hydro Power Development was announced in August 1998. A 
favourable environment has been created to promote private sector investment 
in the field of hydro electric projects. The procedure for transfer of clearances 
have been streamlined and tariff rationalization have made such projects 
attractive. The Ranking St udy recently carried out by the Central Electricity 
Authority (CEA) to create a shelf of feasible projects would facilitate the hydro 
developers to take up the implementation of potential sites in a phased manner 
in order of their ranking. CEA is also in the process of formulating a National 
Action Plan in consultation with the State Governments to harness the entire 
balance potential in the country.

(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) The Standing Conference of 
Public Enterprises (SCOPE) had submitted a Memorandum on Economic Policy 
issues for Union Budget 2002 to th e Finance Minister wherein it was, inter-
alia, emphasized that the hands of the PSUs should be strengthened to augment

the country's energy programme. One of  the suggestions made was that the 
PSUs may be helped to recover their dues from the State entities. It has been 
the Government's constant endeavour to asist the Central Public Sector 
Undertakings of power and coal to recover their outstanding dues from the 
State Electricity Boards (SEBs). The is sue of outstanding dues of the State 
Electricity Boards (SEBs) payable to the Central Public Sector Undertaking 
(CPSUs) was discussed in the conferen ce of Chief Ministers/Power Ministers 
in March, 2001. 
On the basis of the resolution passed in the Conference an Expert Group 
was set up under the Chairmanship of Shri Montek Singh Ahluwalia, former 
Member (Energy), Planning Commission, to: 
(i) Recommend Measures for one time settlement of outstanding dues 
of the State Electricity Boards to wards the Central Public Sector 
Undertakings as also the dues fr om the CPSUs to the State Power 
Utilities; and 
(ii) Suggest a strategy for capital re structuring of the State Electricity 
Boards including the provision of Structural Adjustment Loans so as 
to enable them to tide over the present financial crisis, make them 
operationally viable and improve their credit-rating. 
The recommendations of the Gr oup were accepted with minor 
modifications by the High Level Empowered Group of Chief Ministers. The 
modified scheme for one-time settlement  of outstanding dues was approved 
by the Government recently. The salient features of the scheme are: 
(a) The scheme would come into force from the date of issue of order or 
from the date when the State Government sign the tripartite agreement 
(with the Ministry of Finance in the Government of India and the 
Reserve Bank of India), whichever is later. 
(b) For the States participating in the scheme, 60% of the interest/surcharge 
on the delayed payments as on 30.09.2001 would be waived off. 
(c) The rest of the dues amounting to the full principal amount as well 
as the remaining 40% of the interest/surcharge would be securitised 
through bonds issue by the respective State Governments. 
(d) The bonds would be issued through RBI at a tax-free interest rate 
of 8.5% per annum. The terms of bonds should be structured to 
achieve a moratorium of 5 years on repayment of principal 
99 

RAJYA SABHA [24 April, 2002] 
with the entire principal being repaid between the 6th and 15th 
year. These bonds would be identical to bonds issued in connection 
with the market borrowings of State Governments, with the 
attendant discipline in repayments. The bonds will be subject to 
Iock-in restrictions that will allow release of only 10 per cent of the 
bonds in the secondary market each year. 
(e) Forensuring timely payment of current dues in future, defaults in 
current payment for power/fuel would attract a graded reduction in 
the supply of power from central  power stations and in coal 
supplies. Where such defaults ex ceed 90 days from the date of 
billing, the Ministry of Finance shall recover these dues through 
adjustment against releases due to them from the Centre. 
(f) In order to initiate steps toward s reform of the sector, the State 
Governments/SEBs shall accept reform-based performance 
milestones such as setting up of SERCs, metering of distribution 
feeders, improvement in revenue realisation and other such 
milestones specified in the MoUs signed/to be signed with the 
Ministry of Power. 
(g) The States shall be offered incentives for complying with the 
scheme. If SEBs or their successor entities (other than the ones not 
owned by the State Government) do not default on their current 
dues and adhere to the performance milestones, CPSUs shall pay 
them, during the first year commencing from 1.10.2001, bi-annual 
cash incentives equal to 3 per cent of the value of bonds in the first 
year, 2.5% in the second year and 2% in the third and fourth years. 
Further, if SEBs open and mainta in Letters of Credit (LCs) till the 
end of December 2002, CPSUs shall pay them a one-time cash 
incentive equal to 2 per cent of the value of bonds. In addition, 
States undertaking reforms s h a l l  also be assisted through 
Accelerated Power Development and Reform Programme 
(APRDP) grants and discretionary allocation of Power. The 
100 

[24 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
date for opening of LCs shall be 60 days from the issue of the 
order. 
(h) The States that withhold their consent beyond 60 days after this 
scheme enters into force shall be denied any share in the 
discretionary allocationof 15 per cent from the power stations of 
CPSUs as well as any assistance und er APDRP. If the overdues of 
such States exceeded Rs. 50 crore in respect of any CPSUs, they 
would also attract reduction in power and coal supplies, as 
applicable to the State participating in this scheme. 
(i) Outstanding dues as on 30.09.2001 would form the basis of the.one-
time settlement. Dues that accrue after this date would not form 
part of the scheme. As regard bonds issued in the past in lieu of 
outstanding dues of SEBs, all bonds issued after 1-3-1998 can be 
converted into State Government bonds at the option of the 
respective State Government. These bonds would form part of the 
scheme. However, any agreements entered in the past of which the 
old bonds are a part should not be re-opened. Only conversion of 
bonds under the present scheme shall be permitted. 
(j) The scheme covers the outstanding dues payable by the SEBs to the 
National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC), National Hydro-
electric Power Corporation (N HPC), North Eastern Electr ic  
Power Corporation (NEEPCO), Power Grid Corporation of India 
limited. (PGCIL) & Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) under the 
Ministry of Power, Coal India Limited (CIL) & its subsidiaries and 
Neyveli Lignite Corporation (NLC) under the Department of Coal, 
Nuclear Power Corporation (NPC) under the Department of 
Atomic Energy and the Ministry of Railways. 
(c) The total dues payable by the SEBs to the power and coal CPSUs as 
on 30.09.2001 (the cut-off date for securitisation of the dues) are given in the

Monitoring schemes by the Ministry of Rural Development 
3297. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister 
of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has introduced a new initiative to monitor 
implementation of its schemes; 
(b) if so, the details of such initiatives; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that responsibilities of area officers have 
been streamlined; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M. 
VENKAIAH NAIDU): (a) and (b) A new initiative has been taken to 
strengthen the Monitoring and quality of implementation of Programmes of 
the Ministry by introducing a scheme of District Level Monitoring on pilot 
basis during 2001-02, with the objectives of (i) maintaining the flow of 
timely, authentic and reliable information about the performance of the 
programmes of the Ministry from the District level to the Ministry, (ii) 
obtaining qualitative feedback about the implementation and policy 
environment at the District level, and (iii) to check and verify the physical 
achievements. 
(c) and (d) The Ministry have an Area Officers Scheme, in which all 
Officers of the rank of Deputy Secretary and above have been appointed Area 
Officers for one or more States. The sc heme has been streamlined recently to 
make it more effective. The Area Office rs are required to visit the allocated 
State(s) regularly, with briefs regard ing outstanding issues and details of 
proposals for clearance and release of funds under various Programmes. The 
Area Officers are also required to'visit the DRDAs and the State Headquarters 
(in addition to the selected villages) and help to expedite submission of 
proposals. In addition, they will find out the status of implementation of the 4-
point programme and assess the impact of awareness generation programmes 
through electronic and print media, th e Area Officers are also required to 
review the programme implementation and undertake physical verification of 
the assets created.

t33!4. SHRI RAM NATH  KOVIND: Will the Mi nister of TEXTILES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government had started the weavers loan relief scheme in 
the year 1990 with a view to waiving off the loans to the tune of Rs. 10,000/-
outstanding upto 1989 to be implemented by the State Cooperative Banks; 
(b) whether the loans of the weavers belonging to all the cooperative 
weavers committees have been waived off by the Magadh Central Cooperative 
Bank in Jehanabad but loans of the weavers of Gaya district have not waived 
off till date;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
V. DHAN ANJAY KUMAR); (a) Government of India had formulated a scheme 
known as "Agricultural and Rural Debt Relief Scheme 1990" (ARDRS) which 
was in force during the period from 15th May, 1990 to 31st March, 1991. 
Under the Scheme, the non-wilful defaults of Farmers, Land-less Labourers, 
Artisans and Weavers in rural areas to Public Sector Banks and Regional Rural 
Banks in respect of loans up to Rs. 10,000/- from these banks on or after 1st

formulated by the State Governments on the lines of Government of India 
Scheme. The liabilities arising out of the State Scheme were shared by 
Government of India and the concerned State Governments in equal 
proportion. In the case of weavers' societies where wages and/or yam had been

Providing yam to handloom weavers in A.P. 
3321. DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO: Will the Minister of 
TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken any concrete steps to provide yam 
to handloom weavers of Andhra Pradesh at affordable rates and in sufficient 
quantities; and 
(b) if so, details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OFTEXTILES (SHRI 
V. DHANANJAY KUMAR): (a) Yes, Sir. The Government of India has been 
implementing a scheme for arranging supply of yam to handloom weavers, at 
the prices at which it is available at the mill gate. This scheme is 
implemented throughout  the country. 
(b) The aforesaid scheme is im plemented through the National 
Handloom Development Corporation Ltd. (NHDC), a Central Public Sector 
Undertaking. Under the scheme NHDC makes available all types of yam 
required by handloom weavers and their organizations against indents, at the 
price at which the yarn is available at the mill gate i.e. the place of 
manufacturing. Hence, the weavers do  not have to bear the cost of 
transportation from the spinning mills. Thus, the yam becomes generally 
more affordable than if purchased from the local market. Under the scheme, 
NHDC has supplied 55.68 lakh kg yam worth Rs. 6265.40 lakh in Andhra 
Pradesh in the years 1995-96 to 2001-02 (up to February, 2002.)

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
V. DHANANJAY KUMAR): (a) to (c) Re view of the actions initiated in 
implementation of the National Textile Policy, 2000 is a continuing exercise 
and has been done from time to time. 
Since the announcement of the Policy, the following main initiatives 
have been taken: 
• formulation of new schemes namely, Apparel Parks for Exports Scheme 
and Textile Centres Infrastructure Development Scheme;

Scheme announced in April, 1999, Cotton Technology Mission 
announced in February, 2000 and initiation of new programmes namely, 
modernization of the weaving sector by induction of 50,000 shuttleless 
looms and induction of 2.5 lakh semi automatic/ automatic looms in the 
decentralized powerloom industry; 
• Policy changes, namely, dereservation of the garment sector, raising of 
SSI limit of investment in knitwear industry to Rs. 5 crore; 
• Changes and concessions in the duty and tariff structures to support 
modernization and growth and investment, announced in the budget; 
• Liberalization of quota measures etc.

RE. COMMEMORATION OF THE CENTENARY YEAR OF 
ANUSHILAN SAMITI 
Matter raised with permission of the Chair 
. MR. CHAIRMAN: Shri Manoj Bhattacharya. 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA (West Bengal): Sir, the Anushilan 
Samiti, the organisation of the devout revolutionary freedom fighters of our 
country, was formed in a meeting on 23 rd and 24 th March, 1902, in Calcutta, 
the then epicentre of revolutionary armed struggle against the inhuman British 
rule. 
156 

[24 APRIL, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
This is the centenar y year of this great organisation, which 
contributed immensely to the freedom st ruggle of ours and fought relentlessly 
against the most brutal atrocities of tyrannical imperialism. This organisation 
was founded by none other than Deshbandhu Chittaranjan Das, Sri Arobinda 
(Ghosh), Pramatha Nath Mitra, Surendranath Banerjee and others. 
Sir, the Anushilan Samiti was the pioneer organisation which could 
consciously promote revolutionism a nd emancipation of the common people 
from the yoke of subhuman socio-econ omic and political situation under the 
British colonial rule. Against all possible and impossible odds, the organisation 
could garner formidable strength in entire Northern India and Maharashtra, 
through the Gadar Party, the Hindustan Republican Army, later the Hindustan 
Socialist Republican Army of the great Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, 
Chandrasekhar Azad, Ramprasad Bismil, Asfaqulla, et al., who laid down their 
precious lives for our dear nation. We  can never forget the chanting of 
'Inquilab Zindabad' by the great martyr Bhagat Singh. The great 
revolutionaries of Uttar Pradesh, to name a few Jogesh Chatterjee, Rajen 
Lahiri and Jatin Das, Maharaj Trailokaya Chakaraborty, Masterda Surya Sen, 
Pulin Das. et al. of Bengal were very actively involved in building this 
organisation. This organisation, way back during the first decade of the last 
century, gave a clarion call for emanc ipation of the peasants and toiling 
millions, through mass actions against colonialism. 
We must remember that the founder  of the great Indian National 
Army, the Azad Hind Fauj, that led the armed action against the British rule, 
was none other than the legendary Rashbehari Bose who had been the main 
organiser of the Anushilan Samiti for a long time before he was forced to 
choose a life in exile. In fact, the revolutionary upheaval against the tyranny of 
colonialism shook the entire British Empire. Thousands of brave young men 
and women sacrificed their lives, unsung and unwept. Many consciously 
concealed their identity even before thei r death for the noble cause of their 
ideals. The dreams of these great patrio ts could not be realised even till this 
day. Their lives were their ideals and those are worth emulating, particularly, at 
this hour of national crisis, when t he most dreaded force of communalism is 
out with its fangs open in Gujarat an d elsewhere, the most ugly divisive 
terrorist forces are haunting the entire  nation, particularly, in Jammu and 
Kashmir and in the North-Eastern States. 
Sir, I, on behalf of my party, the Revolutionary Socialist Party, urge 
upon the Government of India to commemorate the centenary year of the 
157 

RAJYA SABHA [24 APRIL, 2002]  
Anushilan Samiti with gaiety, and immediately release a commemorative 
postal stamp on this auspicious occasion. 
SHRI T.N. CHATURVEDI (Uttar Pradesh): Sir, I rise to associate myself with the 
Special Mention of my hon. colleague. The Anushilan Samiti spread the 
revolutionary movement in the country. The heroes of this body have carved out a 
niche for themselves in the history and it is time for us to remember them and issue 
a commemoration. It will be a great inspiration for the generations to come.

SPECIAL MENTION 
Steep Hike in Passport Fee 
SHRI M.P. ABDUSSAMAD SAMADANI (Kerala): Sir, I draw the 
attention of the House to a situation created by the increase in the passport 
fee. The sudden and large increase in the fee for the issuance of the passport 
has dealt a serious blow to the numberless job-seeking young people of the 
country. People are compelled to go abroad mainly for job opportunities. The 
majority of the people travel to the fo reign countries, not for sight-seeing and 
tourism. They leave their families, paren ts and children, in search of some 
employment for their sustenance. The Government's decision to increase the 
passport fee has somehow burdened the unemployed citizens of the country. 
The majority of the people travel abroad because of the serious unemployment 
problem here. The Government is not abl e to provide job opportunities for its 
young generation. What right such a Government has to exploit the poor 
unemployed citizens who intend to go abroad seeking a path for their 
livelihood? Most of those who travel abroad for employment belong to the 
middle class and the poorest sections of  the society. The numberless families 
are living in our country and they depend upon the income from their members 
who work abroad. Why is the Governm ent closing this door of seeking job 
opportunities for its own citizens? It is  nothing but cruel. Those Indians who 
work abroad contribute to a great extent to the national exchequer, through 
foreign exchange. It is not fair to harass them by every means; some times by 
an increase in the 
158 

[24 APRIL, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
passport fee and some times by an incr ease in the airfare. I, therefore, 
request the Government to withdraw this, at the earliest. Thank you.

Protection of material evidence 
SHRI K. B. KRISHNA MURTHY (K arnataka): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I 
wish to state the dispensation of crim inal justice in our country has reached a 
dismal level. The conviction rates in our criminal courts are only 6 per cent. My 
focus in today's Special Mention is with regard to the criminal trial of dons and 
kingpins of organised crime, who thrive on a criminal network and when they 
are arrested for heinous offences and pu t to criminal trial the prosecution 
witnesses are terrorised by the associates of the accused and the witness 
turns hostile and the accused is acquitted. 
159 

RAJYA SABHA [24 APRIL, 2002]  
My suggestion to the Government is that it enacts special laws, which 
may be used in rare cases when the State is prosecuting dangerous criminals. 
I would suggest that this law be called the Protection of Material Evidence Act. 
The legislative intent of this Act would be that in sensitive cases the 
Government should identify important prosecution witness and if in their 
opinion a conviction can be recorded on his testimony by the court of law, he 
should be taken into protective custody before the trial and be given necessary 
protection so that he may truthfully depose in the court without being subject to 
coercion, duress and after the material  witness delivers the testimony he 
should be given protection for a prescribed period, to save him from any 
retribution by the accused or his associates. It is my profound hope that if 
protection is given to a material witness pre and post criminal trial, the ends of 
justice can be met. Thank you. 
Need to set up an international airport with night landing facilities 
at Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Chairman, Sir, 
Visakhapatnam is one of the most developed industrial cities in Andhra 
Pradesh. There are a large number of in dustrial units in Visakhapatnam such 
as Hindustan Shipyards Ltd., petroleum refinery, Visakhapatnam Port Trust, 
Dredging Corporation Ltd. and Visakhapatnam Steel Plant. Besides these, 
other industries are coming up in this area and the city is developing rapidly. 
In spite of the importance of Visa khapatnam, unfortunately, there are 
very poor airport facilities and it also does not have a night landing facilities. 
There is a need to increase the length of the runway at the existing airport for 
landing of larger aircraft. 
In view of the liberalisation of economic policies of the Government of 
India and the keen interest shown by t he foreign investors in establishing the 
industrial units and also thrust on exports and imports through Visakhapatnam 
Port, there is an urgent need for having an international airport at 
Visakhapatnam. 
This issue was raised by me in the Lok Sabha on 28.5.98 and the 
then Minister for Civil Aviation on 27 trv January, 1999, had communicated that 
a High Level Committee to study the possibility of upgrading Visakhapatnam 
airport for AB.320 class of aircraft in all weather conditions was taken up by 
the Government. 
160 

[24 APRIL, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
In view of the above, the Government must take a final decision on 
this issue of setting up an international airport and night landing facilities at 
Visakhapatnam  early.  Thank you.

RAJYA SABHA [24 APRIL. 2002] 
Indian Railways are the lifeline of the nation. They have been prime 
movers to the economy and the society of the Indian sub-continent. It has the 
distinction and pride of being one of the largest railway systems in the world. In 
the process, Railways have become the symbol of our integration and strategic 
instrument for enhancing the country's defence preparedness. Indian Railways 
occupy a place of pride in the growth and development of the nation. 
The Railway network has 63,028 kms. covering 6,853 railway 
stations. It is transporting about 30 m illion passengers and more than one MT 
of freight daily with the help of 1.5 million employees. The assets of the 
Railways are now Rs.63,341 crores. I am sorry to say that the railway lines are 
not given equally to all the States. If you go through the details, we will see 
that the increase in route length bet ween 1999-2000 was only 0.6%. That 
means, while we say that Railways are completing 150 years of its existence, 
we have not been able to provide to all States, at least, the block 
headquarters. In some States like Arun achal Pradesh, which has one km. of 
rail track, Jammu and Kashmir has 96 kms. of rail track, Manipur has 1 km, 
Mizoram has 2 kms, Nagaland has 13 kms; Tripura has 45 kms, Uttaranchal 
has 356 kms, Jharkhand has 1,797 kms, Delhi has 200 kms; Kerala, Himachal 
Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, also got very less share in rail tracks. I don't want to 
name the States which have got more railway lines for various reasons. Only a 
small number of big States  have the lion's share in the railway lines. I suggest 
that this Government should also take a rational decision so that other States, 
who don't have railway lines also get equal share in the railway facilities. 
The money allocated, at present, to the new railway lines is very 
much negligible and it is not according to the requirement. Now the railway 
expenditure is based on two principles : one, the State popul ation, two, the 
revenue generation on the existing railway lines. Both the principles will help 
only the developed States to get more share in the Railway Budget and not the 
backward States. It will not help the backward States where there is no railway 
line, where comparatively the population is small. This will also increase the 
regional imbalance and serious disc ontentment will be there among the 
backward and under-developed States. 
Even accepting the same principle, the Government has completely 
failed to fulfil the hopes and aspirations of the people of the country so far as 
the railways are concerned. As we al l know, ports, railways, transport and 
railway lines are the main infrastructure for attracting investments and

[24 APRIL, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
for setting up of industries. Unless and until ports are developed, and the 
railway lines are connected from the mining areas or industries to the ports, 
our country can't attract investment. I can cite one glaring example from 
Orissa. The Surface Transport Ministry, t he Government of India, the Paradip 
Port and the Railways signed an agreement with the Asian Development Bank 
to get Rs. 700 crores to mechanise the coal handling plant at Paradip, which 
would facilitate for exporting 10 MT of coal per year. The coal handling plant 
has been completed two years ago, but the railways are not able to complete 
the developing work from Talcher to Paradip via Cuttack with two bridges over 
Mahanadi and Birupa. As a result, the target of coal export could not be 
achieved. Hence, the Government is lo sing thousands of crores of rupees, 
both in railways and surface transport. 
In the same way, Haridaspur railway line, Jhakhapur Bansapani 
railway line, Talcher Bimlagarh railway line and Angul Sukinda railway line 
were started for transporting the mining ore from mining head to the Paradip 
Port. Another new railway line from Jajpur Kendujhar railway station to 
Dhamra Port via Jajpur and Aradi was st arted. These proposals, if completed, 
could have earned more money in crores and would have been helpful for 
generating internal resources. But, unfortunately, neither of these railway lines 
is completed nor the Dhamra Port or Gopalpur Port is developed. Even the 
Novapada Gunpur and the Bangrip'osi narrow gauge could not be converted 
into broad gauge. As a result of which, Orissa. which was expecting Rs. 
1,30.000 crores investmen t, could not get even a sing le rupee investment in 
these years. Because of non-completion of the Novapada Gunpur line and 
because of the non-conversion of Bangr iposi narrow gauge into broad gauge, 
the local Tribals are being compelled to sell their produce at lower prices. As a 
result, the Naxalite movement, PWG movements are very much prevalent in 
Koraput and Raigarh areas. 
In the Railway Budget, this year, more allocation has been made to 
seven newly-created Railway Zones, including the East-Coast Zone, Orissa, 
which has got only Rs.4 crores. 
I must thank the hon,. Minister for this. The Prime Minister had 
inaugurated this zone but it is only no w that after being pressurised by the 
people of Orissa and the Government of  Orissa, the hon. Minister has given 
Rs.4 crores. But this has been done without notifying the zone which is very 
much required. When the money is being given to the East-coast Zone, I 
would like the hon. Minister to inform this House whether this zone has been 
notified. The first thing that I would like to know from the hon.

Minister is that whether this zone, wh ich was inaugurated three years back by 
no less than the Prime Minister himself, it has been notified. These zones 
should be completed immediately taki ng Khurda, Chakardharpur, Sambalpur,

division. 
The construction of new lines, doubling lines, progressing gauge 
conversion, accretion of electrified routes, track renewals are also not 
satisfactory. The share of the Railways in the total Plan Outlay has also been

you see the share of Railways in the total Plan Outlay, you will see that in the 
First Plan the share was 11.1 per cent an d in the Ninth Plan it has come down 
to 5.3 per cent. It has been reduced drastically. When we approve the

expenditure was even 40 per cent or 50 pe r cent higher, the job was done in a

the amount rather than actually spending it. In two cases, i.e., in the construction

that he has brought to my notice and act upon them.

*484. DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to do away with the Centrally 
sponsored Integrated Development of Small and Medium Towns (IDSMT) 
scheme; 
(b) whether this scheme was launched in the year 1979-80; 
(c) whether the CAG Report in March, 2001, had criticised Government 
for the scheme's failure to achieve its objectives; 
(d) whether Government have repl aced this with the State Pooled 
Financing Mechanism; and 
(e) the reasons for failure of IDSMT scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION (SHRI ANANTH KUMAR): (a) to (e)A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) No, Sir. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) to (e)The Comptroller & Auditor General (CAG) in its Report No. 2 of 
2002 for the year ended 31 st March, 2002 has observed inadequate coverage of 
towns under the Integrated Development of Small and Medium Towns (IDSMT) 
Scheme, non-satisfactory project execution, non-availability of financial 
resources, etc. 
The Pooled Finance Development Fund (PFDF) has been conceived as a 
State Pooled Financing Mechanism and is not a replacement of the IDSMT 
Scheme. It seeks to enable a group of small and medium urban local bodies to

Statement

per cent in the budget for the year 2002-2003, along with the peak

retained at 25 per cent 
(iii) In addition, the items will attract applicable rate of 
countervailing duty, i.e. duty equal to the Central excise duty 
leviable on such items if domestically manufactured, plus 4 per 
cent Special Additional Duty of customs (SAD).

OFFICE MEMORANDUM 
Subject:   Guidelines for qualification of Bidders seeking to acquire stakes in 
Public Sector Enterprises through the process of disinvestment 
Government has examined the issu e of framing comprehensive and 
transparent guidelines defining the crite ria for bidders interested in PSE 
disinvestment so that the parties selected through competitive bidding could 
inspire public confidence. Earlier, criteria like net worth, experience etc. used 
to be prescribed. Based on experience and inconsultation with concerned 
departments, Government has decided to prescrible the following additional 
criteria for the qualification / disqualification of the parties seeking to acquire 
stakes in Public Sector Enterprises through disinvestment:—  
(a) In regard to matters other then the security and integrity of the country, 
any conviction by a Court of Law or indictment / adverse order by a regulatory 
authority that casts a doubt on the ability of the bidder to manage the public 
sector unit when it is disinvested, or which relates to grave offence would 
constitute disqualification. Grave offence is defined to be of such a nature that 
it outrages the moral sense the community. The decision in regard to the nature 
of the offence would be taken on case to case basis after considering the facts of 
the case and relevant legal principles, by the Government. 
(b) In regard to matters relating to the security and integrity of the country, 
any charge-sheet by an agency of the Government / conviction by a Court of 
Law for an offence committed by the bidding party or by any sister concern of 
the bidding party would result in disqualification. The decision in regard to the 
relationship between the sister concerns would be taken, based on the relevant 
facts and after examining whether the two concerns are substantially controlled 
by the same person / persons.

Government deems appropriate.

disinvestment process, would not be allowed to remain associated with it or get 
associated merely because it has preferred an appeal against the order based on 
which it has been disqualified. The mere pendency of appeal will have no 
effect on the disqualification. 
(e) The disqualification criteria would come into effect immediately and 
would apply to all bidders for various disinvestment transactions, which have 
not been completed as yet. 
(f) Before disqualifying a concern, a Show Cause Notice why it should not 
be disqualified would be issued to it and it would be given an opportunity to 
explain its position. 
(g) Henceforth, these criteria will be  prescribed in the advertisements 
seeking Expression of Interest (EOl) from the interested parties. The interested 
parties would be required to provide the information on the above criteria, along 
with their Expressions of Interest (EOl). The bidders shall be required to provide

authority is pending against them. In case any investigation is pending against 
the concern or its sister concern or ag ainst its CEO or any of its Directors / 
Managers / employees, full details of such investigation including the name of 
the investigating agency, the charge / offence for which the investigation has 
been launched, name and designation of persons against whom the investigation 
has been launched and other relevant in formation should be disclosed, to the

Applications for permission for clinical trials, Bio-equivalence studies 
and marketing of new drugs are examined by the New Drug Division in the 
office of DCG (I). The requirement for granting such approval are specified in 
Rules 122A, 122B, 122C, 122D and 122E and Schedule Y of Drugs and 
Cosmetics Rules. The evaluation of new drug/clinical trial is a complex process 
and varies according to the nature of molecule drug, published data and 
information furnished by applicants. Therefore, depending upon the nature of 
the application, it may take on an averag e more than 5 years for approval of 
investigation New Drug (i.e. a drug molecule not tested on human being 
anywhere in the world) about 1—3 years for the first time approval of the drug 
already approved elsewhere but requiring confirmatory clinical trial and about 
2-3 months for subsequent applications for already approved drugs. This is, 
however, subject to submission of all required data as per provisions of Schedule 
Y of Drug and Cosmetics Rule s. Certain critical drugs e.g. anti-cancer, anti-
HIV etc. which are important from the point of view of public health are also 
cleared on a fast track basis. Permissions are granted after taking into account 
the technical requirements and not on discretion.

56 

[29 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) the number of leprosy cases in the country; and 
(d) by when the country could achieve elimination of the disease? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b)The Government of India is 
implementing the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) in all the 
States/UTs for the elimination of Leprosy. 
National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) is a 100% Centrally 
sponsored scheme with the objective of achieving the elimination of leprosy i.e. 
prevalence Rate of less than 1 case per 10,000 population, at national level, by 
March, 2004. 
The details of the Programme are:— 
(i) Decentralization and Institutional Development under which State 
Leprosy Societies have been formed in 27 major States and District 
Leprosy Societies in all the original 557 districts in the country. 
(ii)  Integration of Leprosy services with General Health Care. 
(iii) Two rounds of Modified Leprosy Elimination Campaigns (MLEC) 
for case detection throughout the country during 2001-02 and 
2002-03. 
(iv) Early Leprosy Case Detection and Free Multi Drug Therapy to all 
patients. 
(v) Special Action Projects for elimination of Leprosy (SAPEL) and 
Leprosy Elimination Campaign (LEC) for difficult/inaccessible/ 
under served Rural and Urban areas, respectively. 
(vi) Intensified Public Awareness Campaigns. 
(vii) Training of Health Staffiri disability prevention and care. 
(viii) Training of General Health Care Staff in Leprosy. 
(c) The number of leprosy patients in the country as per reports received 
till 31 st March, 2002, is 4.92 lakhs. 
(d) Government of India is aiming to achieve the elimination of leprosy by 
March, 2004.
