And, regarding the Agricultural  Bill and other Welfare Bills, I 
know, in my State, Kerala, there are 14 welfare fund schemes, say, 
the Construction Workers Welfare Fund, Agricultural Workers Welfare 
fund, etc., covering various unor ganised sector. But there is no 
financial commitment from the Government. So, the Union 
Government will have to formulate l egislations so as to protect the 
welfare of the workforce. Sir, I am concluding with this point that the 
labour force, the working class in I ndia, is not satisfied. They have no 
peace of mind because of the new economic reforms and labour 
reforms. A country like India cannot  achieve progress when it has a 
discontented working class. Therefore, I would once again urge upon 
the Government to kindly re-consider the labour reforms so that the 
labour is protected in this country and the country is able to achieve 
more progress.

THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Irrigation being a State subject, the responsibility of planning, 
investigation, funding alongwith priority, execution, operation and 
maintenance of irrigation projects (including lift irrigation projects) as also 
flood control and drainage projects primarily rests with the concerned State 
Governments themselves. Minor irrigation lift schemes and major and medium lift 
schemes on Intra-State rivers do not require techno-economic appraisal in the 
Central Water Commission. 
Detailed Project Reports of 8 major and 6 medium lift irrigation schemes on 
inter-State rivers have been submitted by various State Governments for techno-
economic appraisal in the Central Water Commission and are under 
correspondence with them. The details are given in the enclosed Statement 
(See below) 
The Government of Rajasthan had formulated project proposal namely, 
Indira Lift Irrigation Scheme (major) for providing irrigation facilities in Sawai 
Madhopur and Karoli Districts by lifting water from Chambal and submitted to 
Central Water Commission in June, 2000  for techno-economic appraisal. The 
project was considered by the

to:

from Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Karn ataka, Goa, Delhi, All India Kisan

(c) and (d) India is a founder member of the WTO which came into being 
on 1.1.1995 as a successor to the Gene ral Agreement on Tariffs and Trade 
1947 (GATT), of which also India was a founder member. WTO provides a 
predictable rule based multilateral trading system. 
While the Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) has not constrained India's 
domestic policy options for agricultural and rural development, experience 
in implementation of the same has brought out a  number of issues,  which  
deserve  rebalancing.  These  have 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
45 

RAJYA SABHA [30 April, 2002] 
already been flagged by India in its comprehensive proposals submitted in 
WTO. The Indian proposals aim at protecting its food and livelihood security 
and for creating opportunities for the exports of its agricultural surpluses 
while targeting the high tariffs and trade distorting domestic support and 
export subsidies of the developed countries. Further in the Doha Ministerial 
Declaration also the key concerns of India in agriculture have been adequately 
safeguarded. Special and differential treatment for developing countries 
including recognition of food security and rural development has now 
become an integral part of the mandated negotiations on agriculture. 
As regards the fluctuation in prices of agricultural commodities it may be 
noted that prices arc a function of demand and supply factors as well as other 
macro-economic indicators. It will thus not be correct to attribute, in general, 
the decline or rise in prices of agricultural products to any one factor. 
The wholesale prices of different agricultural commodities have shown a 
mixed trend with domestic prices for wheat, jowar, bajra, ragi, maize, 
moong, gram, masoor and edible oils witnessing an increase. Commodities-
like rice, barley, urad, arhar, sugar and cotton have registered a decline in the 
past one year. Government is constantly monitoring the imports of sensitive 
commodities and acting to protect the interests of both the consumers and 
producers. 
In order to ensure that Indian producers including the Small Scale Industries 
are not put to any hardship, the Government have put in place a suitable 
mechanism for monitoring of the imports of sensitive items and are committed 
to providing adequate protection to the domestic producers by resorting to 
various WTO compatible measures whic h include appropriate calibration of 
applied tariffs within the bound tariffs, imposition of anti-dumping, 
countervailing duties and safeguard action under certain specified 
circumstances.

THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a)As per the information received from the States so far, 3596 large 
dams have been constructed and 695 large dams are under construction. As a 
result of this, a live storage capacity of 177 Billion Cubic Metre (BCM) has 
been created. An additional live stages capacity of 75 BCM will be created 
on completion of dams which are under various stages of construction. Besides, 
about 3,76,000 tanks (minor dams) and ponds have also been constructed in the

(b) and (c) Silting of reservoirs is a natural phenomena and provision for 
consequent loss of storage is made at the planning stage itself. It has been 
assessed from the data of capacity survey of 144 reservoirs in the country that 
the weighted average loss of live storage in these reservoirs is around 0.31 per 
cent per year. Capacity surveys of 15 reservoirs got conducted by Central 
Water Commission has indicated that there is no reduction in the useful life 
of these reservoirs due to siltation. 
(d) and (c) In order to augment the av ailability of water for various uses 
and their efficient use, schemes arc planned, investigated, formulated, 
implemented and funded by the State Governments out of their own 
resources and as per their own priorities. The Time by which the schemes arc 
to be completed is depedent on the priority

47 

RAJYA SABHA [30 April, 2002] 
assigned to such schemes by the State Government and the resources 
made available for these schemes. To help the State Governments in 
their efforts to harness the water from natural resources and 
accelerate creation of irrigation potential by early completion of 
ongoing schemes, Government of  India has launched Accelerated 
Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP) since 1996-97. Under the 
programme, financial assistance in form of central loan is being 
extended to State Governments to help them complete the ongoing 
irrigation projects in a time bound manner so that the benefits could 
accrue at the earliest. Accordingly,  the Central Loan Assistance 
(CLA) amounting to Rs. 8480 crore to the State Governments have  been provided 
under AIBP upto the end of 2001-02. An outlay of 
Rs. 2800 crore has been provided for the year 2002-03. Additional 
irrigation potential of over one mi llion hectare upto the end of 
March, 2002 has been created under AIBP. Assistance is also being 
extended to State Governments under Command Area Development 
(CAD) Programme for bridging th e gap between potential created 
and utilised. A expenditure of Rs. 764.15 crore has been incurred 
during Ninth Five Year Plan under CAD programme and an outlay 
of Rs. 202 crore has been proposed for the year 2002-03. 
Government of India is also promoting rain water harvesting through 
Watershed Management Programme, artificial recharge of ground 
water and roof-top rain water harvesting under the sector reform 
project of Accelerated Rural Wa ter Supply Programme under the 
Ministry of Rural Development, for which technical and financial 
assistance is provided to the State Governments and other 
implementing agencies. Central Ground Water Board has also taken 
up a Central Sector Scheme on "Studies of Recharge to Ground 
Water" on pilot basis. For meeting future requirements of water, as a 
long   term   measure,   National   Water   Development   Agency   has   formulated 
National Perspective Plan for water resources 
development which envisages interlinking various Peninsular rivers 
and Himalayan rivers for transfer of water from surplus basins to  water deficit 
basins.

THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SYED SHAHNAWAZ 
HUSSAIN): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) According to the Committee of Inquiry, set up to investigate the cause 
of the accident, this mishap occurred due to the fact that 
56 

[30 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
the pilot while flying through active thunder storm at cruise altitude encountered 
severe updrafts in intense and mature cloud formation and possibly underwent and 
abnormal and abrupt manoeuvre, most probably a steep spiral dive, resulting in 
inflight breakage of the aircraft structure on account of aerodynamic overloads 
leading to total loss of controls followed with heavy impacts with the ground 
causing fatal injuries to all the occupants. The Committee has made 11 
recommendations, details of which arc available in the Statement (See below). 
(c) Action is in progress to implement the recommendations made by the 
Committee of Inquiry. A Task Force has been constituted by the Government to 
monitor implementation of the recommendations. 
Statement 
Recommendations of the Inquiry Committee on Accident of King Air C-90 
Aircraft VT-EFF near Mainpuri 
1. Installation of CVR or a combination of both CVR/FDR should be made 
mandatory on small twin engine general aviation aircraft where 
supplementary type certificate by the manufacturer on modification by an 
organization approved by the regulatory authority is available. 
2. Where information for installation is available either in the form of duly 
approved STC by the manufacturer or a modification leaflet by an approved 
agency, all twin engine aircraft equipped to fly in IMC and/or night 
operations should mandatorily be installed with coloured weather radar. 
3. Considering the age of the ill-fated C-90 Aircraft Reg. No. VT-EFF and the 
fact that during the preceding 12 months only one snag had been reported 
was that of the ATC transponder. It is apparent that the practice of snags 
reporting is not being observed. The reporting and the rectification of 
snags for general aviation aircraft needs to be reviewed and reinforced. 
57 

RAJYA SABHA [30 April, 2002] 
4. The provision of designating on accountable manager as envisaged in 
the CAR should be extended to general aviation organizations with a 
view to make surveillance and safety audit checks more objective and 
meaningful. 
5. Enhanced surveillance of approved maintenance organizations for 
adequacy of required infrastructure as against the specific approved 
scope of maintenance needs to be  enforced to ensure that the 
infrastructure standards are maintained on a continual basis. The 
procurement documents should be made available for auditing by 
such organizations to the regulatory authority. 
6. The requirement of conducting test flight for renewal of Certificate of 
Airworthiness be mandated for aging general aviation aircraft. 
7. Pilots and engineering personnel associated with general aviation 
organizations should undergo periodic classroom and practical training 
at any institute of repute duly approved by the DGCA. 
8. On aircraft equipped with adva nced avionics like GPWS, TCAS, 
ATC transponder, FMS, coloured weather radar etc. the operators 
should ensure initial and periodic recurrent training for pilots and 
engineering personnel for affective man-machine interface. 
9. The Flight Inspection Directorate of the DGCA should have dedicated 
flight inspectors for general aviation aircraft. In the event that adequate 
expertise is not available, the services of experienced 
retired/superannuated pilots from the industry may be utilized on 
contractual basis. In case if expertise is still not forthcoming, 
deputation from defence services may be considered. 
10. The Committee felt that since whether has played significant 
contributory role in the accident, it is recommended that in general 
aviation before exercising the privileges of their licenses, all new 
Captains in their first monsoon seasons should undergo monsoon/bad 
weather operations training with an approved organization. They 
should also undergo a proficiency 

[30 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
check with a approved examiner in structor in actual weather. All 
existing captains must also undergo similar training and checks 
within a stipulated time-frame. 
11. The Committee having gone through the details of the weather briefing 
made available to the pilot before departure feels that the 
meteorological briefing at airports needs considerable improvement. 
The infrared and visible satellite pictures by themselves do not give 
the precise picture, but when the two are compared and plotted 
together on a single chart by the met officer will give a more accurate 
representation of the prevailing weather conditions. The satellite 
pictures arc on a black and white monitor wihout a back up and 
imageries are available every three hours with the delay of one hour. 
The satellite imageries vis-a-vis a route forecast is more accurate and 
factual position of weather than a forecast. The Committee therefore 
recommends that the satellite imageries be made available hourly in 
colour including imageries from all available sources in adverse 
weather. A proper briefing on these imageries with trends should be 
covered by the briefing officer.

Liberalisation of housing loans 
3727. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the housing sector has got a boost after many financial institutions 
have liberalised housing loans in the country; 
(b) if so, whether all the banks and other financial institutions have decided to 
provide loans upto Rs. 1 crore with negligible processing charges; 
(c) if so, to what extent the rates have been reduced; 
(d) whether this reduction of rates has given a boost to the housing development 
in the country; and 
(e) if so, to what extent the liberalisation norms has helped the poor and the

138 

[30 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Reserve Bank of India 
issued instructions to all commercial banks perscribing the annual allocation 
limit for housing finance. Accordingly, each bank is required to compute its 
share of the housing finance allocati on at 3 per cent of its incremental 
deposits. There is no objection to banks exceeding this level having regard to 
their resources position. According to the information furnished by National 
Housing Bank (NHB) the processing fees charged by banks are negligible, 
not exceeding 1 per cent of the loan amount and it is a one time payment. 
However, in most of the cases it is in the range of 0.1 per cent to 0.5 per cent 
and in certain cases it is waived complete ly as an incentive especially during 
festive seasons. Similarly, most of th e housing finance companies have also 
reduced the processing fee from an aver age range of 1.50 per cent 2.00 per 
cent to 0.5 per cent 1.00 per cent. A few HFCs have even waived the 
processing fees completely. 
(c) to (e) The lending rates of banks from time to time are governed by the 
directives on interest rate issued by RBI. As per extant guidelines the interest 
on loans upto Rs. 2 lakh should not exceed Prime Lending Rate (PLR) of the 
bank and beyond Rs. 2 lakhs, banks are free to charge rates over PLR but 
within the maximum spread fixed by bank. There has been reduction in 
PLRs of banks following reduction in Bank Rate and Cash Reserve Ratio by 
RBI. The reduction in the processing fees and rates of interest coupled with 
options of floating rates and increase in the tenure of the loan has enabled the 
common people to access the formal financial sector for assistance at a much 
more affordable rates. This

Clearance of Stock Market Defaulters by Appellate Tribunal 
3729. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that certain entities which had been found guilty of 
rigging of share prices in the stock ma rket by SEBI have been subsequently

(c) whether the Tribunal striking of full SEBI orders consisted of one 
member benches; 
141 

RAJYA SABHA [30 April, 2002]

BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) after 
investigation found certain companies viz., BPL Ltd., Sterlite Industries Ltd., 
Videocon Industries Ltd. and their promoters guilty of indulging in price 
manipulation in the scrips of their own companies on Bombay Stock 
Exchange and therefore debarred all these companies and directed initiation 
of prosecution against the Directors of these comp anies. These companies 
and their promoters filed appeals be fore Securities Appellate Tribunal 
(SAT). SAT in the matter of appeal f iled by Sterlite Industries has struck 
down SEBI orders and has held that power of Section 11 B is only remedial 
and cannot be used to penalise. 
(c) Section 15 K of the SEBI Act, 1992 provides that the Central 
Government shall by notification establish one or more Securities Appellate 
Tribunals. Section 15 L prescribes that  a Securities Appellate Tribunal shall 
consist of only one person (to be referred to as the Presiding Officer of the 
SAT) to be appointed by notification, by the Central Government. 
(d) and (e) These provisions of SEBI Act, 1992 do not violate any quasi-
judicial principles.

Fraud in Oriental Bank of Commerce, Panipat 
3734. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether a fraud was reported in Or iental Bank of Commerce, Panipat 
regarding their letter of credit No. 253/99 for US $285000/-; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the bank failed to handle documents properly 
and acted negligently by not pointing out the major discrepancies in the L/C 
and also misrepresented the facts before appropriate authority; 
(c) if so, the reasons for making haste payment on forged documents and 
putting a huge loss to Government; and 
(d) the steps taken by the Government  against bank officials for their 
negligent act? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) to (d ) No Sir. Oriental Bank of 
Commerce has reported that an import LC for USD 285000/ was opened by 
Panipat Branch on 26.8.1999. The do cuments under LC were received from 
Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank, UAE. The branch pointed out certain 
discrepancies in the documents to the negotiating bank and contacted the 
applicant who accepted all the deficienci es in the documents in writing and 
indicated the same may be conveyed to the beneficiary bank. The bill of 
exchange accepting the documents with all the discrepancies was 
subsequently signed and the acceptan ce was conveyed to the foreign 
negotiating bank. However, before the due date 25.11.1999 the principal 
debtor filed a 
150 

[30 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
case and the Court of Civil Judge, Panipat restrained the bank from making 
payment to the beneficiary. On appeal  the Additional District Judge vacated 
the stay which was again challenged. The litigation between the beneficiary 
and principal debtor continued and on 7.3.2002 the High Court, Chandigarh 
passed an order in favour of beneficiar y. Since the stay was vacated by the 
High Court the negotiating bank sought payment of the LC and the amount 
of US$ 285000 was paid on 26.3.2002. There was no negligence on the part 
of the bank officials and payment was made after the review petition filed by 
the applicant was also dismissed by the court.

wound up on 30.9.2001.

3782. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state:

captioned "Scary summer". Taps dry little underground which appeared in the 
Times of India dated the 21st March, 2002;

(c) the steps proposed to be taken to address the problem of continuously 
depleting table of underground water level as highlighted in the report? 
197 

 
RAJYA SABHA [30 April, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The news-item express concern over  fall in ground water level and 
inadequate water supply in some parts of Delhi in Mehrauli and Najafgarh blocks. 
It is true that decline of 8.35 meters in ground water have been recorded by the 
Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) in Mehrauli and Najafgarh blocks of 
Delhi during 1960—2001. However, in most parts of the alluvial areas of Delhi, 
decline of only 2—6 meters in ground water level has been recorded. 
(c) The Government has taken following steps to check the decline in the 
ground water level in Delhi:—   
(i) Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) has notified South and South 
West district of NCT of Delhi, prohibiting further digging of wells. 
(ii) CGWA has imposed ban on abstraction of ground water resources for sale 
and supply by private agencies/persons from the "Notified areas" except 
Yamuna Flood plain area of NCT of Delhi. 
(ii)Adoption of roof top rain water harvesting system has been made 
mandatory for group housing societies, institutions, schools, hotels, 
industrial establishments and farm houses located in 'notified areas'. 
(iv) CGWB is promoting artificial recharge to ground water in NCT of Delhi by 
financing proposals under its Central Sector Scheme viz. "Studies of 
Recharge to Ground Water" on pilot basis, Besides, the Board has assisted 
various agencies and individuals in preparation of proposals and provided 
technical guidance including design for construction of rain water 
harvesting structures. 
(v) The Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation has 
amended Building Bye-laws, 1983 making provision for water harvesting 
through storing of water run off including rain water in all new buildings on 
plots of 100 square meters and above in Delhf mandatory.

WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the State Government of Andhra Pradesh has formulated Rs. 
216 crores water conservation project to be implemented in 482 water stress 
mandate in 22 districts extending Hyderabad; 
(b) if so, whether these projects would be undertaken with the financial 
assistance of Rs. 151.20 crores from NABARD; 
(c) if so, the total area to be covered; 
(d) whether Government have been urged to provide the remaining funds 
for implementing these projects; and 
(e) if so, by when this project of water conservation is likely to be 
completed in Andhra Pradesh? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (e) As per 
the information received from the Go vernment of Andhra Pradesh, water 
conservation projects costing Rs. 216 crores to be implemented in 22 districts 
(excluding Hyderabad) and to cover an area of 4,70, 607 Ha. has been 
formulated to be taken up with NABARD for financial assistance of Rs. 
151.20 crores. The balance amount is to be met from Food for Work funds. 
The completion of these projects as per Memorandum of Understanding to be 
entered into by the State Government is linked to sanction by NABARD.

Propogation of rain water harvesting 
3788. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether second water convention was recently held in the capital 
depicting the attainment of water harv esting plan in the desert State of 
Rajasthan; 
(b) whether rain water harvesting has en abled the villagers to draw water 
from handpumps in some districts and enabling them to grow two cash crops 
a year; 
222 

[30 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether such plans at Chitrakoot (Madhya Pradesh) have also given 
good results; and 
(d) if so, what steps are being taken by Government to propogate such 
ventures to other needy areas throughout the country so that the villagers 
could reap the benefits of water harvesting? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) The 
Government is not aware of second water convention held in the Capital 
depicting attainment of water harvesitng plan in the desert State of 
Rajasthan. However, the Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) under the 
Ministry of Water Resources has implemented a scheme on "Studies of 
Recharge of Ground Water" on pilot basis during the Ninth Five Year Plan. 
Under this scheme, 18 projects have been approved in Jaipur, Udaipur, Sikar 
and Jhunjhunu districts of Rajasthan.  The demonstration of these schemes 
have proved that the water harvesting schemes are beneficial even in low 
rainfall regions. 
(c) No project has been approved for the district of Chitrakoot in Madhya 
Pradesh under the above pilot scheme. 
(d) Public need to be made aware, mo tivated and involved for successful 
implementation of water harvesting programmes. With a view to popularise 
the water harvesting, the CGWB has approved 174 schemes in various parts of 
the country during Ninth Five Year Plan under the above mentioned pilot 
scheme which has been proposed to be extended during the Tenth Five Year 
Plan with an allocation of Rs. 200.00 crore. 
Conference of National Water Resources Council 
3789. SHRIMATI SAROJ DUBEY: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the National Water Resources Council held a Conference 
presided by the Prime Minister in the first week of April, 2002; 
(b) if so, the main features of the conference; 
(c) whether any consensus has been arrived at the conference; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
223 

RAJYA SABHA [30 April, 2002] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) Yes, Sir. The 
fifth meeting of the National Water Resources Council (NWRC), was held 
under the Chairmanship of Hon'ble Prime Minister on 1st April, 2002 to 
consider the draft revised National Wa ter Policy. In light of the views 
expressed and suggestions made by the members of the Council, certain 
modifications were incorporated in the draft policy with consensus. The 
Revised National Water Policy was adopted and a Resolution to this effect 
was unanimously passed by the Council. The Policy, inter-alia envisages that 
each State should formulate its own State Water Policy backed with an opera-
tional action plan in a time bound manner within a period of two years and 
implement the same in order to achieve the desired objectives as laid down in 
the policy. 
Ground water level In A.P. 
3790. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO:  Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is a severe water crisis in Godavari and Telangana 
regions of Andhia Pradesh on account of scanty rainfall; and 
(b) if so, the measures proposed to save the people from acute water 
shortage in view of rapid depletion of ground water in the affected districts? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) and (b) Water 
being a State subject, measures/initiatives to tackle water shortage are to be 
taken by the concerned State Government. As per information furnished by 
the Government of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana region and Godavari districts 
of the State received defi cit rainfall during the year 2001-2002. Deficit 
rainfall creates deficiency in ground water. 
The Government of Andhra Prades h has launched "Neeru-Meeru" 
programme on a large scale to improve fa cilities of artificial recharge, which 
will reduce the adverse affect of deficit rainfall.

SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Request to ease blanket curbs on borrowing and provide 
assistance of Rs.3000 crores to Tamil Nadu 
SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN (Tam il Nadu): The Tamil Nadu 
Government is facing severe financial crunch, which forced us to open 
this financial year with unpaid liabilities. The Centre has stipulated that 
the State obtain prior permission from the Centre for borrowings of the 
Special Service Vehicles (SPV) wh ich are serviced by the States and 
barred SPV borrowings, which enter the public account and are further 
'on-lent' to the Consolidated Fund of the State. 
Tamil Nadu, which had the third largest percentage of 
unemployment in the country, was forced to prune its Plan outlay for 
2001-2002 by Rs.840 crores. Moreover, the Eleventh Finance 
Commission has recommended reduction in the share of Tamil Nadu 
in the shareable pool of Central reve nues from the previous level set 
by the Tenth Finance Commission. Consequent to this reduction, from 
6.637% to 5.385%, Tamil Nadu will lose Rs. 2,946 crores between 
2000-2005. 
The fiscal condition of the Stat e is aggravated further and we 
suffered a loss of Rs.1,100 crores in the last fiscal year due to the 
Central Government's failure to transfer in full, even the reduced 
devolution. 
Tamil Nadu is a pioneer in the implementation of many welfare 
schemes and developmental programmes. The blanket restriction on 
the powers of the State Governm ents to borrow for developmental 
programmes, at this hour, will hamper the implementation of the 
developmental programmes for the down-trodden. 
I request the Central Government to release an untied grant 
package of Rs.3000 crores and ease blanket curbs on borrowing to 
implement the developmental programmes in the State of Tamil Nadu. 
Thank you.

Relief and rehabilitation of refugees in Kokrajhar, Assam 
SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA (Assam): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I 
am representing Assam, particularly the trouble torn Kokrajhar District 
of Assam. Sir, in the years of 1996 and 1998 two separate incidents of 
ethnic violence occurred in Kokrajhar and Bongaigaon Districts of 
Assam between the Bodos and Adivasis. The reason for which the 
clashes took place was misunderstanding and communal hatred 
created by some anti-national terrorist elements active in the areas of 
Assam and Bhutan border. The age long brotherly relationship and 
peaceful co-existence among various communities has been shattered 
in its worst form. As a result of that, two ethnic clashes, lakhs of 
people have become homeless and presently languishing in the relief 
camps. According to the Government records in total 54 numbers of 
relief camps are there in Kokrajhar District and numbering about 
1,79,872 people from both Bodos and non-Bodos are there in the 
camps. During the last five years, no such, measure of rehabilitation of 
refugees has been taken by the State or the Central Government. 
Around 37 crores of rupees were r equired as rehabilitation grant from 
the Central Government by the State Government. Sir, the situation in 
the area is normal now and rehabilitation process can be started. But a 
large number of refugees are from Reserve Forest and illegal 
encroachers. As per the Supreme Court order, they cannot be allowed 
to re-occupy the forestland. No such policy has been chalked out by 
the same so far. So I urge upon the Central Government to take time 
bound action plan with adequate fundS for the rehabilitation of 
refugees. Thank you.

Water project for Koodankulam Nuclear Project 
PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Chairman. Sir, 
Koodankulam Nuclear Power Plant in Thirunelvelli District of Tamil 
Nadu started the erection work as a joint venture of Indian and 
Russian Governments. The allotment  is 13,000 crores of rupees and 
the estimated production is 2000 MW of power. Enriched uranium will 
be the by-product. This project is a vital one of our country's progress. 
For the success of this scheme good water of large quantity is 
needed. Koodankulam is located in rain shadow region. I learnt that 
they have planned to take water from Pechi Parai Dam in 
Kanyakumari District. Kanyakumari Di strict used to get sufficient rain 
in the southwest monsoon and northeast monsoon. But two-third 
quantum of rainwater goes to sea which could be diverted by 
constructing a dam across Pazhayar in between Suchindram and 
Thamariakulam and lift to Anjugramam and store in a dam. Sufficient 
conducive space is there for constructing dam for storing the good 
water in an elevated placed. Already eleven dams are across 
Pazhayar to feed 13,000 acres of double crop paddy lands. 
The nuclear project authorities plan to take water from Pechi 
Parai Dam constructed a hundred years back, which has to feed 
50,000 acres of paddy crop which is barely sufficient for the irrigation. 
So I request the Government of Indi a to have interaction with experts 
of the project to examine the project of getting water by constructing a 
dam on Pazhayar as specified earlier. I learnt only Rs.100 crores will 
be sufficient for the entire scheme.   I appeal to the Government to 
consider this request.

Misery of Orissa Tribals failure of K.B.K. Plan 
DR. M.N. DAS (Orissa): Sir, my Special Mention relates to the 
poorest of the poor living in our country. The title of my Special 
Mention is: Misery of Orissa tribals - Failure of KBK Plan. Sir, the stark 
face of Indian poverty can be seen  in the Western Orissa's Koraput, 
Bolangir, Kalahandi districts - famo usly known as 'KBK Districts' - 
inhabited mostly by tribal population.  As early as in 1974, the Union 
Government ordered for a comprehensive plan for the development of 
the KBK region. Officers after office rs were appointed to prepare the 
plan, and years passed till the then Prime Minster, Rajiv Gandhi, 
visited the tribal tracts and felt deeply moved at the sufferings of the 
primitive dwellers. As a result, a plan costing Rs. 4,557 crores was 
prepared for roads, water supply, heal th services, education, etc. But, 
most surprisingly, at this distance of time, nobody, either at the Central 
level or at the State level, can actually say how much money was 
released; how much money was received; how much money was 
spent, and for what purpose. One instance will suffice. Only this 
month, in April, 2002, the State Fi nance Minister admitted on the floor 
of the Orissa Assembly that during the last two years, out of the Rs 
140 crores, that were received, only Rs. 3 crores have been spent,   it 
is in public knowledge that in 1998, Rs.

Adverse effects of depiction of violence on Television 
DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY (Nomi nated): Sir, I seek your 
permission to bring to the notice of this House the growing trend of 
media violence, with particular reference to its adverse effect on 
children. Newspapers widely cover s ensational crimes. Directors of 
films prefer to make thriller and horror movies. Television channels 
show violence in many of their programmes. A family with cable 
connection has access to about one hundred television channels. 
Under the provisions of the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) 
Act, permission for cable television operation is given simply through 
registration, and no licence is required. With the changing trends of 
globalisation, access to foreign-based channels has become 
extensive. It is agreed the world over that television violence 
immediately affects the child's behaviour, or, it may manifest some 
years later. While I am a protagoni st of the freedom of speech and 
artistic presentation of soci al facts, I oppose the mode of 
presentation, or, depiction of violence on television. The Centre for 
Advocacy and Research, with the support of UNESCO and UNICEF, 
conducted a study in cities like: De lhi, Lucknow, Kolkata, Ahmedabad 
and Hyderabad. It has revealed growing prevalence of violence in 
television serials. It further disclosed that children are losing their 
childhood in the process. They ar e living and thinking beyond their 
years, involving many risks. Many  countries have initiated effective 
measures to counter it. In America, a National Television Violence 
Study was conducted in collaboration with Universities, Researchers, 
Media Executives, Mental Health Experts and others. I request the

SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN (Maharashtra): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, I stand to oppose the Appropriation (No.3) Bill, - the 
Appropriation Bill amounting to Rs.7,36,000 crores - which has been 
approved by the Lok Sabha and which the Finance Minister wants us 
to sanction. Sir, I oppose this Bill because of the state of the' economy 
which is prevailing under the present NDA Government. It presents a 
sorry state of affairs, beginning with the low GDP growth rate in the 
economy. We were shocked to see the estimates of the Central 
Statistical Organisation, when the growth rate for 2000-01 was scaled 
down to mere a 4 per cent, compared to the previous year's 6.1 per 
cent. Sir, the estimate was scaled down so drastically that one had 
doubts about the credibility of the C entral Government's statistics 
gathering machinery. I understand the Government is proposing to 
reform the whole set-up. But the relia bility of statistics also affects our 
international credibility. It affe cts our credit rating. Now, the 
Government has projected a growth rate of 5.4 per cent for 2001-02. 
But even if this growth rate is scaled down in the final analysis, we do 
not know what is going to happen. The RBI maintains that the growth 
rate will be 5-6 per cent; it can be as low as 5 per cent. And the 
NCAER, the think-tank of Delhi, has projected a growth rate of 4.8 per 
cent; and, this is without factoring certain developments, certain 
negative developments that we all know, have taken place. So, the 
economy, instead of growing at the rate of 8 per cent or 9 per cent, as 
the Prime Minister and the Finance Minister have been telling us, is 
actually down to 4 per cent. 
Sir, the story about the mounting revenue and fiscal deficit is 
equally bad. The revenue deficit which was about 4 per cent in 2001-
02 --when the Congress (I) demitted office in 1996-97, it was as low as 
2.3 per cent. The first deficit - has gone up to 5.7 per cent. It was 
estimated to be 4.7 per cent in t he Budget Estimates but it has gone 
up by 1 whole per cent. Again, we budgeted 5.3 per cent for this year, 
but I do not know whether that figu re will be maintained or, it will, 
probably, overshoot even the 6 per cent mark. There is a revenue 
shortfall. There are signs of the economy slowing down; the economy 
is in recession.    The net revenue 
265 

RAJYA SABHA                [30 APRIL, 2002] 
shortfall last year was over Rs.20,000 crores. The revenue shortfall is 
not just in a particular sector. It is there in personal taxation, customs 
duties, excise duties, everywhere. This revenue shortfall indicates 
clearly that the economy is really  slowing down. Sir, the story of 
industrial growth rate is equally dismal. There has been a tremendous 
slowdown in the industrial growth. We talked of recovery. But there is 
no sign of recovery. Deep recession is before us. From April to 
December, 2001, the industrial growth rate was a mere 2.3 per cent. It 
is the lowest jn a decade. It was 5.8 per cent last year. Compared to 
last year, from 5.8 per cent, we have gone down to 2.3 per cent. 
Again, the advance stat istics given by the CSO indicate an annual 
growth rate of only 3.3%, compared to 6.2% last year. There has been 
a tremendous slow-down. The infrastructure sector, which contributes 
about 27% to the index of industrial  production, has grown only by 2% 
during the period from April, 2001 to November, 2001, compared to 
the previous year's growth rate of 6.4%. The crude oil sector has 
negative growth. The power sector ha s grown barely by 2%. The steel 
sector's growth is almost zero per cent - down to 0.6 per cent growth 
from a growth of 10% last year. The railway freight is down. 
Infrastructure is down. Industrial growth is not picking up. What has 
happened to exports? We all know that  exports are stagnating. And it 
seems that it will be very difficult to meet even the sc aled-down target 
of 3% - scaled down from the 12% ta rget earlier. I think it will be 
difficult even to meet the target of 3% growth. We might even end up 
with a negative growth. The Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy 
expects an export growth rate of ba rely 1.3%. I personally think that 
we may not achieve even that low target. 
Sir, there is drying up of investment. Because of the sorry 
state of Central finances, the plan expenditure is down. If at all the 
plan expenditure is shown to be higher, in real terms, it is either 
negligible, or, even negative, at times. There is no demand in the 
economy. Without a demand push, t he economy will not pick up; the 
industrial growth will not pick up. Local investment is  down. What is 
happening to the FDI? The foreign direct investment figures are also 
negative. From January to November, 2001, according to the 
Government figures, the net FDI was $ 3.7 billion. In the same period 
of 2000, it was 4.5 billion dollars; and in the same period of 1999, it 
was four billion dollars. So, FDI is coming down again. What has 
happened in Gujarat? Everybody whom we have talked to -- the NRIs 
outside, the industry associations, and so on - is gravely concerned 
about foreign investment coming into India.    There is going to be a 
complete 
266 

[30 APRIL, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
drying up of investment, unless the economy revives, unless the 
Gujarat situation is sorted out. There is such a negative feeling all 
over the world about the viability of India as a destination for 
international funds, That foreign so urces of investment are really 
going to dry up. I am not sure if the Finance Minister has seen a 
report of US Government's Organisation, called the OPIC, the 
Overseas Private Investment Corpor ation. It is an organ of the US 
Government. The OPIC has already blacklisted India as a destination 
for American investment.   There was a letter written by the  OPIC to 
the National Security Adviser in November, 2001, very specifically 
threatening that unless a certain project, particularly the Enron 
project, was sorted out to the complete satisfaction of the Enron 
Corporation, there would not be any American investment in India. All 
that is coming here now. We are getting reports from America that 
because of OPIC's assessment and because of whatever has 
happened in Gujarat, there will not be any substantial foreign 
investment coming from America and from the Western world. 
Sir, I talked about the huge revenue shortfall. The tax to GDP 
ratio is coming down. The Finance Bill has substantially modified the 
direct tax proposals. But I do not think it is more than a tinkering. If the 
Finance Minister would recall, his predecessor had launched a major 
exercise to simplify the direct tax code. I remember, the Parliamentary 
Consultative Committee had many sittings to discuss the proposed 
draft Bill for the Direct Tax Code. I think the Finance Minister has given 
up the entire exercise. So much effort had gone into drafting the Direct 
Tax Code to simplify it, but now what we see is, there are 157 clauses 
in the Finance Bill which deal with Direct Tax Code. It is getting more 
and more complicated. The Finance Minister has hit the middle class 
and the salaried class, but he has no political will to go after the huge 
list of defaulters consisting of big companies, corporate sectors and big 
business houses who have defaulted to  the tune of tens of thousands 
of crores of rupees. There has not been big substantial movement in 
this regard. The Finance Minister does take the  credit for simplifying 
the excise duty legislation. But, he is nowhere near achieving the goal 
of full VAT system because the Stat e Governments are not on board. 
There have been a few meetings perfunctorily, but the State 
Governments are completely blank as to how they are going to modify 
their sales tax and octroi laws and how they are going to integrate the 
same with the national laws. I think we are still far away from the 
objective of Value Added Taxation.

Sir, computerisation in the Revenue Department is not 
progressing as fast as it should. Perhaps, there is resentment and 
opposition by the lower level employees. But the Government should 
see to it that all employees are im parted training on computers. There 
is a backlog on imparting training to its employees on computers; 
there is a backlog on computerisat ion; there is still a backlog on 
issuing Permanent Account Numbers. Unless a comprehensive 
Permanent Account Number is given to all the entities who pay tax 
and all of them are cross-checked wi th an All India computer network. 
We will not even be able to cont ain the scourge of black money. I, 
therefore, urge upon the Finance Minister to look at the work done by 
his predecessor in simplifying the Direct Tax Code. He has to come up 
with a very strong policy to get at  the tax arrears and the defaulters 
who are not paying taxes and there has to be a time bound 
programme within which the defaulters will pay their dues. 
Sir, I now come to the critical  area of subsidies. Through the 
Budget, the Finance Minister has tried to reduce the subsidies. He has 
managed to tax only the middle class and the poor people and the 
poor agriculturist. His two main proposals relate to reducing subsidies 
on fertilisers, on LPG and kerosene. Sir, LPG subsidy has been rolled 
back slightly, but there has been no rollback on kerosene. Actually, the 
increase in kerosene price was even higher than the LPG price. The 
Finance Minister has rolled back the LPG price because there was 
pressure from his own party constituents. I appreciate dismantling of 
administered price mechanism in the petroleum sector; and moving 
over to market determined prices. That was a decision taken long 
back. The Finance Minister could have avoided price increase in 
kerosene and LPG by not increasing the Excise Duty from eight per 
cent to 16 per cent CENVAT rate. I think he could have deferred it and 
he need not have to increase the prices of LPG and kerosene which 
are used by poor people. 
The Minister has been able to manage to reduce the fertiliser 
subsidy by about Rs.9,00 crores. Sir, this year, there is a crisis in the 
farm sector and the agriculturists are facing many problems due to 
non-procurement by the Government . The godowns are full of sugar, 
wheat, etc. In such a year, when farmers are committing suicides in 
large numbers, he could have avoided to increase the prices of 
fertilisers. I even appeal to him that when the Finance Bill would be 
taken up for discussion in this House --even though the Finance Bill 
has already been passed by the Lok Sabha -

to reconsider it and not increase the pr ice of fertiliser. We are facing a 
grave agricultural crisis. He has not addressed to the agricultural crisis 
at all. Sir, I remember, in 2000-2001 Budget, the Finance Minister 
delivered a deadly blow to the Public Distribution System by 
increasing the issue price of foodgra ins, meant for consumers living 
Below the Poverty Line. The price of wheat was increased by 68 per 
cent and the price of rice was increased by 50 - 60 per cent. 
What happened? Naturally, the PDS issue price for the BPL 
consumers became higher than the market price, because there was 
already a glut of foodgrains in t he market. Nobody went to the PDS 
shops. The PDS system started collapsing. As a result, the FCI 
godowns are overflowing. It is estimated that by June 2002, the stocks 
in the FCI godowns would start touching 75-80 MT while the food 
security stocks that we need are 18-25 million. What are you going to 
do with this mountain of foodgrains which is rotting? You are not able 
to deliver foodgrains to the people who are starving of hunger. 
Sir, this is the foodgrains crisis before us. If the Government is 
planning not to procure foodgrains at the minimum guaranteed price, 
they are inviting trouble. I think, th ere will be a revolution. It will take 
some time for the Punjab farmers to changeover from wheat and rice 
to alternate crops. They have to be given time. You can't just stop 
procuring foodgrains. This is a serious crisis. The only way out, I think, 
is to find money to give huge expo rt subsidies. The Food-for-Work 
Programme, the Annapoorna Programme and all those programmes 
that you have talked of, would not get food out of this country. The 
food will just go from here to there. The total availability of food will 
remain high. I think, the only way to get rid of the foodgrains is to 
export it at whatever price possible. You have made attempts to 
export foodgrains even below the pric e of what you sell to the poor 
people in the country. You will have to give huge export subsidy to get 
rid of the stocks within the country. Just shifting it from one 
programme to the other would keep the stocks at the same level. By 
this, the crisis is not going to blow over. 
Of course, we need some innovative schemes where food 
actually reaches the poor people. Maybe, you can try food coupons. 
Innovative Food-for-Work Programme s which really work should be 
tried out. The State Governments need to be taken on board. There is 
an impending crisis.

I come from an area which produces sugarcane. There is a 
sugar crisis too. The Minister of State is here and he too comes from 
the same area. The sugar crisis is so grave that sugar stocks in the 
country today are 12 MT, almost two-third of what we need in the 
country, maybe even more than that. Again, the same story, the 
godowns are full. People have kept sugar in the open, under 
tarpaulins. With just one rain, the entire sugar would be wiped out, and 
it would not be fit to be consumed.  What will you do about it? Here, 
again, some innovative schemes to get rid of these stocks and bring 
the stocks to a manageable level, by giving innovative export subsidy,

the agriculture crisis. There is farm  crisis everywhere, in Kerala, in 
Karnataka. Each State has a crisis in a commodity. 
After the WTO regime, when you opened up the farm sector 
for imports, this crisis is getting gr aver. I don't think there is a serious 
attempt. We hear from the Finance Minister is, "A committee had been 
appointed, Food Economy Committee is going to give its report, it has 
given its report, it is being considered." For the last couple of years, 
since we have been hearing about crisis, but nothing is happening on 
the ground. 
Sir, I was talking about subsidies. We need to bring subsidies 
to a manageable level, and we all agree. But subsidies need to be 
targeted. Subsidies, which are going to the richer sections of the 
society have to be removed, and not the subsidies which are going to 
the poorer people. A cut in the fertilizer subsidy, LPG subsidy, and 
kerosene subsidy will hurt poor people the most. The Finance Minister 
has chosen a soft option, by target ing the poor people, who are not 
vocal, who are not an organised class. He has not dared to touch the 
richer sections. 
I come to a few more points which are of grave concern to the 
national economy. One of the points is the grave state of finances of 
the State Governments. 
All the State Governments are facing a huge financial crisis 
and a huge fiscal deficit. Actually, the combined fiscal deficit of the 
States and the Central Government is today higher than what it was in 
1991. Both the Central Government's and the State Governments' 
fiscal deficit are contributing to it. But I am worried about the finance of 
the State Governments. Sir, I will ju st give an example. I do not know 
whether the Finance Minister has seen a recent article by Shri Madhav 
Godbole, an

Government of India, who has been very deeply involved in the 
finances of the State Government of Maharashtra. His article has

The Finance Minister should also plead with the State Governments to

international finance centre. Sir, you all know that Mumbai has 
comparative advantages over any other Indian city. It has well-
developed infrastructure. It is already the business capital of the 
country. It has good hinterland linkages and a good port. It has got a

SHRI YASHWANT SINHA: Sir, I am grateful to all the Members 
who have participated in this discussion and made very important 
contributions to the debate and to the understanding of the economic 
problems of this country.    I would like to briefly touch upon some of the 
287 

RAJYA SABHA               [30 APRIL, 2002] 
points which have been raised -- I find that Jibonbabu is coming back; 
but Shri Prithviraj Chavan is not here. He raised the important point 
about the finances of State Govern ments. And I would like to repeat 
here what I had said in the other Hous e yesterday, that the finances of 
the Government of India -- and this is relevant to the point which 
Jibonbabu also has raised --and the finances -of the State 
Governments have been very severely impacted upon by the famous 
dole-out after the Fifth Pay Commission, by the then Government in 
1997. I just quote one figure because you were talking about the bonus 
of the employees and the fact that this Government is acquiring an 
image of being anti-worker. No Government would like to acquire the 
image of being anti-worker. I would like to say that we are not anti-
worker; we are very much pro-worker. There is a communication gap 
between you and us; and we will, certainly, do our best to bridge that 
communication gap. But, I will draw the attention of the House, through 
you, to the fact and let us look at the domestic savings. As you are 
aware, the domestic savings consist of three elements, household 
savings, public 6ector savings and private sector savings. As far as the 
household savings are concerned, we have the figures up to 2000-
2001, at 20.9 per cent of the GDP, that was the highest achieved so 
far. That was the household saving. The private sector saving was at 
4.2 per cent, which was not bad, compared to the fact that the highest 
that we had achieved was 4.5 per cent  and 4.3 per cent in two years. 
So, at 4.2 per cent, I will not say that  we are doing badly, as far as the 
private sector saving is concerned. Where is it that we are taking a 
beaing, as far as domestic savings, as a whole, are concerned? 
Because the domestic savings has touched, as you are aware, a high 
of over 25 per cent, 25.1 per cent  in 1994-95. After that, there has 
been some deceleration. The latest figure that we have is 23.4 per cent 
in 2000-2001. It is on account of public sector dissaving of 1.7 per 
cent, the highest ever in 2000-2001. The whole public sector consists 
of public authorities which is the Government administration, 
department of commercial enterprises, non-departmental enterprises 
which include the Government companies and statutory corporations. 
Sir, Jibon Royji will be glad  to know that it is not  because of the losses 
of the public sector undertakings t hat the public sector savings have 
gone down and become so much in the red. It is entirely on account of 
the Government administration. The Government administration went 
into the red for the first time in 1986-87. We had a plus of Rs.15 crores 
in 1985-86. That was the last plus. Pranababu will recall because he is 
an old hand at all this. After that, it has been downhill, all the way, 
starting from 1986-87. But, it was not so bad

[30 APRIL, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
until we came to 1997-98 and 1998-99 where the Government 
administration minus the deficit on account of Government 
administration went up from Rs.31,821 crores in 1996-97 to Rs.42,515 
crores in 1997-98 to Rs.88,618 cr ores in 1998-99; and in 2000 it was 
Rs. 106521 crores. This one jump from Rs.31,000 to Rs.88,000 
represents the impact of the Fifth Pay Commission on the Government 
administration. So, if the State financ es are bad, if the Government of 
India finances are bad, if domestic sa ving has contracted, it is entirely 
on account of the amount of money that we are spending on 
ourselves. The means have become the end. We are the means. Why 
are we here for? We are here in order to serve the people of India, but 
we are serving ourselves. We are not serving the people of India. This" 
is a classic case where the means have assumed the dimension of the 
end. We are only interested in ourselves; we are not interested any 
more in the lofty purpose of the State, in the business of the welfare of 
the people. This situation has to be corrected. I entirely agree with Shri 
Prithviraj Chavan when he said that this situation has to be corrected. 
If I am allowed to share a secret, I had a long meeting with the Finance 
Minister of West Bengal this morning. He is the Convenor of the Group 
of State Finance Ministers. He came to represent to me on behalf of 
the State Governments,  and I have agreed with him. I will have a 
meeting with the State Finance Mini sters. We are going to seriously 
discuss this issue of how we can solve this problem, because this 
problem is becoming untenable. This problem is becoming 
unsustainable. Let me tell you with all the responsibility at my 
command that if we go on like this, then, we are surely taking this 
country towards ruination. We have to stop this. We will have to realise 
that we can extend our coat or cut our coat only according to the cloth. 
We can't go beyond that.

Sir, I will plead with Jibanbabu, let us remember our capacity to be

any organisation-whether Government  of India, State Government, 
public sector undertaking or even the private sector undertaking-has to 
take these things into account.

Azad to the Appropriation Bill, and to  the various things that this

for the European economy. The Euro zone is now supposed to be 
doing well. All this has created a new sense of optimism. I was 
looking at our own figures, I found that though we reached a low

we have been moving up,   thanks, largely, of course, to a

better agricultural performance. Jibonji raised a question about the 
demand. He asked, "Where is the demand going to come from?" It is 
a very important question. It is a ve ry relevant question. The demand, 
as far as the Indian economy is concerned, will come from the 70 per 
cent people who live in the rural areas. If their income goes up, if 
agriculture does well, If the rural economy does well, we will have a 
better demand. There is empirical ev idence to suggest that whenever 
agriculture has done well, it has had cascading effect on the services 
sector, on the industrial sector. And, whenever agriculture has done 
badly, we have seen the Indian indu stry also performing badly. Now, 
fortunately, agriculture has done well in the year 2001-2002, and we 
should be able to see the beneficial impact of that in the coming year.

of criticism, especially, if it is constructive criticism. But for God's sake,
